problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The grazing rule defines a finite directed graph whose unique universal target must be a fixed point. Forum proofs combine congruences for iterates of the doubled/reflected position with increasing 2-adic valuation to rule out other cycles and establish convergence. A late post gives the cleanest route: with k/n in lowest terms, each move keeps the odd part of the denominator and halves its power of 2, so an odd divisor other than 3 yields a second invariant set and hence a second cycle.

problems.explanation: T lies on the polar of the external-bisector foot, which yields a harmonic range on BC and makes AU, AV isogonal; tangent-length relations and a homothety centred at the internal-bisector foot then place J on the bisector. An alternative proof uses similar triangles and a cyclic quadrilateral centred at J. With the circumcircle as unit circle, J is redefined as the meeting point of OT with the internal bisector; equal distances to BC and TX reduce, after substituting the external-bisector intersection, to a polynomial identity that vanishes. A late forum proof uses Desargues' involution through X and Y, whose fixed harmonic conjugate shows that triangles ABC and AUV share an Apollonius circle, so the two circumcircles are tangent.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Homotheties at the vertices show that corresponding vertices of the two perpendicular-line triangles are collinear with A, B, C, and the three lines meet at a point of the circumcircle. An angle chase puts that point on both circumcircles, and the homothety centred there makes them tangent. With the circumcircle as unit circle and the two parallel lines written as z + conj(z) = t, the intersection points and the vertices of each perpendicular-line triangle are explicit and linear in t, which gives the homothety centre as minus the product of the vertex variables; that centre is then shown to lie on one of the circles by a direct conjugation identity, so the homothety forces tangency.

problems.explanation: The two triangles share their nine-point circle (a half homothety at H), and the circumcircle, nine-point circle and circle PQR are shown coaxal. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Monge's theorem reduces the incircle to showing that BB' passes through the exsimilicentre of the two incircles. Reim makes B, I, I', B' concyclic, and the exsimilicentre has equal power with respect to that circle and the circumcircle, by Poncelet arguments or Stewart's theorem. A short ratio argument and a DDIT proof also appear. All six vertices are written through the arc midpoints of the two triangles, so both incentres and inradii have closed forms; the tangent-length criterion for the quadrilateral reduces to one relation, which follows by subtracting the two tangency conditions of the given sides to the other incircle and cancelling a non-zero factor.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Coprimality and a uniform size bound confine the recurrence to a finite set. Inverse-power residues modulo d recur by multiplicative periodicity, forcing a return to one and a chain through the target power. Another proof establishes pure periodicity from unique predecessors on the finite orbit and recovers that chain by running backwards.

The answer is ceil(log_a d), with d<a^n<ad because gcd(a,d)=1 excludes d being a positive power of a. Bound: start each addition block below d and divide within a-1 additions, so every term is <ad. Sound return-to-one proofs are supplied by #5’s recurring inverse-power residues and #2/#7/#9’s unique-predecessor argument, after the following explicit corrections. In #2 the block contains a multiple of a, not necessarily d. In #3, choose a term immediately after a positive number of divisions whose residue returns to 1; the literal earliest k>1 with x_k=1 mod d can still lie in the initial addition block and need not be a division step. #4’s complete residue system assertion is false: inverse powers visit only the cyclic subgroup generated by a modulo d, which suffices to return to 1. #5’s isolated +a must be +d; #7’s predecessor k+d must be k-d. Reversibility is asserted on the actual bounded orbit, not as a permutation of every integer below ad; gcd(x_k,d)=1 excludes the boundary x_k=d, and the predecessor is ax_k below d or x_k-d above d. Backward powers up to the first a^n>d therefore occur. #6 reports the power a^k where the requested answer is its exponent; #9’s terminal 2^k should read a^k. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Angle chasing shows AC is tangent to circle APQ and that A, B, R, C and C, Q, R and the intersection point are concyclic, so the intersection of AQ with CD lies on BR; one proof instead reduces to a similarity giving BC² = CR·CP. problems.explanation: Each polygon's area is at most the sum of the triangles it forms with the lattice centre, and each such triangle is at most half the product, hence half the mean of squares, of the two distances; summing gives a bound attained by concentric squares about the centre. problems.explanation: A hypothetical occurrence of every target proportion gives distinct integer hitting times. Monotonic counts of both colors constrain their relative sizes, and choosing maximal earlier times forces one past the allowed range.

Since p is prime, every occurrence of a/p is at a distinct positive multiple of p. Scale these times as k_i, so all k_i<(p^2-1)/4. If k_i<k_j, monotone red and blue counts give j*k_j>=i*k_i and (p-j)*k_j>=(p-i)*k_i. Swap colors to put k_1<k_(p-1). With h=(p-1)/2, if all k_1,...,k_h precede k_(p-1), their maximal time is at least h and forces k_(p-1)>=h*(p-h)=(p^2-1)/4. Otherwise let ell>=1 be maximal with k_1,...,k_ell before k_(p-1). problems.explanation: Interpreting the angle ratios with auxiliary isosceles triangles shows that the two given bisectors are perpendicular bisectors of segments from P to arc midpoints of circle PAB, or equivalently that A, O, P, D are concyclic with O the circumcentre of PAB; hence all three lines pass through that circumcentre. problems.explanation: Reflecting ℓ in the three perpendicular bisectors gives lines concurrent at a point T of Ω by angle chasing; Θ is homothetic to the arc-midpoint triangle with centre T, so its circumcircle is tangent to Ω there. Writing the vertices as squares on the unit circle with the line vertical, the three perpendicular bisectors are linear equations and their pairwise intersections are values of a single affine map of the unit circle at three points, so that map sends the unit circle to the circumcircle of the triangle they form. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Angle chasing shows AH is tangent to circle PQH; power of a point from A then identifies P and Q as projections of the ends of a segment through H parallel to BC, whose midpoint is the circumcentre and lies on the median. Harmonic-bundle/Brocard and ratio-linearity proofs are alternatives. With the circumcircle as unit circle, P and Q are found as intersections of the diameter through A with the chords through B and C and the reflections of H; shifted by H they are scalar multiples of two points whose circumcentre with the origin is known, which gives the circumcentre of HPQ in closed form. problems.explanation: D is the circumcentre of ABC and B, C, D, F are concyclic; angle chasing then shows X lies on that circle, that AMXE, FAXD and MFED are parallelograms and that B, F, E are collinear, so the three lines pass through the centre of an isosceles trapezoid. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: E and F are the touch points of the A-mixtilinear incircle; a sqrt(bc) inversion sends them to excircle touch points, putting A, X and an isogonal-conjugate point on a line, and a cross-ratio comparison on BC then forces XD to pass through the second intersection of AM with Γ. A spiral-similarity plus butterfly-theorem proof is the proposer's route. Since AE = AF = bc/s, the powers of B and C give the equation of circle AEF, so line AX is the radical axis with Γ and X has explicit coordinates; the second intersection of AM with Γ is (−a²:b²+c²:b²+c²), and a determinant shows it is collinear with X and the incircle contact point D.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Rewritten in the excentral triangle, the lines become isogonals in the orthic triangle passing through a known common point on the Euler line (via a cyclic quadrilateral through H and O). For the angle, Poncelet's porism reduces it to an inversion relation between that point and the orthocentre in the nine-point circle. The reflected excentres have explicit coordinates, the three cevians visibly concur, and the isogonal conjugate of their common point is a linear combination of O and I. For part (b) a Poncelet-porism lemma reduces the angle to showing P lies on the radical axis of the circumcircle and circle AIO, whose equation is solved by Cramer's rule (hybrid). A late forum proof notes that the extouch point is the midpoint of I_A I_A', so reflecting the harmonic pencil A(I_A, I_A'; extouch, altitude direction) in AI shows ℓ_A meets OI at the harmonic conjugate of I with respect to O and the exsimilicentre X56, which is the inverse of I in the circumcircle; then PX·PY = PO·PI and d(O,XY) = R/2 give 120°.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The angle condition makes each side a rotation of the opposite side by one common angle; adding the alternate side vectors shows that either the rotation is a half-turn (three parallelograms, so the diagonals share a midpoint) or the alternate sides close up into triangles. In the second case, translating sides builds three parallelograms whose new vertices are equidistant from opposite vertices of the hexagon (SAS after an angle chase), so the three diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of one triangle and meet at its circumcentre. Writing the six side vectors as complex numbers, the equal-length and angle conditions make alternate side vectors rotations of one another by a common unit factor w; either w = -1 (central symmetry) or a+c+e = b+d+f, and then a conjugate-symmetric identity shows the line-intersection formulas for AD with BE and with CF give the same point.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: SAS congruences with the excircle tangent lengths show the arc midpoints are equidistant from pairs of the contact points, so the circumcentre of A1B1C1 is one of them. After synthetic steps in the excentral triangle (arc midpoints are equidistant from pairs of contact points, so one of them is the circumcentre, which forces a side of A1B1C1 to be parallel to an internal bisector), barycentric displacement vectors turn that parallelism into a² = b² + c² (hybrid).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Since O lies inside the angle B'OC' of ω, the inscribed-angle comparison 2A < 90° + A/2 forces angle A < 60°; then OL is at least the distance from O to BC, R cos A > R/2, so ω contains points both inside and outside the circumcircle. A reflection of O in BC gives the same angle bound. The two circles meet as soon as the radius of the tangent circle exceeds R(1 - cos A): the angle bisector theorem and the law of cosines give that radius and an upper bound for R from the tangent length, and the comparison reduces to sin A <= 1. Alternatively, with the circumcentre as origin, the bisector foot is a weighted average of B and C and its squared distance from O is bounded below via cos 2A > -1/2.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Each term is minus the reciprocal of the power of a vertex with respect to the circle through the other three; with P the intersection of two diagonals, power-of-a-point products show that opposite terms pair up to the same expression with opposite signs. Writing each circle as x²+y² plus a linear part, a weighted sum of the four circle equations minus 1 vanishes at all four (non-concyclic) points, so it is identically zero, and its x²+y² coefficient is the required sum. In barycentric coordinates the circle equation directly gives the power, and the sum collapses.

problems.explanation: By symmetry of circle DBC, BE bisects angle ABD, so E is the incentre of ABD and AF is perpendicular to FC with D the centre of circle AFC. Then I is the radical centre of the circles AFC, DBC and ABFE, so CI is a radical axis; this gives DK·DB = DA², so DA is tangent to circle ABK and an angle chase shows AI bisects angle BAK. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Equal tangent lengths from the concentric condition give DC = DE, FE = FA, AB = BC, and congruent triangles give equal base angles. problems.explanation: Since triangles ABF and AEC are similar, AE·AF = AB·AC = AI·AI_a, so triangles AFI_a and AIE are similar; as D is the midpoint of II_a, the line DG is parallel to FI_a and the angle chase puts the intersection of EI and DG on the circumcircle. With the circumcircle as the unit circle and square-root parametrisation of the vertices, the point on the circle with chord parallel to BC gives F as a chord intersection, G as a midpoint, and the second intersection of EI with the circle in closed form; the ratio (G - D)/(K - D) factors and equals its own conjugate, so K, G, D are collinear.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The Miquel point of X, Y, Z sees each side of ABC under 60° plus the opposite angle, so it is fixed; a √(bc) inversion at A turns the claim that I is outside triangle AYZ into the excentre lying inside a circle through A, which reduces to a length inequality CE + BF > a about an equilateral triangle on BC, settled by the law of sines. Assuming I and A on the same side of YZ, a homothety at A puts I on YZ; distances to BC are computed by trigonometry, the collinearity becomes a reciprocal-length identity, and Cauchy–Schwarz with a smoothing/derivative argument reduces everything to an inequality in the angles that holds for acute triangles (hybrid).

problems.explanation: With I the incentre of ABC, angle IDK is 45°, so reflecting E in the bisector CI to a point F on BC gives angle IFK = 45° too; either F = D (the equilateral case, 60°) or I, K, D, F are concyclic, which forces a right angle at K and, by an angle sum in triangle BEC, angle A = 90°. Both values are then checked. Writing IK/KC once by the angle bisector theorem in triangle IDC and once by the ratio lemma in triangle IEC gives a single trigonometric equation in a quarter of angle A, which product-to-sum formulas reduce to sin(90° − θ) = sin 5θ, i.e. A = 60° or 90°.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: At P, the circumcentre and orthocentre lines are isogonal and PH/PO = 2cos P in both triangles, so one spiral similarity at P maps O1, O2 to H1 and a reflection of H1; the two perpendiculars are parallel to PH2 and PH1, and Menelaus in the resulting triangle shows they meet H1H2 at the same point. With P as origin, the nine-point centres are E1 = (A + B + H1)/4 and E2 = (C + D + H2)/4; the two perpendicularity conditions plus the altitude relations H1·C = A·C etc. show the intersection point X satisfies X·(A − B + C − D) = H1·(A − B + C − D) = H2·(A − B + C − D), so X lies on H1H2.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Two of the circles both pass through H and their centres are midpoints of two sides, so their radical axis is the altitude through H and contains the third vertex; equal powers from that vertex make each set of four intersection points concyclic. The three circles obtained must coincide (else their radical axes, the sides, would concur), or directly their common centre is the circumcentre. With the circumcentre as origin, each of the six points is at squared distance OM^2 + MH^2 from O, where M is the midpoint of the corresponding side and H = a + b + c; expanding this in complex numbers on the unit circle (or with dot products) gives an expression symmetric in the three vertices, so all six points lie on one circle centred at O.

problems.explanation: B and D are homothety centres of ω with ω1 and ω2, so by Monge–d'Alembert the diagonal intersection is the internal centre of ω1 and ω2. problems.explanation: The bisector at C makes equal angles with the two perpendicular bisectors, so the circumcentre O is equidistant from P and Q; hence P and Q have equal power with respect to the circumcircle, PR·PC = QR·QC, and with the similar right triangles CPK and CQL this gives PR·PK = QR·QL. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The homothety at C with ratio ½ maps A, F, G to the midpoints of BD, CF, CG, which are therefore collinear; the feet from E to CF and CG lie on that line, so it is the Simson line of E with respect to BCD and E is equidistant from B and D. Similar triangles then show the line is parallel to the bisector of angle DAB. Take the circumcircle of CFG as the unit circle with E at the origin; the homothety at G expresses A, B and the fourth parallelogram vertex through one real scale factor k, the cyclic condition becomes the statement that a quotient is real, and after cross-multiplying the difference factors so that c^2 = fg, i.e. CF = CG, from which the bisector conclusion is an angle equality.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The angle conditions make triangles ABC, ACD, ADE similar, so a spiral similarity at A maps quadrilateral ABCD to ACDE; corresponding diagonal intersections divide the diagonals in equal ratios and Ceva shows AP meets CD at its midpoint. Equivalently, similar triangles ABD and AEC make circles ABCP and AEDP tangent to CD, and equal tangent lengths from the midpoint finish. The three similar triangles at A make the vertices successive powers of one complex number when A is the origin and one vertex is 1; the intersection P of two diagonals then has a short closed form, and the quotient of P by the midpoint of CD simplifies to a real number, so AP passes through that midpoint.

problems.explanation: The condition AC + BC = 3AB makes the tangent length from C equal to AB, which identifies the reflection of C in I as the C-excentre; then A, B, I and this excentre lie on the circle with diameter joining them, and K, L (reflections of the touch points) see that diameter at right angles, so all lie on one circle. problems.explanation: Equal hexagon sides make isosceles triangles at each vertex, and an angle chase shows lines C1A1 and C2A2 (and the analogous pairs) meet at 60°, so a spiral similarity with angle 60° maps triangle A1B1C1 to A2B2C2. Equal hexagon sides make the three triangles at its centre congruent, which puts the centre on each of the three lines. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The spiral similarity centred at the second intersection T of circles APD and BPC maps D to B and A to C, hence (since BE = DF) F to E; then T lies on circles FQD and BEQ, and by Miquel's theorem on the circumcircle of PQR, independent of E and F. Equivalently T is the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of AC and BD. A hybrid route: the law of sines shows that the points cut on the moving segment divide it in fixed ratios, so every triangle formed by the moving segment and the circumcentre is directly similar; writing the endpoints as linear functions of one real parameter in the complex plane, the circumcentre is then also a linear function of that parameter and runs along a fixed line, and the second common point is the reflection of P in it.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: With X, Y the feet of the altitudes from B and C, the equal angles at D and E give similar triangles BDH and CEH, so XE/EC = YD/DB; hence the second intersection Q of the two circles is the Miquel point of both quadrilaterals and lies on the circle with diameter AH. Then angle AQH = 90°, and since H, M and the antipode of A are collinear, HM ⊥ AQ. In barycentric coordinates the collinearity of D, H and E fixes the common length AD = AE, the circle ADE has an explicit equation, subtracting the circumcircle gives the common chord, and the perpendicularity formula shows that the chord is perpendicular to MH. A unit-circle complex computation of the centre of ADE gives the same parallelism of OO1 and MH.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The radical axis PQ passes through the midpoints of the two common-tangent segments on BX and AX, so it is the midline of the trapezoid formed by the two touch chords. By the Iran lemma each touch chord meets the A-midline at a fixed point on a bisector of ABC, so PQ passes through the midpoint of these two fixed points. The difference of powers with respect to the two incircles is a linear function; its values at A, B, C follow from tangent lengths, and in barycentrics the point (2a : a − b − c : a + b + c) makes the weighted sum vanish for every position of X.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: With G = AB ∩ CD, the point H = EF ∩ CD gives a harmonic range (C, D; H, G), so GH·GM = GC·GD = GA·GB and H lies on circle ABM. The condition on N makes ANBM harmonic; projecting from H matches the two harmonic divisions on AB, so HN and HE meet AB at the same point and N lies on EF. Pascal shows E, F and the poles U, V of AB and CD are collinear; with the circumcircle as unit circle, the harmonic condition gives n = (m(a + b) − 2ab)/(2m − (a + b)), and checking that N lies on UV (or that ON is perpendicular to the inverse of G) is a short conjugation computation (hybrid).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The feet from D lie on the Simson line, and the cyclic quadrilaterals on DB and DA make triangles DPR ~ DBC and DQR ~ DBA, so PQ = QR becomes DC/CB = DA/AB; by the angle bisector theorem this says the two bisectors meet AC at the same point. The extended law of sines in the circles on diameters DA and DC gives the same ratio. With the circumcircle as unit circle, the feet have the standard form p = ½(d + b + c − bc/d) etc., and |p − q| = |q − r| reduces to |a − b|·|c − d| = |b − c|·|a − d|, i.e. AB·CD = BC·AD, the bisector condition.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Among the six angles formed by the three main diagonals, one is at least 60°. A circle lemma shows the segment from a side's midpoint to the diagonal intersection is at most √3/2 times the side when the opposite angle is at least 60°, with equality only for an equilateral triangle; the triangle inequality forces equality, and repeating the argument gives all angles 120°. Writing the vertices as vectors, the hypothesis and the triangle inequality give three inequalities |y − z| ≥ √3|x| (cyclically) for suitable side-difference vectors x, y, z; squaring and adding yields −|x + y + z|² ≥ 0, so all inequalities are equalities, opposite sides are parallel, and the angle conditions follow.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: F is the Fermat point, so equilateral triangles ACY and ABX erected outside make F, D, Y and F, E, X collinear with AFCY, AFBX cyclic. An area or Ptolemy comparison gives FD ≤ FY/4 and FE ≤ FX/4, and since angle DFE = 120° the law of cosines yields DE ≤ XY/4 ≤ (AX + AY)/4 = (AB + AC)/4. With the three distances from the Fermat point as variables, the law of cosines gives the sides, the 60-degree bisector property gives FE = ab/(a+b) and FD = ac/(a+c), DE follows from the law of cosines again, and the inequality reduces to an algebraic inequality settled by AM-GM/GM-HM and a sum of squares. A trigonometric variant compares FE with the distance to an equilateral apex.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The answer is the golden ratio, attained by the regular pentagon. A point inside a triangle of the others forces ratio ≥ 3, so the points are in convex position; taking the triangle of maximal area, an affine map and the parallelogram constraint on the remaining two points give 1 + 1/θ ≤ θ for the area ratio θ. After an affine normalisation the largest triangle is fixed with explicit coordinates; if a point lies inside a triangle the ratio is at least 3, otherwise the other two points are confined to regions bounded by lines, the shoelace formula gives the three relevant areas as simple expressions in two parameters, and a short optimisation shows the smallest of them is at most (sqrt 5 - 1)/2.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The line KM passes through the A-excentre (midpoint-of-altitude lemma via the homothety taking the incircle to the excircle). Power of a point gives KN·KT = r·r_A = BK·KC for T the midpoint of K and the excentre, so B, N, C, T are concyclic with T on the perpendicular bisector of BC, and the homothety at N mapping the incircle to circle BNC finishes. A harmonic/Apollonius-circle argument shows NK bisects angle BNC, which gives the same homothety. A hybrid route: by the Archimedes lemma it suffices that N lies on the Apollonius circle on KK'; with the incircle as the unit circle the intouch points give K', the midpoint M and then N as a second chord intersection, and the quotient (k' - n)/(k - n) is shown to be purely imaginary. A tangent-length computation with tan and r r_A = (s-b)(s-c) gives a trigonometric alternative.

problems.explanation: The homothety at A taking the inscribed square on BC to the square erected outward on BC fixes the line through A and the centre, so AA1, BB1, CC1 are the lines to the centres of the outer squares. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The answer is 4. Writing each ratio as an area ratio gives 3 + ([ADE] + [BEF] + [CFD])/[DEF]. The points D, E, F are circumcentres of three triangles that, by Miquel's theorem, share a common point M, and each pair of circles is symmetric in its line of centres, so [ADE] + [BEF] + [CFD] = [DEF]. With circumradius 1, similar-triangle ratios give AD, AE and the angle between them, the law of cosines gives DE, showing DEF is similar to ABC with an explicit ratio; the sine area formula then gives [ADE] + [BEF] + [CFD] = [DEF], and the requested sum of ratios equals 3 plus this area ratio, i.e. 4.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Reflect H in BC to a point on the circumcircle and let D be where O joined to that point meets BC; then OD + DH equals the circumradius, and likewise on the other sides. Angle chasing at the reflected point gives BD/DC = sin B / sin C (by the law of sines), and multiplying the three ratios gives 1, so Ceva yields the concurrency. A hybrid route: reflecting H in the sides puts the reflections on the circumcircle, so the points D, E, F where O joins them meet the sides give the constant sum R; the concurrency is then checked by Ceva, computing each side ratio either from the complex intersection formula on the unit circle or from the law of sines as a ratio cos 2B / cos 2C.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: If the polygon is cyclic with vertices at angles 2θ_j on a circle of radius R, chords are 2R sin(θ_j − θ_i), so b_j = √(2R) sin θ_j and c_j = √(2R) cos θ_j work. Conversely, the assigned pairs make A_iA_j·A_kA_l + A_jA_k·A_iA_l = A_iA_k·A_jA_l for every four vertices in order (an algebraic identity), so Ptolemy's converse shows each four vertices are concyclic. If the polygon is inscribed in a circle of radius R, writing the vertices with half-angles theta_i makes each chord 2R sin(theta_j - theta_i), which expands into the required determinant form with b_j, c_j proportional to sin and cos of theta_j; conversely the algebraic Ptolemy identity for such determinants and the converse of Ptolemy's theorem force every four vertices to be concyclic.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: AP and BR are symmedians, so with L, M the midpoints of BC, CA and X, Y the second intersections of the medians with the circumcircle, triangles ABQ ~ AXM and BAS ~ BYL; the equality of the angles reduces to L, X, Y, M concyclic, which follows from GA·GX = GB·GY at the centroid. Comparing the cotangent formula identifies the triangles where the angle is largest. In barycentrics P = (0 : b² : c²) and R = (a² : 0 : c²), so Q = (b² + c² : b² : c²), S = (a² : a² + c² : c²) and BQ ∩ AS = (b² + c² : a² + c² : c²); the distance formula gives equal distances to A and B. The law of sines version gives cot ∠ABQ = 2cot A + 2cot B + cot C, which also settles the maximum.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The angle conditions make triangles ADX and BCX similar. Placing two points M, N on the perpendicular bisector of AB with triangle AMN similar to ADX, the spiral similarities at A and B give MD = MC, so M lies on both perpendicular bisectors and is Y, whence ∠AYB = 2∠AYN = 2∠ADX. With X at the origin, the opposite similarity of ADX and BCX lets one write A = wD and B = w-bar C for a unit complex number w; the perpendicular-bisector intersection formula gives Y, and the condition on the angle at Y becomes the reality of 1/((1 - w)(1 - w-bar)), which is clear.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Every reflection in a perpendicular bisector fixes the centroid, so all points lie on a sphere about it, and any plane through three or more points cuts out a regular polygon. If the set is not planar, every face of its convex hull is an equilateral triangle (a larger face would give a non-regular plane section), so the hull is a regular deltahedron; the icosahedron fails on an antipodal pair, leaving the tetrahedron and octahedron.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The three circles are orthogonal to the incircle, so inversion in the incircle fixes them; it sends each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side of the intouch triangle, so A′, B′, C′ are those midpoints and their circumcircle is the nine-point circle of the intouch triangle, with radius r/2. A hybrid trigonometric finish: the incentre is the radical centre of the three circles, similar triangles give the sides of A'B'C' in terms of the inradius and the distances from I, and the sine area formula together with the extended law of sines shows that the circumradius of A'B'C' is half the inradius.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: If ABCD is cyclic with perpendicular diagonals, P is the circumcentre and the angles APB and CPD are supplementary, so the two triangles have equal areas by the half-R²-sine formula. Conversely, with M, N the midpoints of AB, CD and T the intersection of the diagonals, TM = AM and TN = DN; equal areas give PM·TM = PN·TN, and an angle chase shows triangles TMN and PNM are congruent, so TMPN is a parallelogram. The perpendicular sides then make triangles TAM and DTN similar, which gives equal angles TAB and TDC, so ABCD is cyclic. Put the perpendicular diagonals on the axes; the perpendicular bisectors of AB and CD meet at an explicit point P, the two triangle areas are computed from the distance to each side, and equality of the areas factors as (ac - bd) times a positive quantity, while ac = bd is exactly the power-of-the-origin condition for ABCD to be cyclic.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let G be the intersection of lines AD and BC. Triangles GAB and GCD are similar (cyclic quadrilateral) with ratio AB : CD, which is also AE : CF, so triangles GEA and GFC are similar too. Hence GE : GF = AB : CD = PE : PF, so GP bisects angle AGB and P is equidistant from AD and BC; the two areas are then in the ratio AD : BC. If AD and BC are parallel the trapezoid is isosceles and the claim is immediate. Because P divides EF in the ratio AB : CD, its distances (or areas) to AD and BC are weighted averages of those of E and F; writing these with the sine area formula and using that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral have equal sines, the ratio of the two areas reduces to AD/BC, independent of E and F.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Since BI is perpendicular to RS, the angle RIS is acute exactly when BI² exceeds BR·BS. An angle chase gives similar triangles BSK and BMR (M the touch point on the side through B), so BR·BS = BM·BK, which is the square of the tangent length from B; this is less than BI², since BI is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with that tangent as a leg. A hybrid trigonometric route: similar triangles at B give the tangents of the two angles that IR and IS make with BI as products of half-angle cosines; their product is cos^2(B/2) < 1, so the two angles sum to less than a right angle and the angle RIS is acute.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: M and N are isogonal conjugates. Let ray AN meet circle BNC again at A1 (and similarly for B1, C1). The equal angles from isogonality make triangles ABM and AA1C similar, so AM·AN/(AB·AC) = AN/AA1; the three such ratios are the cevian ratios of N in the triangles it cuts off, and they sum to 1 by an area argument. Variants place the auxiliary points by spiral similarity or through circles through N. M and N are isogonal conjugates, so each quotient (m - a)(n - a)/((b - a)(c - a)) is a positive real equal to the corresponding product of length ratios; summing the three quotients over a common denominator, the terms in mn and m + n cancel cyclically and the sum is exactly 1.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: OH = 2R exactly when the nine-point centre N lies on the circumcircle. The reflection triangle DEF is the image of the pedal triangle of N under the homothety at the centroid with ratio 4 (checked with two applications of Menelaus, or with vectors), so D, E, F are collinear iff the feet from N are collinear, which by the Simson line theorem means N is on the circumcircle. With the circumcircle as the unit circle, the reflections are b + c − bc/a and its cyclic versions, and the orthocentre is a + b + c. The collinearity condition (a quotient equal to its conjugate) factors to a symmetric polynomial condition, and |a + b + c|² = 4 expands to the same condition.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Build P outside with triangle EDP similar to EFA. The condition that angles B, D, F sum to 360° makes angle CDP equal to angle CBA, and the side-ratio condition makes PD : CD = AB : BC, so triangles CDP and CBA are similar. The spiral similarities at C and at E then express AP in two ways, as BD·AC/BC and as FD·AE/FE, which is the required identity. Alternatively, the circles ABC, CDE, EFA share a point, and inverting there gives the result. Treat the vertices as complex numbers. The angle condition makes the product (a−b)(c−d)(e−f)/((c−b)(e−d)(a−f)) a positive real, and the ratio condition gives it modulus 1, so it equals 1 (up to the sign convention). A cubic polynomial identity in the six affixes turns this into the corresponding identity for the target product, and taking moduli finishes.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Reflect B and C in D, so the segment BC is cut into equal thirds; the angle relation to prove becomes an isosceles condition between a vertex-to-point length and a segment along BC. The angle-doubling condition gives a point T on BC with TA = TB = AC, and a difference-of-squares computation along the altitude foot (a power-type identity) shows the two lengths agree. Put B = −1, D = 0, C = 2 on the real line, so E = −a for A = a. Each angle condition (with the convexity bound that pins the multiple of 180°) is the realness of a cubic in the free variable, and the two cubics are carried into each other by a ↦ −a, so one is real iff the other is. Unit-circle versions use b = a³ with c = 1.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let M be the foot of the altitude from A (the midpoint of AE) and T the intersection of AZ with BC. Projecting the harmonic range formed by A, X, the midpoint Y and the point at infinity of AX from B onto the circle, and then from A onto BC, shows T is the midpoint of DM. Since (D, M; B, C) is harmonic, TD² = TB·TC, which is the power of T and so equals TZ·TA; hence BD is tangent to circle ADZ. A hybrid route: inverting in the circumcircle sends D to the foot F of the perpendicular from A to BD, so it suffices that AZ is perpendicular to FZ; with BC as a diameter on the unit circle, E, F, X, Y and the second intersection Z are explicit and the perpendicularity reduces to a one-line identity.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let BT meet the circumcircle again at X. Reflection in the perpendicular bisector of AB fixes the circle and the point V, so it swaps the chords AU and BX, and BX = AU. An angle chase shows the angles TCX and TXC are both equal to angle A, so TX = TC; the condition that A is the smallest angle places T between B and X, so AU = BX = TB + TC. Writing the two parts of angle A cut by AU as x and y, the angle BTC equals 2A; the sine rule in triangle BTC expresses TB and TC through a, sin 2A and the angles B − x and C − y, and a sum-to-product step turns TB + TC into 2R times the sine of the angle that AU subtends, which is AU.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Three circles through I have collinear centres exactly when they are coaxial, so it suffices to find a second common point. Inverting in the incircle sends the sides to equal circles on diameters from I to the touch points, sends the vertices to the midpoints of the contact triangle's sides, and sends each circle C_i to a common external tangent of two of the equal circles, which is parallel to a side of the contact triangle. The image triangles of the A_i and of the B_i are therefore homothetic, so the lines joining corresponding images concur, which is the required coaxality.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The line QR is parallel to EF, which is antiparallel to BC, so B, R, C, Q are concyclic and DQ·DR = DB·DC. The complete quadrilateral formed by the cevians through the orthocentre makes (P, D; B, C) harmonic, and with M the midpoint of BC this gives DB·DC = DM·DP. Hence DQ·DR = DM·DP, and the converse of the power of a point puts M on circle PQR. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The forward direction is the extended sine law. For the converse, drop perpendiculars from K to the four sides; each side of this pedal quadrilateral is a chord of a circle on a diameter such as KA, so it equals KA sin A, and the condition says the two pairs of opposite pedal sides have equal sums. Splitting each pedal side into two projections turns the condition into a sum of four distance-times-cosine-difference terms, which all have the same sign by comparing angles (a vertex outside or inside the circle through the other three) and the monotonicity of cosine. So every term vanishes and the quadrilateral is cyclic. A hybrid trigonometric route: each term in the condition is a side of the pedal quadrilateral of K (a chord of the circle on AK as diameter), so the condition says that two pairs of opposite pedal sides have equal sums; writing each pedal side as a sum of projections with cosines of the angles at the vertices, the difference becomes a sum of four terms that all have the same sign unless the opposite angle pairs are equal, which forces ABCD to be cyclic.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Since AQBP and APCR are parallelograms, the angle at R equals angle ABC, which equals angle AHC, so A, H, C, R are concyclic (and likewise A, H, B, Q). An angle chase then shows HR is perpendicular to AQ, so X lies on the circle with diameter AH, which also passes through E; one more chase in that circle gives EX parallel to AP. Equivalently, triangle AQR is the translate of PBC and H is its orthocentre. With the circumcentre as origin, H = A + B + C and R = A + C − P, so the dot product of P − B with H − R reduces to |P|² − |B|² = 0; hence HR is perpendicular to BP and so to AQ. The rest is the same short cyclic-quadrilateral chase with the circle on diameter AH (hybrid).

problems.explanation: By the angle bisector theorem the three lines concur exactly when AB : BP = AC : CP. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Reflect H in AB to a point H' on the circumcircle, so F is the midpoint of HH'. Since the line through F perpendicular to OF cuts a chord bisected at F, the butterfly theorem for chords AB and CH' shows F is also the midpoint of the segment from P to the point where that line meets BH'. The two triangles are then congruent by SAS, so HP is parallel to BH' and the required angle equals angle CH'B = angle A. Another route notes that O and H are isogonal conjugates in triangle AFP. Take the circumcircle as the unit circle, so h = a + b + c and F is the foot from c to chord AB. problems.explanation: In each corner triangle the angle is 60°, so the law of cosines gives a squared side of the cevian triangle as x² + y² − xy, which is at least xy for the two segments x, y adjacent to that corner. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Inversion in the circumcircle sends the circle BOC to line BC, so OA' times the distance from O to the point where AO meets BC is R², and similarly for the other two. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Drop perpendiculars from X to every sideline. By Pythagoras, the two pieces of each side cut by the foot are square roots of differences of squares of a vertex distance and a sideline distance, and the perimeter is at most the sum of these pieces. Cauchy–Schwarz on the factorisations (a − b)(a + b) then bounds p² by 4(d − h)(d + h). Write each side by the law of cosines in the triangle XA_iA_{i+1} and each distance to a sideline as twice that triangle's area over the side. Cauchy–Schwarz reduces the inequality to one term per side, which is a polynomial identity in the two distances and the cosine of the angle at X, with a manifestly nonnegative remainder.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: P lies on the radical axis XY of the two diameter circles, so PM·PC = PN·PB and B, C, M, N are concyclic. The right angles at M and N then give an angle chase showing A, M, N, D are concyclic, and AM, DN, XY are the three radical axes of that circle and the two given circles, so they concur at the radical centre. Equivalently, the right angles at M and Z make AMPZ cyclic and power-of-a-point gives the same intersection point on XY from both sides. A Cartesian route: put Z at the origin with the common line of A, B, C, D as the x-axis and the radical axis XY as the y-axis; since AM and DN are perpendicular to PC and PB, both lines are written down directly from their slopes, and they meet the y-axis at the same height exactly when ac = bd, which is the power of Z with respect to the two circles.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Each equality is a difference-of-squares condition, so by Pythagoras X must lie on a fixed line perpendicular to a side: the reflection of the corresponding altitude in the perpendicular bisector of that side. With A', B', C' the antipodes of the vertices, these three lines are the altitudes of triangle A'B'C', so they meet in exactly one point (the reflection of H in O). Equivalently, X is the radical centre of three circles centred at the vertices with radii the opposite sides. Put B and C at (−1, 0) and (1, 0) and A at (a, b) with b ≠ 0. After subtracting the common quadratic part, the two equations become linear in the coordinates of X, and their determinant is a nonzero multiple of b, so there is exactly one solution. A dot-product version with the circumcentre as origin shows the three conditions are the perpendicularities that define the reflected orthocentre.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Since BF = BD = BZ and CE = CD = CY, Menelaus (or the harmonic property of the Gergonne cevians) puts the intersection of EF with BC and the intersection of YZ with BC at the same point T, the harmonic conjugate of D with respect to B and C. Then TE·TF = TD² = TZ·TY by the tangent-secant theorem for the two incircles, so E, F, Z, Y are concyclic. Barycentric coordinates locate the intersection of EF with BC as (0 : s − c : −(s − b)), a point determined only by the touch point D; the same computation in triangle XBC gives the same point for YZ, and the radical-axis converse finishes (hybrid).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: A solid-geometry problem. Each product GA_i·GA'_i is the power of the centroid with respect to the circumsphere, R² − OG², and the Leibniz relation shows this power is a quarter of the sum of the squares GA_i². The first inequality is then AM–GM on the four squares, and the second becomes GA_1 + … ≤ GA'_1 + …, which follows from Chebyshev (or Cauchy–Schwarz twice) using the same identity. With position vectors from the circumcentre, each GA_i² expands to OG² + R² − 2 G·A_i; summing and using that the vertex vectors sum to four times G gives the sum of squares 4(R² − OG²). The rest is AM–GM and Cauchy–Schwarz on the four distances (hybrid).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Consider the circles with diameters AB and CD. F has equal power AF·FB = CF·FD with respect to both, by the circle ABCD. For the orthocentre of EAD, the feet of its altitudes from A and D lie on these two diameter circles and on a common circle through A and D, so its power to both diameter circles is the same; the same holds for the orthocentre of EBC. All three points lie on the radical axis, hence are collinear. A complex-number route on the circumcircle of ABCD as the unit circle: each orthocentre is the intersection of two chord-perpendicular lines, F is the chord intersection of AB and CD, and the quotient (F - H1)/(F - H2) simplifies to an expression that equals its own conjugate, so F, H1, H2 are collinear.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let the two tangents meet at P and drop the perpendicular from P to the diameter line. Similar right triangles (with the centre and the tangency points) give ratios which, together with the equal tangent lengths from P, satisfy Ceva's condition in triangle ABP, so AC, BD and that perpendicular concur; hence its foot is F and P, E, F are collinear. The tangency points, F and the centre lie on the circle with diameter OP, so the two angles at F are inscribed angles over equal chords. A polar/harmonic route reaches the same collinearity. A hybrid Cartesian route: with the circle as the unit circle and the diameter on the x-axis, the tangent points give A and B directly, and solving for the intersections shows that E and the pole Q of the chord CD (the meet of the two tangents) have the same abscissa, so Q lies on EF; a short cyclic-quadrilateral argument with equal tangents then gives the bisection.

problems.explanation: Midpoint relations make the four triangles NBC, NCM, NMD, NDA equal in area. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: OB and OC are perpendicular to the equal sides. If OQ is perpendicular to EF, the right angles make OQEB and OQCF cyclic, and an angle chase gives OE = OF, so Q is the midpoint. Conversely, if QE = QF, Menelaus in triangle AEF with line BC gives BE = CF, so triangles OBE and OCF are congruent, OE = OF and the median OQ is perpendicular to EF. Place B, C at (−1, 0), (1, 0) and A at (0, m), so O = (0, −1/m). With E on line AB and Q = (k, 0), the perpendicularity condition factors as (k + 1)(k − n − 1) = 0 and the midpoint condition factors to the same nondegenerate relation, so the two conditions coincide.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The points O, A, E, B, M lie on the circle with diameter OM, and E, C, D, M on the circle with diameter EM. If AB meets OE at H, then OH·OE = OA² by similar right triangles, so H is fixed. An angle chase shows the foot from E to AB lies on CD (a Simson line), and then the right angle at that foot makes F the midpoint of EH, which is fixed. A complex-number route with the circle as the unit circle and OE along the imaginary axis: the tangent intersection M, the foot E, and the feet C and D come out as explicit rational expressions in the tangency points, and intersecting CD with the imaginary axis shows that F is the midpoint of E and the inverse of E in the circle, which does not depend on M.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The homothety at the tangency point with the circumcircle sends the touch points on CA and CB to the midpoints of the arcs cut off by those sides, so the lines from the tangency point through D and E pass through those arc midpoints. Pascal's theorem on the hexagon formed by the vertices, the arc midpoints and the tangency point then puts I on DE, and since CD = CE with CI the bisector, I is the midpoint. Inversion (centre C or at the incircle) and Casey's theorem give other routes. Let the small circle have radius t and centre P on the bisector of C. The power of P with respect to the circumcircle, computed once from OP and once along the bisector chord through C and the arc midpoint (law of sines for that chord), gives t·cos²(C/2) = 4R·sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2) = r. Then the foot of the bisector on DE is at distance t·cos²(C/2)/sin(C/2) = r/sin(C/2) = CI from C.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The tangency point splits the side into the tangent lengths s − b and s − c of the small triangle, and their reciprocal sum equals the side over the product of the tangent lengths. Heron's formula with the area written as ah/2 and as rs, and r = (s − a)tan(A/2), turn this into 4cot(A/2)/h, where h is the altitude from A. Both triangles share the altitude from A and the angle at A (by the hypothesis), so the two sums agree. Writing the tangent lengths through the inradius and the half-angles at B, at D and at A, each tangent length becomes 2R·sin C·tan(θ) over a sum or difference involving tan(B/2) and tan(θ), where 2θ is the common angle at A. Adding the reciprocals cancels the tan(θ) terms and leaves 1/(R·tanθ·sinA·sinB), which is symmetric in B and C, so the other triangle gives the same value.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Use the Fermat–Torricelli point T. The segments TA, TB, TC make 120° with each other, as do the sides of the equilateral triangle, so each of TA, TB, TC meets the opposite side of DEF at the same angle; splitting ABC into three quadrilaterals with diagonals TA and EF, etc., bounds twice the area by (TA + TB + TC)·DE. The law of cosines with 120° angles and the areas of the three triangles at T give 2(TA + TB + TC)² = a² + b² + c² + 4√3·S; when one angle is at least 120° the same argument works with a signed sum. Equality is attained by the pedal triangle of the isodynamic point.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Write m as twice the area over the longest side. A point inside or on a triangle cannot create a longer side than the triangle's longest side, and a point on a side gives a sub-triangle with no larger m (scaling by a parallel). Then split by position of X: inside the triangle, add the three areas over the common bound; when a vertex lies inside the triangle of X and the other two, or the four points are convex, shrink to sub-triangles through the intersection of the diagonals and reduce to the first case.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: A circle with centre P bisects a circle with centre A exactly when A lies on their radical axis, i.e. r² = PA² + r_A². For two of the circles this forces PB² − PA² to be a constant, so the admissible centres form a fixed line perpendicular to AB. For non-collinear centres two such lines meet in exactly one point; for collinear centres the lines are parallel to each other (no circle) or coincide, and then every admissible circle meets the line of centres at the same two points, found from the power of A and B.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Invert at A. The angle condition becomes a right angle at the image of B in the image triangle, and the length condition becomes equality of the two legs at that vertex, so the image triangle is an isosceles right triangle; the required ratio is its hypotenuse over a leg, √2. The circle through A, C, D becomes the line through the images of C and D, which is a diameter of the image of the other circle, so the circles are orthogonal (equivalently, the angles at A and B subtending CD add up to 90°). A spiral similarity at B produces the same isosceles right triangle without inversion. With complex coordinates, the quotient (b − d)(a − c)/((a − d)(b − c)) has modulus 1 by the length condition and argument 90° by the angle condition (C and D on the same side), so it equals i. The identity (a − b)(c − d) = (a − c)(b − d) − (a − d)(b − c) then gives (a − b)(c − d) = (i − 1)(a − d)(b − c), so the ratio is |i − 1| = √2. Orthogonality is handled by the angle chase (hybrid).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: A quarter-turn about a vertex of the quadrilateral maps each side line of the first quadrilateral to the corresponding side line of the second, and the same quarter-turn is obtained about any point of the bisector of the right angle where those two lines meet. That bisector passes through the vertex and through the apex of the isosceles right triangle erected on the opposite diagonal (a cyclic quadrilateral with two right angles). Because the diagonals are perpendicular, the two squares built on the diagonals have parallel sides, so they are homothetic and the four bisectors concur at the centre of homothety; one quarter-turn about that point maps one quadrilateral onto the other.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Two segments joining opposite centres are perpendicular exactly when the sums of squares of opposite sides of the centre quadrilateral agree. The law of cosines at a vertex (the centres are at distance side/√3 and the angle grows by 60°) expresses each squared side; expanding the cosine and using the law of cosines for a diagonal and the area of the quadrilateral, one opposite pair sums to a symmetric expression plus BD²/3 and the other to the same expression plus AC²/3. Each centre is (a − εb)/(1 − ε) with ε a primitive cube root of unity. Writing x = a − c and y = b − d, the quotient of the two connecting vectors is pure imaginary exactly when x·x̄ = y·ȳ after conjugating and clearing denominators, i.e. when AC = BD.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: A homothety at P sending the incircle to the excircle opposite P maps the point of the incircle diametrically opposite the tangency point T to the excircle's tangency point on L, which is the reflection of T in the midpoint of QR. So P lies on the line joining the antipode of T to the reflection of T in M. Conversely, from any point of that line beyond the antipode the tangents meet L in Q, R with midpoint M, while points on the other side cannot produce a triangle with the circle as incircle, so the locus is the open ray.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Each small circle touches the chord BC and the big circle, so the line through its two tangency points passes through the midpoint Q of the arc BC opposite A (homothety at the contact point). An angle chase makes the four tangency points concyclic, so Q has equal power with respect to the two small circles and lies on their common tangent AI; hence AQ bisects angle A. Similar triangles give QB² equal to that power, which is QI², so QB = QI and the incentre–excentre lemma identifies I as the incentre.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: By the Erdős–Mordell inequality the distances from P to the vertices sum to at least twice the distances to the sides, so for some vertex the distance to the vertex is at least twice the distance to the adjacent side; the corresponding angle then has sine at most 1/2, and the case of an angle of at least 150° makes another of the three angles small. Alternatively, the law of cosines in the three sub-triangles and the area split give a² + b² + c² < 4√3·[ABC], contradicting Weitzenböck's inequality. If all three angles exceeded 30°, trigonometric Ceva would make the product of the sines of the other three angles at the vertices exceed 1/8, so the product of all six sines exceeds 1/64. The six angles sum to 180°, and concavity of log sin (Jensen) bounds that product by sin⁶30° = 1/64, a contradiction.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The angle bisector theorem applied twice (in the whole triangle and in a sub-triangle) gives AI/AA′ = (b+c)/(a+b+c), so the ratio equals (a+b)(b+c)(c+a)/(a+b+c)³. The upper bound is AM–GM on the three sums, and the strict lower bound follows from the Ravi substitution, where the product exceeds twice the cube of the semiperimeter. In areal (barycentric) coordinates with I = (p, q, r), AI/AA′ equals 1 − p = q + r, so the ratio is (p+q)(q+r)(r+p); AM–GM gives the upper bound for any interior point, and substituting the incenter (a : b : c) reduces the lower bound to the same algebraic inequality.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: A solid-geometry problem. The three sum conditions are linear in the edge lengths and force each pair of opposite edges to be equal. Then the segments joining midpoints of opposite edges are common perpendicular bisectors meeting at their common midpoint, which is equidistant from the vertices and so is O; the midpoint quadrilaterals are rhombi (their sides are halves of equal opposite edges), and the required angles are the right angles between rhombus diagonals.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: A solid-geometry problem. The part containing the apex is a cone over the elliptical section, so its volume is one third of the ellipse area times the apex-to-plane distance. In the axial cross-section the major axis is a side of a triangle with the apex, and the Dandelin spheres appear as the incircle and excircle of that triangle, so the focal distance (and hence the minor axis) comes from tangent lengths; the ratio is 1/(3√3). Coordinates in the axial plane give the far end of the major axis and the foot of the perpendicular from the apex as intersections of explicit lines, yielding the major axis and the apex-to-plane distance; combined with the Dandelin-sphere step for the minor axis this gives the volume ratio.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Alternate angles make the triangles cut off by the parallel line isosceles, so CG = CB and CE = CA, and the parallel gives GF/FB = CB/AB and DE/DA = CA/AB. If CB > CA then the bisector segment BG exceeds AE, so FB > DA, and multiplying the two strict inequalities forces GF > DE, a contradiction; by symmetry CA = CB. The law of sines in the two small triangles at C, with the angle-bisector lengths CF and CD, turns GF = DE into (a+c)b/((b+c)a) = sin(A/2)/sin(B/2); assuming a ≥ b the right side is at least 1, which forces b ≥ a.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The diagonals must meet at the A-Dumpty point. Take the spiral similarity at that point sending CA to AB; applied to a pair of opposite vertices and their midpoint it produces cyclic quadrilaterals and a directly similar triangle, which shows that a midpoint other than the Dumpty point determines the whole diagonal line. Two diagonals sharing such a midpoint would coincide, so the common midpoint is the Dumpty point, which lies on circle BOC. With the parallelogram centre as origin, the two angle conditions say two quotients are real; subtracting them shows that unless bc equals a squared the vertex X has a fixed argument, and the same for Y, which would make the parallelogram degenerate. So bc = a^2, i.e. the centre is the Dumpty point.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Split the points into two classes: a minimum-area triangle with vertices in both classes is nice for both of its sides that cross the split, since any third point keeps such a side crossing. problems.explanation: Composing the tangency homotheties (Monge–d'Alembert) shows the fourth circle is also tangent to the first, and parallel radii from these homotheties make the four centres a parallelogram. Double counting extra edges that jump over each vertex gives a vertex jumped by about k²/(2n) of them, while every pair of such edges forms a different cycle and there are at most n cycles; hence k = O(n^(3/4)).

If 2019 is the only root, f(x + f(x)) = 0 gives f(x) = 2019−x; another root yields f(x) = f(kx) with k ≠ 1, which makes f periodic unless f vanishes away from 0, and a nonzero period then forces f to be constant. The leftover family is f = 0 off zero with arbitrary f(0).

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Q(x) = x^d with p ≡ 1 (mod d) takes only 1+(p−1)/d values, which rules out c < d. For c ≥ d view Q as a functional digraph on residues: all residues outside the image plus one point on each isolated cycle suffice, and since values have at most d preimages and Q(x) = x has at most d roots, this is at most (d−1)p/d + 1 ≤ (2c−1)p/(2c+1).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Invert in the fixed circle Gamma: the vertices become midpoints of the sides of the triangle formed by the fixed contact point and the two moving contact points, so the circumcircle becomes a nine-point circle of a triangle inscribed in Gamma. Its radius is fixed, and the centroid homothety along the Euler line moves its centre on a fixed circle, so it is tangent to two fixed concentric circles; invert back. With Gamma the unit circle and the fixed tangent as a vertical line, the circumcircle has an explicit equation in terms of the moving point; the substitution t -> 1/t turns it into a circle of radius 1/2 whose centre is an affine image of 1/x, so as the point runs over a circle the image circles stay tangent to two fixed circles.

problems.explanation: The answer is 2n−2, attained by all (n−1)-subsets with n−2 singletons. For the bound induct on n, merging elements that no set separates; otherwise the sets avoiding the least frequent element cover the rest and are not tight, so some element lies in exactly one of them, and deleting that set and at most one other makes two elements inseparable, so merging finishes.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Treat each parabola as a conic tangent to the line at infinity at the vertical direction; Pascal (or a harmonic projection) shows the two tangent intersections lie on the vertical line through the midpoint of the common chord. If that line were not perpendicular to the chord, comparing the two pairs of opposite tangent lengths contradicts Pitot's condition, so it is the common axis. Direct coordinates: the tangents at two points of a parabola with vertical axis meet above the midpoint of the chord, so both tangent intersections share that x-coordinate; tangent-length equality from the incircle plus the law of cosines then forces the chord to be horizontal.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The locus is the part of the A-angle bisector inside the triangle. An inversion at A with power AB·AC composed with the bisector reflection swaps the two circles, so their centres are isogonal; similar right triangles give the ratio of radii, and the angle-bisector theorem puts the insimilicentre on the bisector, with continuity covering the whole segment. A trigonometric computation on the medial triangle expresses both radii and the distances to the bisector through the angles of the configuration; the required ratio identity is then verified directly.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: λ is completely multiplicative and +1 on squares. For two +1s, look around 2^(2^n): if λ(2^(2^n)+1) is eventually −1, then whenever λ(2^(2^n)−1) = −1 the product formula makes λ(2^(2^(n+1))−1) = +1, so a pair appears at step n or n+1. For two −1s, the Pell-type equation 3s² − 2r² = 1 has infinitely many solutions, and 2r², 3s² are consecutive with λ = −1.

problems.explanation: For (i), the Chinese remainder theorem places |P| consecutive numbers each divisible by a different prime, and when min(P) ≤ |P| one prime can serve twice to give one more; when min(P) > |P| pigeonhole forbids |P|+1 covered consecutive numbers. For (ii), inclusion–exclusion over the run with rounding errors of 1 gives N·∏(1−1/p) ≤ 2^|P| − 1, and the product over distinct primes is at least 1/(|P|+1).

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: C_n = (n−1)/(2n). A weighted combination of the values at all-ones, all-zeros and the n points with a single zero, of total weight 2n, telescopes to n−1, so one of them has absolute value at least (n−1)/(2n). Conversely f_i(x) = x^n/n − (n−1)/(2n²) works: Σx_i^n/n − ∏x_i lies in [0, (n−1)/n] by AM–GM and by convexity in each variable, which pushes extremes to the vertices.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Assume one concurrence. Monge–d'Alembert applied to an auxiliary circle tangent to two of the four circles identifies it and shows it is also tangent at the given point; a tangent-length chase then shows the other two points are midpoints of common tangents, hence on the radical axis of the remaining pair, and the radical axis theorem gives the second concurrence. By the law of sines (area ratios), each collinearity is equivalent to a product of ratios equalling 1; right-triangle similarities express the ratios through the radii, and the two products turn out identical.

problems.explanation: p-adic valuations show only finitely many primes, with bounded exponents, can occur in denominators that do not blow up under iteration, so periodic points and all iterated preimages of a fixed value have denominators dividing a fixed integer; as |f(x)| > |x| for large |x| these sets are bounded, hence finite. A value in every image then has a preimage reaching it twice, so it is periodic, and there are finitely many periodic points.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: k points give C(k,2) distinct squared distances. For the first bound, sort the absolute coordinate differences: vectors equal up to permutation have equal length, and counting sorted vectors in [0, n−1]³ bounds C(k,2) by about n³/6. For the second, the sum of all squared distances is at least 1+2+…+C(k,2) yet at most 3·k²(n−1)²/4 coordinate by coordinate, giving k < n√6.

problems.explanation: Composing with f reduces the task to writing the identity as u + v with u, v bijections. Build u and v as odd functions step by step: each new odd argument of u is sent to minus the smallest positive integer not yet attained, each new even argument of v likewise, and the partner function takes the complementary value; this back-and-forth choice hits every integer and stays injective.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Colour each monomial by the set of variables it actually contains. Every 0/1 substitution kills f, because the product contains the factor x1+…+xn−|S|; so for each set S the colour sums over the nonempty subsets of S add to zero, and induction on |S| (Möbius inversion, or: a multilinear polynomial vanishing on the cube is zero) makes each colour sum vanish. Every colour is used because the top-degree part (x1+…+xn)^(n+1) contains monomials of every support. The vanishing of the support-coloured coefficient sums is a polynomial method: a multilinear polynomial vanishing on {0,1}^n is zero.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: A term is −1 exactly when the short interval ((a−1)k/p, ak/p) contains an integer; call such k bad. Bad indices are closed under addition. After absorbing bad indices into b one may assume b+1 is good or b = p−1, and then each pair {k, b+1−k} contains a good index, so good terms are at least half. Alternatively, the bad k up to c are lattice points of a thin triangle, bounded by Pick's theorem. Additive structure: bad indices form a sum-closed set, so pairs k, b+1-k cannot both be bad when b+1 is good.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Assume every area-1 rectangle has a point inside. By induction on n, for every ε > 0 some region of area below ε (an ellipse, or a triangle) contains n points: an area-preserving affine map makes the current small region round, an area-1 rectangle placed just beside it must contain a new point, and a slightly larger region of still tiny area covers both. A rectangle of comparable area around a region with 2026 points has area below 1, and enlarging it to area 1 gives more than 2025 points. The induction is driven by area bounds, and the covering-rectangle lemma uses the longest chord of the polygon.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The answer is α = 3/2: a k×k block of red points has about k³ total label, so α ≥ 3/2. For the bound, a label is at most the number of red points in its row and at most the number in its column. In a row with r red points the labels therefore sum to at most min(r², n) ≤ r√n, and summing over rows gives n^(3/2). Equivalently, bound each label by the geometric mean of its row and column counts and apply Cauchy–Schwarz. Equivalently, a degree-sum bound in the bipartite row/column graph: each label is at most min of the two degrees.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The common tangents meet BC at X and Y with M the midpoint of XY (angle chase through the midpoints of the tangent segments, or Desargues' involution), so the centre Z of ω is the arc midpoint of XY on the bisector of angle XTY at the exsimilicentre T. The line TZ is the line of centres, i.e. the perpendicular bisector of AM. An inversion at T swapping the two circles gives angle ZTA, which matches the angle at the arc midpoint W of BC, so A, Z, W, T are concyclic; the radical axis theorem for this circle, ω and Γ finishes. With T at the origin and the tangents y = ±kx, put X = (a, ka), Y = (b, −kb). Equal tangent lengths from points of BC force M to be the midpoint of XY; then the circumcentre, the arc midpoint, the point on the bisector and on the perpendicular bisector of AM, and the circle ω all get explicit coordinates, and the two powers of that point come out equal. Forum routes add power of a point, spiral similarity and Brokard (poles and polars) for the M-midpoint claim and the bisector claim.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Modulo a prime p, a³+b³+abc ≡ 0 has only p²−p+1 solutions (one c for each pair with ab ≢ 0, plus a ≡ b ≡ 0), a proportion below 1. Take many primes not dividing the common difference with the product of these proportions tiny. By the CRT, triples up to PN whose value is divisible by P = p1⋯pk are rare, while the progression contains a fixed proportion of multiples of P; since a ≥ b ≥ c keeps a, b, c below the cube root of the value, counting gives a contradiction. The contradiction is a density argument for the arithmetic progression, made possible by choosing many primes with a divergent product.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The answer is 171 = 83 + 89 − 1. Ana's integers must cover every residue class modulo all but at most one candidate prime, or two indicator functions fool her. For the two largest remaining primes p and q, join two chosen integers when they agree modulo p or modulo q; replacing each clique by a path shows the graph has at most n − 2 edges when n ≤ p + q − 2, so it is disconnected, and colouring its components gives functions of two different periods with the same values. Conversely, 171 consecutive multiples of 97 work, since the graph on 171 indices joining differences 83 and 89 is a tree. Bound and construction are a winning strategy plus an adversary argument; the table view (rows mod q, columns mod p) is a grid connectivity argument.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Let r, s, t be the roots of λ³ − a1λ² + b1λ − 1, so rst = 1. By Vieta and induction, a_n and b_n are the power sums of r, s, t and of their reciprocals with exponent 2^(n−1): squaring a power sum and subtracting twice the pairwise products, which are reciprocals because rst = 1, doubles the exponent. Since a1 > b1 the cubic is negative at 1, so it has a real root r > 1. If all roots are real the root of largest modulus dominates; if two are complex conjugates they have modulus below 1, so a_n stays within 2 of a fast-growing power of r. Either way a_n is eventually increasing. An elementary route (two cases with explicit inequality bounds) avoids the cubic substitution.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: P and Q are isogonal conjugates in the polygon. The reflections of P in the sides form a polygon whose vertices are equidistant from Q (the line from each vertex to Q is the perpendicular bisector of two consecutive reflections), so it is cyclic. Each circumcentre step preserves the angles that P makes with consecutive vertices, so after n steps the polygon is spirally similar about P to the reflected one, proving (a). The rotation angles of the spiral similarities at P and Q are opposite and their law-of-sines scale factors coincide because the angle condition swaps the sines, so P, Q, O_Q, O_P form an isosceles trapezoid, proving (b). Forum routes add directed angle chasing, homotheties to pedal polygons and an inversion-plus-spiral-similarity map.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Since AY = AZ and reflection in a side through A preserves distances from A, the points Y, Z, Y′, Z′ lie on a circle centred at A, so the circumcentre S of X′Y′Z′ has AS ⊥ Y′Z′, and similarly BS ⊥ Z′X′, CS ⊥ X′Y′. Writing the direction of Y′Z′ through the reflections of the common line in CA and AB and subtracting the analogous expression for Z′X′ gives ∠ASB = ∠ACB, so S lies on the circumcircle. (The author's solution instead identifies S through the anticomplementary triangle and a Steiner line.) With the circumcircle as unit circle and the line given by Re(z/δ) = λ, the projection of A onto the line is the midpoint of YZ, so X, Y, Z come from the three projections. Reflecting X in BC gives X′, and adding abc/δ² to it gives an expression symmetric in a, b, c, so X′, Y′, Z′ are equidistant from −abc/δ², a point of the unit circle. Further synthetic routes: radical axis concurrence, and the anticomplementary-triangle nine-point-circle configuration.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Let π send each pad to the destination of its jump; it has exactly two cycles. The jumps cover 2025ℓ positions in total, so the average jump is ℓ ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}, and ℓ = 2 or 5 makes π a single translation with one or five cycles. For ℓ = 3 or 4, subtract ℓ from every jump: the cycles of the shifted permutation have zero net displacement, which forces short cycles of a few explicit types on consecutive pads. Following three or four auxiliary frogs through these blocks shows how they are permuted; only ℓ = 4 with the frogs' paths pairing up gives exactly two cycles, and then each frog makes two laps. The decisive step is an invariant: the auxiliary frogs are only ever permuted evenly.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Work with polynomials first: by the Chinese remainder theorem in Q[x], each choice of signs gives a polynomial f of degree at most 23 with f ≡ ±cx modulo c²x² + 1 for c = 1, …, 12, so every f² + 1 is divisible by the degree-24 product of these quadratics. Clearing denominators and evaluating at large multiples of a fixed integer gives 2025 integers whose squares plus one share a factor of size about x^24, while the integers themselves are only about x^23, so any ε below 1/23 works. A purely integer construction with primes ≡ 1 (mod 4), Hensel lifting and the CRT also works. An integer route uses square roots of -1 modulo p^2 for primes p = 1 mod 4.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: The answer is C = 3/2: one a_i just below 2 and many equal large a_i force the reciprocal sum to be either at most 1 or close to 3/2. For the bound, start with every b_i equal to the ceiling (sum below 1) and switch them to floors one at a time; the sum rises monotonically to above 1, and each switch adds 1/(m(m+1)) ≤ 1/2, so the first time it exceeds 1 it is still below 3/2. Alternatively, if some a_i < 2 use b_i = 1 and ceilings elsewhere, and otherwise floors lose at most a factor 3/2. The bounds are floor estimates, and one forum proof picks the rounding with the largest sum not exceeding 1.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: An angle chase reduces the claim to BP = BQ, i.e. to the line PQ making a fixed angle with AP. problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Encode the subset sums in the generating function P(x) = Σ x^(sum of S) over k-subsets. Since p divides C(n, k), Legendre's formula (or Lucas) gives a power p^r with n mod p^r < k mod p^r, and then the cyclotomic polynomial Φ_{p^r} divides P: either from the q-binomial product formula, or by substituting a primitive p^r-th root of unity into Π(1 + x^i y) and seeing that the y^k coefficient vanishes. Divisibility by Φ_{p^r} means the counts of sums in residues j, j + p^(r−1), … modulo p^r are equal, so grouping residues by their block gives p equal classes.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The answer is 11, from 1, 2, …, 2024 and the powers of 2. In an arithmetic progression of 2024 terms (after removing a common factor), ν_p of the terms takes at most ⌊log_p 2023⌋ + 2 values, because only one term can have valuation above that of every index difference. Common terms with a geometric sequence have pairwise different ν_p for any prime p dividing the ratio, so an odd prime gives at most 8. If the ratio is a power of 2 the bound is 12, and the twelfth term is excluded because the progression, containing the odd term b and 2b, cannot reach 2^11·b. A forum proof uses that the common difference divides all differences of common terms and bounds a powers-minus-powers quotient.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: The solutions are the constants and f(x) = x + 1. The engine is that a nonconstant solution has no nonzero period: substituting y + d for y shows f(dx) = f(0). Comparing two substitutions gives the symmetry f(f(x) + y) = f(f(y) + x), and iterating it shows any defect in f(f(x) + y) = f(x) + f(y) would be a period. Then f(0) = 1 and f(x + 1) = f(x) + 1, which upgrade to f(x + y) + 1 = f(x) + f(y), and one more application of the no-period principle forces f(x) = x + 1. Forum finishes solve the resulting substitution system for a zero of f.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: With 2n points the maximum is 2n² − 2n + 2, reached by alternating hops of lengths n and n − 1 with one adjustment. For the bound, draw the n diameters through the midpoints between adjacent points: a hop's length is the number of diameters it crosses, every diameter is crossed an even number of times because the tour is closed, and at most one diameter can be crossed by every hop (two such diameters would leave whole arcs unvisited). Summing crossings gives the bound. Alternatively, pair consecutive hops and compare with the tour through the odd-indexed points. A forum proof reduces from 2n to 2n-2 points by deleting a diametral pair.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Invert in the circle on diameter BC: the circles BME and CMF become the lines BE and CF, the common tangents become the two circles through M tangent to both lines, and K goes to their second intersection, which is the reflection of M in the bisector of angle BHC, so HK* is a symmedian of BHC. K on the circumcircle means K* lies on circle BHC, making (H, K*; B, C) harmonic, so BC bisects angle HMK and K is the reflection of H in BC, i.e. AK ⟂ BC. Other official proofs use the Miquel point Q of BCEF and show QBKC is harmonic. With the circumcircle as unit circle, compute the Miquel point Q, the centres O1, O2 of circles BME and CMF and the point T = −bc/a on the altitude. Q, M and T all have the same distance ratio to O1 and O2, equal to the ratio of the radii, which is also K's ratio since K is the exsimilicentre; so Q, M, T, K lie on one Apollonian circle, and K on the circumcircle forces K = T. Further synthetic routes use the coaxiality lemma, a homothety lemma, external-bisector ratios or power of a point; a barycentric computation is also complete.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Writing 300 = s(s+1)/2 with s = 24 and k = 20, the answer is ks(ks+1)/2 = 115440, from f(n) = max(s − n, 0) and g(n) = max(ks − n, 0). For the bound take g as large as allowed; then the complement of g's Young diagram is the k-fold sumset of the complement of f's, a description symmetric under reflecting the diagrams in the diagonal, so f and g may be replaced by their conjugate partitions. Three estimates follow — Hermite's identity bounding g by f at floors of n/k, the same for the conjugates, and a direct count using where f vanishes — and in every case one of them gives the bound. The first bound spreads n into k nearly equal parts (Hermite identity, floors and ceilings).
