problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The map x ↦ x ⊕ ax is injective exactly for even a. If 2^k exactly divides a, the last k bits of x ⊕ ax are those of x, which determine k more bits of ax and hence the next k bits of x, and so on up the binary expansion. If a is odd, take x = 2^n − 1 and y = 2^n + 1 with 2^n > a: both x ⊕ ax and y ⊕ ay equal the n-bit string of a − 1 written twice. Forum proofs compare 2-adic valuations of x - y and x xor y; the odd case is an explicit collision.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: If gcd(m, n) = d > 1, labellings with all 1×d sums zero are valid, so every row needs a question and no finite number suffices. If gcd(m, n) = 1 the answer is (m−1)² + (n−1)²: labellings with zero m-sums along rows and columns form a space of dimension (m−1)², similarly for n, and they meet only in zero, giving the lower bound. For the upper bound, valid labellings are mn-periodic (Chicken McNugget), so they are polynomials modulo x^mn − 1 and y^mn − 1, and evaluating at pairs of mn-th roots of unity shows at most (m−1)² + (n−1)² evaluations can be nonzero, bounding the dimension. Coprimality drives the periodicity (Bézout/Chicken McNugget) and the Euclid-style recovery lemma.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Suppose |Δ| ≤ N. Then f is injective, so its arrow graph n → f(n) is a union of chains and cycles. Boundedness rules out cycles (iterates would collide), allows at most 2N + 1 chains, and then shows there is a single half-infinite chain, so every integer is f^k(c) for a starting point c. In the index g(k) = f^k(c) the condition says g(x) − x is injective and |g(g(b+1)+a) − g(g(a+1)+b)| ≤ N; since g is a bijection, g(x) − x is unbounded below, and choosing B with g(B) far below B forces infinitely many values of B − g(B) into a bounded window, a contradiction. The chain structure is pinned down by counting values in windows, and the finish takes a maximal preimage.

problems.explanation: Exactly the composite s work. If s = (w + x)(y + z), the products a = wy, b = wz, c = xy, d = xz make the symmetric sum equal to wxyz·s. Composite s come from an explicit factorised choice, and the prime case is a mod-p manipulation with inverses.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The fixed point is K = AF ∩ BE, where AE and BF are the chords of Γ parallel to the two given lines. For X = AC ∩ BD, the powers of any point with respect to circles XAB, XCD, XAD, XBC satisfy pow(XAB) + pow(XCD) = pow(XAD) + pow(XBC), because the difference is linear and vanishes at A, B, C, D. By Reim's theorem circles XAD and XBC pass through fixed points on AF and BE, so K's power with respect to each of them is a fixed product, and so is its power to Γ; hence its power to circle XCD is fixed. The authors instead show K lies on every radical axis using Reim and Pascal. Using that the difference of powers with respect to circle XCD and Γ is a linear function of the point, evaluate it at D and at L = AX ∩ DK and interpolate to K; the law of sines turns the result into (AK·β + BK·α)/sin∠AXB, where α and β are the fixed distances from the two given lines to the parallel chords, and ∠AXB is fixed on the arc. Official and forum routes add a common radical axis, a cross-ratio finish and a barycentric computation.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: The solutions are the concave quadratics ay² + by + c with a ≤ 0. The condition says the slope of each chord is a supergradient (a tangent-line bound) at the chord's midpoint; this makes f concave and hence continuous. Comparing the inequality at nearby symmetric points shows the one-sided slopes at any point converge, so the supergradient is unique; two chords with the same midpoint then have equal slopes, giving the third-difference identity f(x+3d) − 3f(x+2d) + 3f(x+d) − f(x) = 0. So f is quadratic on each lattice (1/n)Z, the quadratics agree, and continuity finishes. The finish identifies f with an interpolating quadratic, via a third-difference recurrence on arithmetic progressions.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: The possible values are exactly 0 ≤ r ≤ 1/2. Induction with strict decrease and integrality gives b_n ≤ n(n+1)/2, so the ratios b_n/n² stay at most 1/2 + 1/(2n) and r ≤ 1/2; r = 0 and r = 1/2 come from b_n = 1 and b_n = n(n+1)/2. For 0 < r < 1/2, start with the triangular numbers and switch to b_n = ⌈rn² + n⌉ from some point on: the extra +n keeps the ratios strictly decreasing despite the ceiling, and they tend to r. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Invert at T swapping the two circles; it sends A, B, C, D to points E, F, V, W. T and Y both lie on the radical axis of circles ADE and BCF (equal tangent-style products from T, and YA·YD = YB·YC). X also has equal power: X lies on lines VE and FW by radical axes with the two given circles, making it the centre of a negative inversion between circles ADE and BCF, which are congruent (equal chords AE = BF and supplementary inscribed angles). So T, X, Y lie on one radical axis. A projective route chases cross-ratios through the inversion at T. Similar triangles YAC and YBD give d(Y, AC)/d(Y, BD) = AC/BD. For T, the distances to AC and BD are TA·sin and TB·sin of the angles these chords make with the tangents, and since TA/TB = r1/r2 and a chord equals the diameter times the sine of its tangent–chord angle, the ratio is also AC/BD. Both T and Y lie inside the same angle at X, so they are on one line through X. Forum proofs add Brokard polars after a homothety, a Desargues–Pascal route, and barycentric and complex computations.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Hephaestus wins exactly for α > 2. With α > 2 he first walls off one side of the (diamond-shaped) flood, keeps lengthening that wall while the water spreads sideways, then closes two side walls at once and finally the far side, the slack α − 2 paying for each sudden addition. For α = 2, follow a shortest flooding path c0, …, cn of cells; it is an induced path, so its boundary has 2n + 4 edges, and shining a ray from each cell toward each boundary edge hits distinct walls of the closed levee, so at least 2n + 4 walls are needed after n + 1 turns. The winning side follows an explicit staged wall-building strategy.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Triangles of G survive in G', and a vertex of degree at least 3 with two non-adjacent neighbours creates a new triangle, so if G is isomorphic to G'' no such vertex exists and every component is a clique, a cycle or a path. Isolated vertices, odd cycles and cliques of size at least 3 are fixed by the operation, while even cycles and paths split into more components, which can never merge back; so G consists only of fixed components and G ≅ G'. Forum proofs look at a maximum clique, and every proof ends by classifying the stable components.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Such P exists exactly when some prime p divides n while a smaller prime does not (rad n is not a primorial). The first time an iterate of 0 vanishes modulo n is the lcm of the same quantity modulo each prime power, by the CRT. Modulo p^e it has only prime factors at most p: by induction, after reaching 0 modulo p^(e−1), the further iterates stay among the p multiples of p^(e−1). For the construction, an interpolation polynomial over Z/p^e cycles 0 → 1 → … → k−1 → 0 for any k < p, and P ≡ x elsewhere glues these by the CRT. The answer is governed by the period of the iteration modulo each prime power.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let K_i be the foot from P to P_{i−1}P_{i+1}; equal products PP_i·PK_i show by inversion at P that the K_i are concyclic. Reflecting P in the centre of that circle gives a point E with matching perpendicular feet E_i. Using the orthocentres H_i of triangles P P_i P_{i+1}, Reim's theorem and an isogonality, E, Q_i and E_i are collinear, and the triangles EQ_iQ_{i+1} and PK_iK_{i+1} have parallel sides; so the Q-polygon is homothetic to the concyclic K-polygon. A generalisation uses P and the circumcentre as isogonal conjugates and a power-ratio circle. With the circumcircle as unit circle, the perpendicularity conditions say the dot products PP_j·PP_{j+1} equal a constant k. Neighbours of a vertex c are then the roots of an explicit quadratic, so by Vieta each Q_i comes out as ((c − p) + f(p + c))/(c·p̄ − 1) with f depending only on p and k. As c runs over the unit circle this is a Möbius image of a circle, so all Q_i lie on one fixed circle. Official and forum routes add Reim angle chases, powers and power ratios, a coaxal-circle locus and similar triangles.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Take Y as the second tangency point from X to the circle AMN. Because MX is the M-symmedian of triangle AMY and the midline from M to the midpoint of AY is parallel to BY, XM is tangent to circle BMY, so ω_B passes through Y; likewise ω_C passes through Y. Since AMYN is cyclic, Miquel's theorem in triangle ABC puts the second intersection of ω_B and ω_C on BC. Other complete routes: two similar-triangle chains through the point where ω_B meets BC, the isogonal conjugate of X in AMN reflected in MN, and a moving-points argument in which X ↦ D is a projective map checked at three positions of X. Put the circumcircle as the unit circle and X on the tangent at A. Solving the tangency and incidence conditions gives the centre of ω_B as an explicit rational expression in a, b and x, and the second intersection of ω_B with BC comes out as ((a + b)(a + c) − 2(b + c)x)/(4(a − x)), which is symmetric in b and c; so ω_C meets BC at the same point.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The answer is all n with no prime factor up to 101 (take g the identity). For the converse let p ≤ 101 be the smallest prime factor of n. Summing (g(x) + Tx)^k over x gives the same value modulo n for T = 0, …, k, so the k-th finite difference in T yields k!·Σx^k ≡ 0 (mod n) for k < p; equivalently, a polynomial of degree at most p − 1 vanishing at 0, …, p − 1 modulo p^e has all coefficients divisible by p^e. Hence Σx^(p−1) ≡ 0 modulo p^e = p^(v_p(n)). But summing over a primitive root and lifting the exponent shows that 1^(p−1) + … + (p^e − 1)^(p−1) has p-adic valuation exactly e − 1 (alternatively, summing the falling factorial (x−1)…(x−p+1) gives (p−1)!·C(n, p), not divisible by n).

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Yes, for every ratio below 1. Split most of the board into r long blocks, each filled by a back-and-forth path that can be run in either direction, joined into one big cycle by short corridors, with two spare columns acting as shortcuts. A snake covering r − 1 of the blocks circulates around the cycle; on each lap it reroutes through a shortcut so that one more block is traversed in the reversed direction, and after r laps the whole snake has reversed. Abstractly this is a planar graph made of main, linking and transit paths in which a snake of length (r − 1)ℓ can turn around, embedded almost perfectly into the grid. Brian Lawrence's alternative deforms a single loop two cells at a time to reach length (n − 1)(n − 2) − 1.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Place the four sequences on the four half-axes of one infinite array, so the three given great functions fill three quadrants and every 2 × 2 block has determinant ±1 with quadrant-dependent sign. Fill the last quadrant cell by cell: if a 3 × 3 window lacks only its corner and its centre is y ≠ 0, the three known determinant relations reduce modulo y to give that the product of the two neighbours of the missing cell is ≡ −1 (mod y), so the corner can be an integer (y = 0 forces ±1 entries and is handled directly). Alternatively, A ∼ B holds exactly when a_0 | a_1b_1 + 1 and every a_n, b_n divides the sum of its two neighbours (the rows obey integer three-term recurrences), and the first condition chains around A, B, C, D.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Cut the necklace between any two equal neighbours, giving alternating runs (zigzags); the no-three-equal condition says no run has length 1. Every removal either merges two runs (one divider fewer) or splits one (one more), so a win needs at most 2n dividers. Conversely, with at most 2n dividers both players can always move at the end of a run: since the colours balance, odd runs ending in T and odd runs ending in S come in equal numbers, and if all runs are even one of length at least 4 exists because the average length is 3; such end moves never create a run of length 1. The criterion does not depend on who starts.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Without the cyclic hypothesis, the Miquel point Z of BFEC (incircle touch points E, F) lies on AD by radical axes, and the spiral similarity at Z makes ZFE similar to AC_1B_1; angle chasing then gives that AD is tangent to circle AB_1C_1 and that IM ∥ B_1C_1 for the midpoint M of AD. The hypothesis forces A_1 to be the Bevan point, so the angles at B_1 and C_1 are right, and Pappus on the lines through the excentres and BC puts I, hence M, on B_1C_1. Then MD² = MA² = MB_1·MC_1 gives the tangency. A second route inverts in the circle BIC and uses harmonic bisectors. In barycentrics, the perpendicularity AI ⟂ ID fixes D on BC explicitly; the cyclic hypothesis becomes (b + c)(s − b)(s − c) = a·s·(s − a). With the circle through D, B_1 and C_1 written out, the power of A equals AD², which is the tangency.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Equality holds exactly for prime powers. Count the integers in [1, σ(n)] that are coprime to n by cutting the interval into consecutive blocks whose lengths are the divisors d of n: a block of d consecutive integers contains exactly φ(d) integers coprime to d, hence at most φ(d) coprime to n, and Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n, so at most n of the first σ(n) integers are coprime to n. If two primes p < q divide n, placing the block of length q first puts p inside it, so the count is strict. Alternatively, inclusion–exclusion with floor errors bounds the count by 2^(k−1) + Π(p_i^(e_i) − 1/p_i), and a short inequality on the primes shows this is below n once n has two prime factors.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Only the constant functions work. Iterating the averaging rule n times writes f(x, y) as a binomial average of the values on the antidiagonal n steps back; subtracting the same expansion for the neighbouring point of the antidiagonal leaves coefficients C(n, i) − C(n, i − 1), whose absolute values telescope to 2C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) = o(2^n). So f is constant along antidiagonals, and the rule then makes it constant. Other complete routes: couple two left/down random walks until they meet (f along a walk is a bounded martingale and the walks meet with probability 1), or take the supremum of the differences between neighbours on an antidiagonal, which obey the same averaging rule, and push a nearly maximal difference backwards until the accumulated differences exceed the range [0, 1].

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: In graph language: maximise the sum over edges of the smaller endpoint degree among graphs with 2017 = C(64, 2) + 1 edges. The answer is 63·C(64, 2) + 1 = 127009, from K_64 with one pendant edge. For the bound, take a vertex of minimum degree and move each of its edges to a missing edge at the same neighbour (repairing doubled edges): no degree drops and the moved edges get larger labels, so one may assume a vertex adjacent to all others. Deleting that vertex changes the sum by an explicit amount, and induction on k over the edge counts C(k, 2) and C(k, 2) + 1 finishes (C_4 is the exception at k = 3). Contestant route: order vertices by degree and charge each edge to its later endpoint to get S ≤ d_2 + 2d_3 + … + 63d_64 + d_65, smooth the degree sequence under the handshake total to reach 127010, and rule out the single degree sequence that would attain it.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Induct on the string length n, with base n = 2 (there the majority of an odd multiset of strings is one of the strings). If S has P_ℓ but some majority y of 2k + 1 strings of S is missing, delete one coordinate: the projected set still has P_ℓ, so by induction it has P_k, which forces the string differing from y only in that coordinate to lie in S. Using these n neighbours of y in nearly equal multiplicities (2ℓ + 1 strings, n ≥ 3) gives majority y, a contradiction. Circuit route: P_k gives P_1 by repeating inputs; conversely, when the overall majority is 0, the 3-majority of x_i, x_j and a (2k+1)-majority of the others equals x_i AND x_j, and the (2k+1)-majority of consecutive ANDs recovers the (2k+3)-majority, so P_1 and P_k give P_{k+1}. Probabilistic variants show that random nested majority gates realise the larger majority with positive probability.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Since M and N are the circumcentres of the right triangles BHC and CHD, the lines MH and NH are perpendicular to AD and AB, so S and T lie on the circle with diameter AH and BTSD is cyclic. Take E as the second intersection of that circle with (ABCD), which is the Miquel point of BTSD; an angle chase through the antipode F of A (E, H, F collinear and CF ∥ BD) shows that EH bisects ∠BES and ∠TED. For ∠BEM = ∠NED: the circumcentre of BTSD, the midpoint of HF, lies on the circles BMS and DNT through E, which gives the equality; alternatively E is the ISL 2011 G4 point of triangle BCD, so (EMN) is tangent to (ABCD) and the homothety at E sends MN to a chord parallel to BD; or the dual Desargues involution at E on B, M, D, N, C and the centroid G is the reflection in the bisector of ∠BED; or EC and EG are isogonal and the isogonality lemma transfers this to EM and EN. Inverting at H (swapping A with C and B with D) turns STBD into a rectangle and shows where E must be.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Bob learns the number N of points and, for each of the linear forms x, y, x + y and x − y, the multiset of its values over the set, hence every power sum of these forms. The identity 12x²y² = (x + y)⁴ + (x − y)⁴ − 2x⁴ − 2y⁴ lets him compute the total weight Σ(x² + y²)(m + n − x² − y²) for every candidate pair (m, n) up to a bound he can read off. Each point contributes independently: points of the annulus have weight ≥ 0 and all other lattice points negative weight, so S is the unique N-point set of maximal weight, and any set giving Bob the same data has the same weight, hence equals S. Equivalently, Σ(r² − m)(r² − n) is an invariant of indistinguishable sets; after cancelling common points it is ≤ 0 on the annulus part and > 0 on the rest.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The answer is ⌈n/t⌉; leagues of that many teams with disjoint colour sets show it cannot be larger. For the bound, take a family of teams of minimum size that still uses all n colours: if some team in it had no colour of its own, it could be dropped, so every team owns a private colour and the family is colour-identifiable, and it has at least ⌈n/t⌉ teams because each team brings at most t colours. Equivalently, repeatedly delete a team all of whose colours appear elsewhere. Constructive route: pick a least-used colour and a team using it, delete that team's colours and every team using the chosen colour; minimality of the colour shows no other colour loses all its users, so each step spends at most t colours (also run as an induction on n).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The circle on diameter AT is orthogonal to the circumcircle, so inverting in the circumcircle fixes it and sends circle BOC to line BC; hence A1 and A2 are the inverses of T and of the foot D of the A-altitude. Since A1 is the inverse of T it lies on the polar of T, the A-symmedian, so A1 is the midpoint of the symmedian chord and part (a) concurs at the symmedian point. For (b), line AA2 inverts to circle AOD, and the orthocentre has equal power HA·HD = HB·HE = HC·HF with respect to the three circles AOD, BOE, COF, which also share O; they are coaxial with axis OH, so the lines meet on the Euler line. Official route: A2 is the Miquel point of the tangential quadrilateral, KA bisects the angle at K, and the homothety from the circumcircle to the circumcircle of the tangential triangle shows AK passes through their exsimilicentre on the Euler line. Barycentric coordinates: the circle on diameter AT and circle BOC are written explicitly; their radical axis gives A1 = (b² + c² − a² : b² : c²) (so AA1 is the symmedian), and Vieta on the remaining quadratic gives A2 = (· : b²f(b)/S_B : c²f(c)/S_C) with f(b) = a⁴ + b⁴ + c⁴ − 2a²b² − 2b²c². The three lines meet at (a²f(a)/S_A : b²f(b)/S_B : c²f(c)/S_C), whose Euler-line determinant expands to 0. Complex numbers on the unit circle give A2 = 2abc/(ab + ac + bc − a²) and the concurrency point 2abc(a + b + c)/(abc + (a + b + c)(ab + bc + ca)), visibly on the line through 0 and a + b + c.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Work over the complex numbers. Derivative route: if P + λ_iQ = R_i² for four values, differentiating shows each R_i divides the Wronskian P'Q − PQ'; the R_i are pairwise coprime (a common root would be a common root of P and Q), so their product divides it, but after shifting P by a multiple of Q so that the degrees differ, the product has larger degree than the Wronskian. Hence P'Q = PQ', i.e. P/Q is constant, contradicting coprimality. Descent route: a Möbius change of the pair (P, Q) puts the four square combinations at P, Q, P − Q and P − kQ with P = A², Q = B²; then A ± B and A ± √k·B are coprime factors of squares, hence squares, so (A, B) is a smaller bad pair. The bound three is sharp (check_2017.py gives an example).

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Normalise scores so that you never change and, in each relevant round, the group you copy loses a point while the correct group gains one (rounds where you are right or everyone agrees only help). Key pairing: if a set S of contestants gained in an earlier round and later all answer alike, copying S cancels both rounds. Strategy: keep a list of winning sets; when some group with a common answer is on the list, copy it and strike it off; otherwise copy a group of size at least n/2 when possible and record the winning group. The list never repeats a set and only holds sets of size at most n/2, so an opponent's gain is bounded by the number of such sets containing them, at most 2^(n−2); a lead of 2^(n−2) + 1 already wins.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Take V and N on the perpendicular bisector of AE; it suffices that the midpoint L of AE bisects VN. The incentre I lies on DL (midpoint-of-altitude lemma, by homothety at D). The tangents from I to the excircle touch it at the points where circle BICJ (J the excentre) meets it, so BC, FG and that chord concur at a radical centre H; thus H lies on the polar of I, so I lies on the polar of H, and DI meets the excircle again at the second tangency point T from H. Then DFTG is harmonic, and projecting from D onto the line through L parallel to BC gives (∞, L; V, N) = −1. Variants: the excircle version of ISL 2002 G7 (circle BTC tangent to the excircle), length computations giving HD² = HB·HC, or a negative inversion at D with Reim's theorem. Complex numbers with the excircle as unit circle (touch points x, y, z) reach the same conclusion via Vieta on the quadratic for F and G.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Use primes p ≡ 1 (mod 3). The polynomial (x + 1)^p − x^p − 1 has every coefficient divisible by p, and a primitive cube root of unity ω is a double root: (1 + ω)^p − ω^p − 1 = 0 because 1 + ω is a sixth root of unity, and the derivative p((x + 1)^(p−1) − x^(p−1)) also vanishes at ω since 6 | p − 1. So p(a² + ab + b²)² divides (a + b)^p − a^p − b^p. For the exam's p³ it then suffices to take b = 1 and a < p of multiplicative order 3 modulo p (a power of a primitive root), so p | a² + a + 1. The official file proves the stronger p⁵: an order-3 element modulo p² is written as a ratio of two residues below p by Thue's pigeonhole lemma (or p = s² + st + t² gives a² + ab + b² = p² with (s² − t², 2st + t²)); p = 2017 works.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Put s(g) = n − c(g); the claim becomes s(f1∘…∘fk) ≤ s(f1) + … + s(fk), and by induction on k only k = 2 matters. Key fact: s(g) is the least number of transpositions whose product is g, because a cycle of length ℓ is a product of ℓ − 1 transpositions while composing with one transposition merges two cycles or splits one, changing c by exactly 1. Concatenating minimal transposition words for the factors then gives the triangle inequality. Graph route: draw the orbits of f1 and f2 on the same vertex set; every orbit of the composition stays inside one connected component of the union, and adding the cycles of the second permutation one at a time (or counting the edges of a bipartite orbit-incidence graph, at most n) shows the union has at least c(f1) + c(f2) − n components. Other complete routes: induction on n by deleting a common or one-sided fixed point, and the linear-algebra version where c(f) is the dimension of the fixed space of the permutation matrix.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let E be the excircle's touch point on BC. Angle chase: since MKDT is cyclic, line TD meets the circumcircle again at the reflection of A in the perpendicular bisector of BC; reflecting that collinearity across the bisector shows AT is isogonal to the Nagel cevian AE, so T is the A-mixtilinear touch point. Because MD = ME and the angles at K are supplementary, circles DKM and EKM have equal radii and are mirror images in line AKM; hence the reflection S of E in the angle bisector lies on circle DKM, on the excircle (whose centre is on that bisector) and on AT. Inversion variant: the √(bc) inversion swaps K and M, fixes circle DKM up to reflection, and swaps T with E and the mixtilinear incircle with the excircle, giving AS·AT = AK·AM directly. Barycentric coordinates: with D = (0 : s − c : s − b), K = (0 : b : c) and M on the circumcircle, circle DKM has linear part (bc, ac(s − b)/(b + c), ab(s − c)/(b + c)); Vieta on the quadratic with the circumcircle gives T = (−a(s − b)(s − c) : b²(s − c) : c²(s − b)), and the second point of line AT on circle DKM is S = (−(b − c)²s : b²(s − c) : c²(s − b)), which satisfies the excircle equation after cancelling abc, bc and s. Cartesian route: put A at the origin with the bisector as the x-axis and M = (1, 0); with λ = a/(b + c) the circle DKM, the line AT of slope λq/(1 − λ + q²) and the point S come out in closed form, and S is at the excircle radius from the excentre (1 + λ, 0).

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Work in F_p[x]. Ψ is additive and, by the Frobenius identity (u + v)^p = u^p + v^p with c^p = c for constants, Ψ(xP) = Ψ(P)^p; more generally Ψ(RP) = Ψ(R)∘Ψ(P), so Ψ turns products into compositions. Since every Ψ(R) has zero constant term, P | Q implies Ψ(P) | Ψ(Q), which gives Ψ(gcd) | gcd(Ψ(F), Ψ(G)). For the reverse, write gcd(F, G) = AF + BG by Bezout and apply Ψ: both terms are divisible by gcd(Ψ(F), Ψ(G)); both sides are monic. Equivalently, run the Euclidean algorithm on (F, G) and on (Ψ(F), Ψ(G)) in parallel, since subtracting x^k·F corresponds to subtracting Ψ(F)^(p^k). Field-theoretic routes: the roots of an irreducible factor are permuted by Frobenius, so divisibility by it is a linear-recurrence condition (ABCDE), or the roots of each Ψ(F) form an F_p-vector space (KevinYang2.71).

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: If b_n, …, b_2n all vanish, then with k = ⌊2^(n−1)√3⌋ the fractional part of 2^(n−1)√3 is below 2^−(n+1), i.e. k < 2^(n−1)√3 < k + 2^−(n+1). Squaring and using k < 2^n gives k² < 3·4^(n−1) < k² + k/2^n + 4^−(n+1) < k² + 1, impossible for the integer 3·4^(n−1). Equivalently, a non-square integer N satisfies {√N} > 1/(2√N) by rationalising √N − ⌊√N⌋, which already beats 2^−(n+1). Variants: ⌊2^(2n)√3⌋ would be divisible by 2^(n+1) and two multiples of 2^(2n+2) cannot fit in the window between consecutive squares; or the near-equality forces 3·4^(n−1) − m² = 1, ruled out modulo 3 or 4.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Diagonal values never occur, so they are free; the answer is W(a, b) = 1 for all a ≠ b or W(a, b) = −1 for all a ≠ b. Write X_abc = W(a, b)W(b, c). Three well-chosen partitions with singleton parts, say ({1}, {3}, rest), ({2}, {3}, rest) and ({1, 2}, {3}, the remainder), have sums that cancel all terms involving the other indices, leaving X_132 + X_231 = 2; the same trick in the other orientation gives X_132 + X_312 = 2. Comparing, W(2, 3)W(3, 1) = W(3, 1)W(1, 2), and W is never zero off the diagonal (a partition with one singleton A and one singleton B would otherwise give 0 = n − 2), so W(a, b) = W(b, c) for all distinct a, b, c. With n ≥ 4 this forces a common off-diagonal value k, and 2k² = 2.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The answer is the incentre, circumcentre and orthocentre, all of which work. Suppose P is neither O nor H, let B1C1 meet BC at T and the lines BP, CP at Q and R. Ceva together with Menelaus makes (B, C; T, A1) harmonic, so A1 lies on the line through P and BR ∩ CQ. The angle condition turns into an angle chase showing BCQR is cyclic, and Brocard's theorem for this quadrilateral puts its centre on BC, so the angles BQC and BRC are right and BR ∩ CQ is the orthocentre of triangle PBC; chasing angles in the resulting cyclic quadrilaterals through the feet shows that BP and CP bisect the angles at B and C, so P = I. A second synthetic route uses isogonal conjugates: the angle condition says P, its isogonal conjugate P* and O are collinear (TelvCohl derives this with a homothety of the pedal and circumcevian triangles and Sondat's theorem, then shows the pedal perspector would have to be H), and the pedal concurrency says P, P* and the de Longchamps point are collinear, so either P = P* (P = I) or P and P* both lie on the Euler line, giving O or H. Trigonometric route: with x1, x2, x3 the angles PAB, PBC, PCA and y1, y2, y3 their partners PAC, PBA, PCB, trig Ceva gives equal products of sines, Ceva on the pedal feet (AC1 = PA cos x1 and so on) gives equal products of cosines, and both triples sum to 90°. Then tan x_i and tan y_i have the same three symmetric functions (from cos(x1 + x2 + x3) = 0 and sin(x1 + x2 + x3) = 1), so the triples coincide as sets; scalene-ness rules out swaps of adjacent pairs, and the three remaining matchings are exactly I, O and H. Complex numbers: encoding the angles as unit complex numbers turns the two conditions into polynomial identities whose monic cubics agree at 0 and ±1; the official solution instead writes both conditions as cubic curves in p and p̄ with ABC on the unit circle and uses Bezout: nine known intersections (vertices, excentres, I, O, H) exhaust them.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Say AB < AC; we get the right angle at E. Because the angle AQD is right, line AQ passes through the antipode D' of D on the incircle, and the homothety at A carrying the incircle to the A-excircle sends D' to the extouch point T; so A, D', Q, T are collinear, and since M is the midpoint of DT and the angle DQT is right, Q lies on the circle centred at M through D. By the Iran lemma, AI, DE and the midline through M parallel to AC meet at one point P'; triangle DMP' is then similar to the isosceles triangle DCE, so MP' = MD and P = P' lies on DE. Finally ID is tangent at D to the circle (M, MD), so the tangent–chord angle gives angle PQD = angle D'DE = angle D'QE, and adding the right angle D'QD gives the right angle PQE. Spiral-similarity route: Q is the centre of the spiral similarity taking circle (M, MD) to the incircle (T to D, D to D'); it sends I to the pole of line AQ, which lies on EF by La Hire, so it maps AI onto EF and P onto E or F. Harmonic route: the intersections of DE and DF with QE' and QF' (E', F' antipodes) both lie on circle (M, MD), and projecting the harmonic quadrilateral D'EQF from D shows that they lie on AI. Complex numbers with the incircle as the unit circle and AI as the real axis (E = e, F = 1/e, D = d): A = 2e/(e² + 1), the point AI ∩ DE is (d + e)/(de + 1), and the second point of line A–(−d) on the unit circle is Q = (A + d)/(Ad + 1); then |m − p| = |m − d| identifies P, and (p − q)/(q − e) is purely imaginary, which is the right angle PQE. Barycentric variant for the collinearity: a point (t : b : c) of AI is collinear with D = (0 : s − c : s − b) and F = (s − b : s − a : 0) exactly when t = c − b, and the displacement formula gives MP² = MD² = (b − c)²/4.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Build the set by induction, recording only the gaps d_1, …, d_(n−1) between consecutive elements: with s_i the partial sums and t_(i,j) the block sums, it suffices that no two block sums divide one another and that the CRT system a ≡ −s_i (mod t_(i,j)) is solvable, after which a + s_1, …, a + s_n works. To add an element, multiply every old gap by a large M (a multiple of all old block sums, coprime to p) and append a new gap equal to a prime p not dividing the old gaps: the new block sums p + M·t are coprime to everything else, so non-divisibility survives and the new congruences can be added by CRT. pi37's variant goes directly from {a_1, …, a_n} with b = a_1⋯a_n to {ab² − 1, ab² + ba_1, …, ab² + ba_n}: the moduli ba_i + 1 are pairwise coprime and coprime to b, so CRT gives a with ab² ≡ 1 modulo all of them; old differences scale by b and still divide only their own pair, and ba_i + 1 dividing another element would force it to divide b(a_i − a_j), a divisor of b². Other complete routes add a large prime offset (with Dirichlet in one version), use linear lifts k·a_i + s, or the exponential lift 2^M − 2^(a_i) based on gcd(2^x − 1, 2^y − 1) = 2^gcd(x, y) − 1.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The answer is no. Track simultaneously the m + 1 "staircase" starting states in which, for a fixed labelling, exactly the first k usamons are charged. A diode from a lower label to a higher one moves the charge exactly in the staircases where one of the two is charged, which is the same as swapping the two labels; a diode the other way never does anything. So after any sequence of moves the set of possible states still contains all m + 1 staircases for some labelling, and any two usamons are in different states in one of them. Official sorting-network view: give the usamons distinct real numbers and let a diode swap the values when the source is larger; the 0/1 picture is the threshold image of this, so if the two chosen usamons end with values a < b, declaring exactly the values ≥ b charged is a counterexample (the 0–1 principle). Monotonicity route: the move sequence induces a map on charged sets that preserves size and inclusion, so a maximal chain ∅ ⊂ E_1 ⊂ … ⊂ U has a chain of images that must separate the two usamons at some step.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: No. Modulo 1, f induces an additive map from Q to Q/Z, and the required c exists only if this map is multiplication by a single rational. The proposer's formula f(p/q) = (p/q)(1! + 2! + ⋯ + q!) (lowest terms, q > 0) works: for fractions whose denominators divide N, every factorial from N! on is a multiple of N, so modulo 1 the function is x ↦ x·(1! + ⋯ + N!), additive on them; but c would have to be congruent to 1! + ⋯ + q! modulo every q, which no integer satisfies. Evan Chen's construction fixes f on powers of 2 through a sequence with 2x_(k+1) − x_k alternating 0 and 1 and extends through the odd part. Structural view: Q/Z is the direct sum of its p-parts Z[1/p]/Z, so multiplying each part by a different integer a_p glues to a valid f; more generally any profinite integer acts, which classifies all solutions. CRT-compatible residues k_q (k_(qn) ≡ k_q mod q) with different behaviour on two infinite sets of primes, and a step-by-step extension that rules out each rational c in turn, give further complete counterexamples.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The answer is ⌈log₂ n⌉. No colour class contains a path u → v → w, so for each colour every vertex is only a tail or only a head of that colour, and each colour class sits inside a complete "all edges from A to B" bipartite graph. Lower bound by induction: split the vertices by one colour into its tails and the rest; the larger part has at least n/2 vertices and no edge of that colour, so χ ≥ 1 + log₂(n/2). Pigeonhole version: the sets of colours on the out-edges of two different vertices cannot coincide, since the colour of the edge joining them would both leave one vertex and enter the other, hence n ≤ 2^χ. Construction: number the vertices in binary and orient and colour each edge by the lowest bit where the endpoints differ (from 0 to 1); equivalently, double a construction and join the copies by a new colour, then delete vertices.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let Ha, Hb, Hc be the feet of the altitudes. The sine rule in triangles AM_cX and AM_bX, the concyclicity of the midpoints and feet on the nine-point circle, and trig Ceva show that AX, BY, CZ concur if and only if HaX, HbY, HcZ concur, because M_aX, M_bY, M_cZ already pass through S. These three lines in fact meet on the Euler line: with N_b, N_c the midpoints of BH and CH (antipodes of M_b, M_c on the nine-point circle), Pascal on the hexagon M_bN_bH_bM_cN_cH_c puts M_cH_b ∩ M_bH_c on the Euler line, and Pascal on M_bYH_bM_cZH_c then makes H_bY ∩ H_cZ collinear with S and that point. Projective route: the map S ↦ X ↦ (HaX ∩ Euler line) is a composition of two perspectivities through the nine-point circle, hence projective, so the three such maps coincide once they agree for three positions of S (circumcentre, nine-point centre, a point of the nine-point circle). Cross-ratio and polar variants and a Jerabek/cevian-nest argument also appear. Barycentric coordinates on the medial triangle (official first solution): by the cevian nest theorem and isotomic conjugation it suffices that M_aX', M_bY', M_cZ' concur, where X' is X reflected in the midpoint of M_bM_c; with S = (a²S_A + t : b²S_B + t : c²S_C + t) on the Euler line the second intersection X with the nine-point circle and then X' have coordinates that factor so that Ceva's condition holds by symmetry. Degree count (Gopal Goel): writing X = (1 − t)M_a + tS and imposing |X − N|² = R²/4 with dot products gives t as a linear function over a quadratic in the Euler-line parameter, so X, Y, Z have quadratic barycentric coordinates and the Ceva condition is a polynomial of degree at most 6 that vanishes at seven explicit positions of S (nine-point centre, centroid, the two points on the nine-point circle, and the three points on the sides of the medial triangle).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The fixed point is the orthocentre H. Line PQ is the Simson line of X, and R lies on it and on the B-altitude, so RH and XP are both perpendicular to CA; once the Simson line is known to bisect XH, the quadrilateral HPXR is a parallelogram and the line through P parallel to XR is PH. The bisection lemma is proved by reflecting X in BC and CA: both reflections lie on a line through H (an angle chase using the reflection of H in BC on the circumcircle and C as circumcentre of X and its two reflections), and the homothety at X with ratio 1/2 carries that line to the Simson line. Direct route without the lemma: with K the second intersection of XP with the circumcircle, the cyclic quadrilaterals XCKB and XQPC give the parallelogram RBKP, and the reflection of K in CA is the orthocentre of XAC, whose distance to X equals BH; adding lengths gives RH = PX. Complex numbers on the unit circle: the feet are p = (a + c + x − ac/x)/2 and q = (b + c + x − bc/x)/2, intersecting line PQ with the B-altitude gives r = b + (a + c + x + ac/x)/2, and then p + r = x + (a + b + c) = x + h, which is the parallelogram HPXR. Equivalently, reflect P in the midpoint of XH and check that the image lies on the B-altitude via a purely imaginary ratio. Trigonometric route: with angle BCX = α, the sine rule in BQR and the right triangles at X give BR and RM = XP as products of sines and cosines of A − α and C + α, and their difference BM = −(a/sin A)cos(A + C) does not depend on α.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Every term is a square, and it suffices to show that for each prime p the exponent ν_p(a_i) does not depend on i; then one divides the whole sequence by p² and inducts (only averages of length at most p are used, so the division stays legitimate). Averages of length p show a_i ≡ a_(i+p) (mod p). If p divides a_1, compare the averages of a_1..a_k and of a_2..a_k: both are quadratic residues, and they are congruent up to the factors k and k − 1, so whenever k/(k − 1) is a non-residue the partial sum must vanish mod p. Taking k the least non-residue (or two consecutive "pivots" k with 1 − 1/k a non-residue, which exist by counting) forces p | a_(k+1), hence p divides a whole arithmetic progression of indices with difference coprime to p, and with the period-p structure every term. The p = 2 case follows from the averages of two consecutive terms.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Prove the stronger bound "amicable pairs ≥ E − V/2" for every graph; with E = n²/4 and V = n this is 2·C(n/2, 2), attained by K_(n/2, n/2). A vertex v forms an amicable pair with every other neighbour of each of its neighbours, so it lies in at least m(v) − 1 pairs, m(v) the largest degree among its neighbours. The friendship-paradox inequality gives Σ m(v) ≥ Σ (average neighbour degree) = Σ over edges (d_u/d_v + d_v/d_u) ≥ 2E, by AM–GM. Inductive route: delete both ends of any edge uv; the remaining graph has two fewer vertices and d_u + d_v − 1 fewer edges, while u is amicable with every other neighbour of v and vice versa, which pays for the lost edges. A Hall-matching proof pairs each vertex whose degree exceeds every neighbour's with a distinct neighbour, and a weighted double count (1/T(x, y) ≥ average of 1/d_x and 1/d_y) also finishes.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Show the polynomial is positive everywhere. All c_i lie in (0, 2), so the signs make every term nonnegative for x ≤ 0. For x > 0 write c_i = 1 + d_i with Σ|d_i| < 1 and split the polynomial as (x^n − x^(n−1) + ⋯ + 1) + (x^n + 1) − Σ ±d_i x^i: the alternating geometric sum equals (x^(n+1) + 1)/(x + 1) > 0, and x^n + 1 exceeds every x^i with 1 ≤ i ≤ n − 1, so it beats the perturbation term by the triangle inequality. Variants split at x = 1 (bounding the perturbation by x or by x^(n−1), or using the symmetry x ↔ 1/x of the problem), or note that for fixed x the perturbation is a linear function of the d_i maximised by putting all the weight on the largest power, reducing to one-term inequalities.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The homothety at A with ratio 2 sends triangle AHE to ADB, so W is the midpoint of A and the orthocentre of ABD; hence AW is perpendicular to BD with length equal to half of that orthocentre distance, R|cos A| (equivalently AW is a fixed multiple of BD determined by the inscribed angle). The same holds for CY with the supplementary angle at C, so AW and CY are equal and parallel, AWYC is a parallelogram, and likewise BXZD. Thus WY and XZ are translates of AC and BD, the diagonals of WXYZ have the same lengths and the same angle as those of ABCD, and the area formula ½·d₁·d₂·sin θ gives equal areas. Area variant: translating two opposite vertices by the same vector keeps one diagonal and shifts the two heights to it by opposite amounts, so the area is unchanged (applied twice). Complex numbers with the circumcircle as unit circle (official): the orthocentre of ABD is a + b + d, so the homothety gives w = (2a + b + d)/2 and cyclically x, y, z; then w − y = a − c and x − z = b − d, so the diagonals of WXYZ are translates of those of ABCD and the areas agree. Full shoelace version: both areas equal (i/4)(a/b − b/a + b/c − c/b + c/d − d/c + d/a − a/d) via the complex area determinant. Vector version: with O the circumcentre, YW = CA and ZX = DB as vectors, and the area is half the cross product of the diagonals.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Take n not divisible by 3, a prime p ≡ 1 (mod n), and α of order n, so S is the set of n-th roots of unity mod p. A relation a + b = c in S scales to 1 + α^k = α^m, making α^k a common root of X^n − 1 and (X + 1)^n − 1 modulo p. Over the complex numbers these polynomials share no root, since |ω| = |1 + ω| = 1 forces ω to be a primitive cube root of unity, impossible when 3 ∤ n; so Bézout in Z[X] gives a(X)(X^n − 1) + b(X)((X + 1)^n − 1) = c with a nonzero integer c, and every prime p > c (infinitely many p ≡ 1 mod n by Dirichlet) works. Dirichlet-free variants choose p as a prime divisor of Φ_q(α) for an integer α divisible by the Bézout constants (Schur), use the irreducibility of cyclotomic polynomials to get coprimality, or work with n = 2^N and a parity argument on f(x)f(−x).

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Colour the edges of K_(2k+1) by language; the answer is C(2k+1, 3) − k(2k+1) = (2/3)k(k − 2)(2k + 1). With no monochromatic triangle, every non-rainbow triple has exactly one apex, the member who speaks the same language to the other two, so these triples are counted at their apexes: a member with d_i partners in language i (Σ d_i = 2k) is the apex of Σ C(d_i, 2) ≥ k triples by convexity (Jensen, Cauchy–Schwarz or smoothing). Equality needs every member to speak each language with exactly two others, i.e. each language class is a spanning union of cycles of length at least 4; a Hamiltonian decomposition of K_(2k+1) (Walecki: a hub plus rotated zig-zag paths on a 2k-gon) supplies it. The naive "colour by cyclic difference" rule fails when 3 divides 2k + 1, because the difference (2k + 1)/3 forms monochromatic triangles, and needs a local recolouring.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The only solution is (2, 251, 252). Reducing modulo x gives x | 4024 = 2³·503; comparing 503-adic valuations (503³ would divide the left side but only 503 divides the right) excludes 503 | x, and 2-adic valuations exclude 4 | x, so x ∈ {1, 2}. Then 503 divides y³ + z³ = (y + z)(y² − yz + z²), and since 3 does not divide 502, cubing is injective modulo 503 (an order argument; equivalently −3 is a quadratic non-residue, so the quadratic factor is not divisible by 503); hence y + z = 503k. Cancelling gives k(y² − yz + z²) = yz + 1 for x = 2, forcing k = 1 and (z − y)² = 1, and k(y² − yz + z²) = 4(yz + 2) for x = 1, where size gives k ≤ 4 and parity together with residues modulo 5 (or 13) leave no solution.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let ω_A, ω_B be the circles about A and B through C; they are orthogonal and CD is their radical axis, so with K′, L′ the second intersections of AX with ω_B and of BX with ω_A, the points K, K′, L, L′ are concyclic on a circle ω whose centre is the orthocentre of XAB (it lies on CD). Orthogonality makes AL, AL′ and BK, BK′ tangent to ω, so KLK′L′ is harmonic and XAB is self-polar; hence D is the inverse of X in ω, i.e. the Miquel point of the quadrilateral, which identifies T as KL′ ∩ LK′. Brokard puts S = KL ∩ K′L′ on AB with (A, B; S, T) = −1, and the power of ω's centre with respect to the circles on diameters AB and ST shows the angle SCT is right; a right angle at C over a harmonic pair makes CT the internal bisector. A metric alternative proves GK = GL from the IMO 2012/5 configuration (G the orthocentre of the auxiliary triangle ABG), then parallels TM ∥ BX, TN ∥ AX give AT/TB = AC/BC. Cartesian route (#24): invert in the circle on diameter CD, place C at the origin and D at (cos θ, sin θ); the circles about A and B through C become the lines x = cos θ/2 and y = sin θ/2, the images of K and L are found explicitly as (cos θ/2 + √(2r − 1)/2, sin θ/2) and the symmetric point, and the image of the bisector foot is the arc midpoint ((sin θ + cos θ)/2, (sin θ + cos θ)/2); the segment joining it to D's image and the segment K′L′ have slope −1 and a common perpendicular bisector of slope 1, so the four points form an isosceles trapezoid and are concyclic. Barycentric route (#33): with X = (a²: b²: x), K = (k: b²: x) with k from BK = BC, the circle through D, T = (a: b: 0) and K is written down and the equality of its z-coefficient computed from K and from L is verified by expansion.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Suppose k_n ≤ M for all n. The functional graph of f has no cycle (the largest element of a cycle could never move up by k), so the orbit 1, f(1), f²(1), … consists of distinct numbers. Joining each index i to i + 2k(f^i(1)) splits the indices into chains; the chains are disjoint (two arrows into one index would contradict the minimality of k), and each meets every window of 2M consecutive indices, so there are at most 2M of them. Along a chain f^i(1) − i/2 is constant, so f^i(1) ≤ i/2 + C for all i; but i + 1 distinct positive integers cannot all lie below i/2 + C once i is large. Equivalent versions phrase this as a density count: the sets where f^i(1) − i/2 takes a fixed value each have lower density at least 1/(2M).

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Yes, infinitely many. In a pair of pals one triangle has sides p, q and median m to the third side while the other has sides p, m and median q (otherwise they are congruent); the third sides are fixed by the median formula, and equating the areas (Heron, or completing each triangle to a parallelogram whose half-triangle has sides p, q, 2m) collapses to 2p² = 5(q² + m²) once q ≠ m. It remains to build infinitely many pairwise coprime solutions that also satisfy the triangle inequalities of both triangles (which force 2m + q > p and 2q + m > p, so q and m cannot be tiny). A Pythagorean parametrisation does it: with u² + v² = t², q = u + 3v, m = 3u − v, p = 5t, e.g. t = 4a² + 1, u = 4a² − 1, v = 4a, with a ≢ 1 (mod 5) for coprimality; a Gaussian-integer factorisation of 10B² = q² + m² or suitable Pell families give alternatives.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: With H the orthocentre and D the foot from C, the circles on diameters AC and BC meet again at D, so H lies on their radical axis CD and the power of H gives HK·HM = HL·HN: K, L, M, N are concyclic, and C lies on the perpendicular bisectors of KM and LN, so it is the centre. Right angles at the points of the circles on diameters make AL, AN, BK, BM tangent to this circle, so A and B are the poles of LN and KM and line AB is the polar of H (equivalently CH·CD = CK², so D is the inverse of H). Brokard's theorem puts ML ∩ NK on the polar of H, i.e. on AB. Alternatives: the harmonic divisions (A, H; K, M) = (B, H; L, N) = −1 projected through a common point (prism lemma), Pascal on degenerate hexagons such as KKNNLM with the tangents at the double points, or an angle chase showing triangles DYK and DLX similar. Barycentric coordinates on ABC (#24): the circle on diameter BC is a²yz + b²zx + c²xy = S_A·x(x + y + z), and intersecting it with the A-altitude (t: S_C: S_B) gives K and M with first coordinate S_BC ± 2S√(S_BC), and N, L symmetrically; a 3×3 determinant then shows that NK meets AB at (√S_B : √S_A : 0), which is symmetric in the construction, so ML passes through the same point.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Encode each row by the shifted zero positions b_(k,i) = a_(k,i) − i ∈ [0, n]; membership in F means b is weakly increasing along rows and weakly decreasing down columns. (a) The k-th row of f(C) has its ones at a_(n+1−j,k) − k + j, which for fixed j is non-decreasing in k, and the column condition on the i-th zeros is equivalent to the same condition on the i-th ones (counting zeros in initial segments of rows). (b) A word lemma converts "the i-th one sits at t" into "exactly t − i zeros precede t", which turns f into inequality rules b′_(k,i) ≥ j ⇔ b_(n+1−j,k) ≤ i − 1 and b′_(k,i) ≤ j ⇔ b_(n−j,k) ≥ i; applying them three times gives b‴_(n+1−k,n+1−i) = n − b_(k,i), so f³ rotates the table by 180° and f⁶ is the identity. An induction on the number of rows, deleting the bottom row and tracking how the moves of the "bugs" change, proves the same rotation statement in a generalised m × n setting.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Yes. Every positive non-square is a² + b with 1 ≤ b ≤ 2a, and nothing of that form is a square, since it lies strictly between a² and (a + 1)². Two positive variables realise a² + b with 1 ≤ b < a (a = x + y − 1, b = y − 1 or similar), and a third variable z restricted to {1, 2} doubles the range: (x + y − 1)² + 2y − 2 + z covers the odd and even b up to 2a. Multiplying by 1 − c(z − 1)(z − 2) with a large constant c (or by −z² + 3z − 1) leaves z = 1, 2 untouched and makes every value with z ≥ 3 negative. A different construction uses Pell: z²(x² − zy² − 1)² + z equals z on solutions of x² − zy² = 1 (which exist exactly when z is not a square) and otherwise lies strictly between two consecutive squares.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The fixed point is the orthocentre H; putting P at the midpoint of BC makes D and E the feet of the altitudes from C and B, which suggests it. Since PD = PB and PE = PC, the midpoints of BD and CE are the feet of the perpendiculars from P, so D and E move linearly (at constant speeds) as P slides along BC. With the altitude feet Z on AB and Y on AC, the ratio DZ : EY stays equal to BZ : CY = HZ : HY, so the right triangles HZD and HYE are similar for every P; the spiral similarity at H carrying Z to Y then carries D to E, which gives ∠DHE = 180° − ∠A and puts H on circle ADE. Other synthetic routes: circle PDE meets BC again at a point Q, and QDE is similar to the orthic triangle, so H is its incentre and the Miquel point of D, E, Q; the altitudes from B and C meet PE and PD at points X and Y with PX = PB = PD and PY = PC = PE, so PD·PY = PE·PX, and power of a point plus three radical axes force A, D, E, H, X, Y onto one circle; or the linearity of the power of a point (power with respect to circle ADE minus power with respect to the circumcircle) is checked at one position of P. Moving-point arguments (D and E move projectively, so three positions of P suffice) give the same conclusion. Barycentric route: with P = (0 : p : 1 − p), the isosceles triangles give BD = 2·BP·cos B and CE = 2·CP·cos C, so D and E have coordinates linear in p; the circle through A, D, E is −a²yz − b²zx − c²xy + (vy + wz)(x + y + z) = 0 with v = 2S_B(1 − p) and w = 2S_C·p, and substituting H = (S_BS_C : S_CS_A : S_AS_B) makes the p-terms cancel and the rest vanish identically, so H is on every such circle (two of these circles share the radical axis y : z = S_C : S_B through A and H). Complex route: on the unit circle with h = a + b + c, D and E come from reflecting P's projections, and the cross-ratio of D, E, A, H is shown to be real.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Answer: f(x) = cx with c ≥ 0. Writing x = 0 gives f(y²) − f(0) = |yf(y)|, so g = f − f(0) satisfies g(x + t) = g(x) + g(t) for t ≥ 0 and g ≥ 0 on [0, ∞); comparing y with −y gives |f(y)| = |f(−y)|, and x = −y² gives f(y²) + f(−y²) = 2f(0). The decisive step is f(0) = 0: either f is even at some point and then constant (only f ≡ 0 survives), or the sign information at y = 1, 2 (or f(1) < 0 leading to contradictions at 2, 3, 4) forces it. Then f is odd and additive, and since f(x + t) ≥ f(x) for t ≥ 0 it is monotone, which rules out the pathological Cauchy solutions; a squeeze by rationals (or the bound on [0, ∞)) gives f(x) = cx, and the absolute value forces c ≥ 0.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Yes, such integers exist. The left side minus 6abc is the norm of a + b·∛2 + c·∛4 from Q(∛2): the product of the three conjugates a + bω^k∛2 + cω^(2k)∛4 (equivalently the determinant of a circulant-type matrix), so it is multiplicative. The triple (1, 1, 1) has norm 1, because 1 + ∛2 + ∛4 is a unit with inverse ∛2 − 1, so multiplying by it preserves norm 1; on coordinates this is the linear map (a, b, c) ↦ (a + 2b + 2c, a + b + 2c, a + b + c), which can also be found by matching coefficients. Iterating from (1, 1, 1) gives solutions whose entries grow without bound, the first above 2010 being (4159, 3301, 2620).

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: 63756. Run the process backwards from everyone in one room: a reverse move sends one student from a room of size a to a room of size at most a − 2, and the process can be continued as long as two rooms differ by 2 or more. With rooms kept sorted, any reverse move between non-adjacent rooms can be split into unit toggles across the gaps in between, and an exchange argument on a maximal process shows one may always toggle adjacent rooms first. Phase 1 toggles adjacent rooms until the sizes form the staircase 62, 61, …, 57, 57, 56, …, 1, counting the toggles across each gap (41649 moves); in phase 2 every move lowers the sum of squares by at least 2, and the bound is attained by moves between rooms differing by exactly 2, from 84624 down to the balanced 90·20² + 10·21² (22107 moves). The sum of squares is the monovariant that caps the count.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Answer: n = 1. For n = 1, with u = x − y, v = y − z, w = z − x and u + v + w = 0, both u² + v² + w² and the square root of P_1 are multiples of u² + uv + v², so Q_1 = 4P_1. For n ≥ 2, specialise to a one-variable polynomial (z = 0, y = 1, x = 1 + t): the divisor is monic with integer coefficients, so by Gauss's lemma the quotient must have integer coefficients, and evaluating at a convenient point gives 2^(2n+1) + 1 | 3^(2n), i.e. 2^(2n+1) + 1 is a power of 3. Lifting the exponent gives v₃(2^(2n+1) + 1) = 1 + v₃(2n + 1), far too small once n ≥ 2 (Zsigmondy or Mihăilescu also finish). A root-of-unity alternative: any root x of the specialised P_n makes (x − 1)^(2n) and x^(2n) the two primitive cube roots of unity, so x and x − 1 are roots of unity, x is a primitive sixth root, P_n would equal (x² − x + 1)^(2n), and x = 2 compares 1 + 2^(2n+1) with 3^(2n).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The right triangles PEB and PFC are inversely similar (∠PBE = ∠PCF on the circle), so PE and PF are isogonal in angle BPC, as are PB and PC. Let R = AB ∩ CD; the right angles at E and F put R on circle PEF with PR a diameter. By the isogonal line lemma (or Desargues' involution theorem on the quadrilateral formed by B, E, C, F) the lines from P to BF ∩ CE = Q and to BE ∩ CF = R are isogonal too, and the isogonal of the circumdiameter PR in triangle PEF is the altitude from P, so PQ ⊥ EF. Alternatives: trigonometric Ceva in triangle PBC, a cross-ratio transfer via a reflection-and-scaling about the bisector of angle BPC, Jacobi's theorem with the point at infinity of the altitude, or a radical-axis argument (the feet of P on BF and CE together with E, F are concyclic, so Q lies on the radical axis of two circles through P and the foot on EF); inversion at P and polars with respect to a circle centred at P give further routes. Complex numbers with P = 0 (#13): the right angle at E gives B = e(1 + ki) for a real k, and the inverse similarity of PEB and PFC gives C = f(1 − ki); writing the two collinearity conditions for Q = q on BF and on CE and adding them leaves q(ē − f̄) = q̄(f − e), which is exactly the condition that PQ is perpendicular to EF. Only ∠PBE = ∠PCF is used.

synthetic.explanation: The right triangles PEB and PFC are inversely similar (∠PBE = ∠PCF on the circle), so PE and PF are isogonal in angle BPC, as are PB and PC. Let R = AB ∩ CD; the right angles at E and F put R on circle PEF with PR a diameter. By the isogonal line lemma (or Desargues' involution theorem on the quadrilateral formed by B, E, C, F) the lines from P to BF ∩ CE = Q and to BE ∩ CF = R are isogonal too, and the isogonal of the circumdiameter PR in triangle PEF is the altitude from P, so PQ ⊥ EF. Alternatives: trigonometric Ceva in triangle PBC, a cross-ratio transfer via a reflection-and-scaling about the bisector of angle BPC, Jacobi's theorem with the point at infinity of the altitude, or a radical-axis argument (the feet of P on BF and CE together with E, F are concyclic, so Q lies on the radical axis of two circles through P and the foot on EF); inversion at P and polars with respect to a circle centred at P give further routes.

Only ∠PBE = ∠PCF is used.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: every n ≥ 4 (for n = 2, 3 the sequences 1, 2 and 2, 1, 2 have no block with integer mean). A block a_(i+1), …, a_j has integer mean as soon as its sum is 2(j − i), so track S_k = a_1 + … + a_k − 2k: it starts at 0, ends at −1, and each step changes it by at least −1, so it cannot jump downwards past a value. If no block works, no value of S can repeat at indices two or more apart; following the walk from both ends forces a_1 + a_2 ≤ 3 and the same for the last terms, and an n ≥ 4 then cannot reach the total 2n − 1. Alternatives prove by induction that a sequence with no good block and sum at most 2n − 1 must alternate 1, 2, 1, 2, …, whose sum is too small; parity (adjacent terms of opposite parity) and a 2-adic refinement (sums of 2^k consecutive terms are ≡ 2^(k−1) mod 2^k) give further proofs, as does taking the largest index whose prefix exceeds twice its length.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The condition says that a^n − 1 has no primitive prime divisor, i.e. no prime p with ord_p(a) = n. Zsigmondy's theorem says such a prime exists for a ≥ 2 except when (a, n) = (2, 1), (2, 6), or n = 2 with a + 1 a power of 2. Checking the exceptions: n = 1 needs a − 1 to have no prime factor, so a = 2; (2, 6) works because 63 = 3²·7 with 3 | 2² − 1 and 7 | 2³ − 1; and a = 2^k − 1 with n = 2 works because every odd prime factor of a² − 1 = 2^(k+1)(2^(k−1) − 1) divides a − 1 = 2(2^(k−1) − 1). Finally a = 1 makes a^n − 1 = 0, and m = 1 serves every prime once n ≥ 2. So the solutions are (1, n) for n ≥ 2, (2, 1), (2, 6), and (2^k − 1, 2) for k ≥ 2.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Answer: HQ/HR = 1. In the orthic triangle DEF the orthocentre H is the incentre and A is the excentre opposite D, so Q (foot from H to EF) is the incircle touch point and P (foot from A) is the excircle touch point on EF. The homothety at D taking the incircle to the excircle sends the point of the incircle diametrically opposite Q to P, so line DP passes through that antipode; hence R is the reflection of Q in H and HR = HQ (the "diameter of the incircle" lemma). Other synthetic routes: a chain of ratios through the similar triangles HEF ~ HCB and AEF ~ ABC whose product is 1; Menelaus and Ceva showing that D and the point EF ∩ AH divide AH harmonically, then projecting from P onto line QR, where the image of A is the point at infinity, so H is the midpoint of QR. Barycentric route with the orthic triangle DEF as reference: H is its incentre (a : b : c in the side lengths of DEF), R is the intersection of DP with line QH computed by determinants, and the coordinates satisfy Q + R = 2H componentwise, so H is the midpoint of QR.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Treat cities and roads as a multigraph with edge weights 1 and 2 and odd weighted degree at every vertex. Reduction: two roads uv and vw of equal capacity can be replaced by a single road uw of that capacity (orient it, then orient the two originals as a path through v), which keeps every parity and every in–out difference; repeating this (induction on the number of edges, or a minimal counterexample) leaves a graph where at each vertex at most one 1-road and at most one 2-road meet. Since the weighted degree is odd, every vertex has exactly one 1-road, so the 1-roads form a perfect matching and the 2-roads a partial matching; the components are alternating paths and cycles, which are oriented consistently along their length, giving difference exactly 1 at every city. Variants delete monochromatic cycles first and orient alternating paths, or decompose the 1-edges and 2-edges into forests and orient trees edge by edge.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The alternating binomial sum is (up to sign) the m-th finite difference of the sequence at 0. Key lemma: a sequence is a p-pod iff for every e it agrees modulo p^e with an integer-valued polynomial, i.e. its expansion in the binomial basis C(n, k) has coefficients that are eventually divisible by p^e. Writing z_n = Σ b_k C(n, k) (Newton interpolation), the m-th alternating sum is ±b_m, so the p-pod condition says b_m → 0 p-adically; then x_n y_n is, modulo p^e, a product of two integer-valued polynomials, which is again integer-valued, and its higher differences vanish modulo p^e. A second proof uses the Leibniz rule for finite differences of a product, Δ^m(xy) = Σ C(m, j) Δ^j x · Δ^(m−j) (shifted y), and shows by induction that truncated p-pods remain p-pods. A third view: p-pods are exactly the sequences extending to continuous functions on the p-adic integers (Mahler's theorem), and products of continuous functions are continuous.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: t = 30(1 + √5). For any point X on the boundary, the sum of its distances to the four corners is at least 1 + √5 (Jensen on √(1 + u²); equality at the side midpoints), while the sum of its distances to the four side midpoints is at most 1 + √5 (equality at the corners). Swapping the order of summation, the four corners have total distance sum at least 120(1 + √5) to the given points, so some corner has sum at least 30(1 + √5), and likewise some midpoint has sum at most 30(1 + √5). The distance sum is continuous along the connected boundary, so the intermediate value theorem gives Q. Uniqueness of t follows from the equality configurations (all points at the corners, or all at the midpoints). An alternative existence proof: for each configuration the attained values form a closed interval, and any two such intervals intersect by a double-counting symmetry Σ_i Σ_j |A_iB_j| = Σ_j Σ_i |B_jA_i|, so all intervals share a point (Helly in one dimension).

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The sum Σ_{i < 2^n} c_i is the Catalan number C_{n+1}. Bijective route: read the binary expansion of i as a lattice path and interpret c_i as the number of non-crossing paths (or balanced parenthesisations with prescribed digits in fixed positions) compatible with it; the two recursions c_{2n+1} = c_n and c_{2n} = c_n + c_{n−2^e} become the first-step decomposition of these objects, so summing over all i counts Dyck paths of semilength n + 1. Algebraic route: split the sum according to the 2-adic valuation of the index, define auxiliary sums over blocks of indices, derive a recursion for them (or for the generating polynomial G_n(x) with G_n(0) = 1 + G_{n−1}(1)), and check by induction that it reproduces the Catalan recursion C_{n+1} = Σ C_k C_{n−k}.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Work with formal power series: P is nice exactly when P(x)/(1 − x) has all coefficients 0 or 1 (its coefficients are the partial sums of the alternating ±1 coefficients) and P(0) = 1. Then Q(x)/(1 − x) = [P(x^n)/(1 − x^n)] · (1 + x^m + x^{2m} + … + x^{(n−1)m}), and P(x^n)/(1 − x^n) has 0/1 coefficients supported on multiples of n. A coefficient of x^k in the product counts the pairs (a, j) with 0 ≤ a < n, k = am + jn and the j-th coefficient equal to 1; since gcd(m, n) = 1 the residue of k modulo n fixes a uniquely, so every coefficient is 0 or 1 and Q is nice (when P has an odd number of terms one first multiplies by 1 − x^d to stay with polynomials). An alternative describes the coefficients through the numerical semigroup generated by m and n, classifying numbers am + bn as good, bad or neutral and proving the structure by induction on k, or splits into the cases P(1) = 0 and P(1) = 1 and counts representations.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Both conditions single out the Miquel point of B, C, D, E (the second intersection of circle AED with Ω). Triangles PBD and PCE share an incentre iff the angle bisectors of ∠BPD and ∠CPE coincide, iff ∠BPE = ∠CPD, iff P is the centre of the spiral similarity taking EB to DC (triangles PEB and PDC similar), i.e. the Miquel point. For concurrency: the Miquel point is the inverse in ω of Q = BD ∩ CE, so O, Q, P are collinear, and OP is perpendicular to the polar line through A and R = BC ∩ DE (Brocard). Conversely, at the Miquel point the quadrilaterals PBOD and PCOE are cyclic and O is the midpoint of the arcs BD and CE of these circles, so OP bisects ∠BPD and ∠CPE; the common incentre is OP ∩ ω by the incentre–excentre lemma. Further routes: the radical centre of Ω, ω and circle AED with polars and harmonic pencils P(B, D; U, R) = −1 giving the bisectors, or spiral similarity with the midpoints of BD and CE and Brocard's theorem.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Divide and conquer: the bound n·2^n already suffices (the stated n·2^(n+1) is twice what is needed). Split {1, …, 2^n} into halves; pairs inside each half are handled by induction, so it is enough that at most 2^n pairs cross the midpoint when the configuration is absent, giving f(n) ≤ 2f(n − 1) + 2^n = n·2^n. For the crossing pairs, view them as a bipartite graph between the halves: it has no cycle, because in a cycle the smallest left vertex and its two neighbours produce the forbidden triple (a, c), (b, d), (a, d), so it is a forest with fewer than 2^n edges. In the grid picture (pair (a, b) as a lattice point) the crossing pairs fill a 2^(n−1) × 2^(n−1) square in which no point has another point both below it and to its right; points with a point below shoot rays to the right that occupy distinct rows, and at most one point per column shoots none, so the square holds at most 2^n points. A sharper count (lasers to the boundary cells, pigeonhole) gives the exact maximum (n − 1)2^n + 1.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Answer: yes, such sets exist. Let P(x) be the difference of the two sums. If the power sums Σ a^i and Σ b^i agree for 0 ≤ i ≤ 2011 (equivalently the sums of C(a, i) agree), then all derivatives of P up to order 2011 vanish at 1, so (1 − x)^2012 divides P; conversely (1 − x)^2011 | P is necessary, since otherwise P is too large near x = 1. Existence by pigeonhole: among the C(N, 2011²) subsets of {1, …, N} of size 2011², the vector of power sums up to degree 2011 takes at most about 2011^(2·2012)·N^(2011·2012/2) values, which is smaller for large N because 2011² > 2011·2012/2; two different subsets share the vector. Finally shift both sets by a large c: |x^c P(x)| = (1 − x)^2012·|x^c R(x)|, and x^c(1 − x) can be made uniformly small on (0, 1) (AM–GM gives x^c(1 − x) < 1/c, or split (0, 1) at a point r near 1 and use compactness), so the strict inequality holds. The explicit Prouhet–Thue–Morse construction gives equal power sums too but needs 2^2010 elements, far more than allowed.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Write Ψ(n) for the gcd. Since a − b divides P(a) − P(b), n always divides Ψ(n). Fixed-divisor lemma: if a prime q divides Ψ(n) but not n, then P vanishes at every multiple of n, hence at every residue mod q, contradicting gcd(P(0), P(1), …) = 1; so Ψ(n) has only the prime factors of n. Take n = p a large prime: if p² | Ψ(p), then Q(x) = (P(x + p) − P(x))/p vanishes identically mod p, so by Lagrange's theorem over F_p either p divides every coefficient of Q (impossible for the leading coefficient d·a_d once p is large) or p is below the degree. Hence Ψ(p) = p for all large primes. Variant: with P = x^k Q(x), n = p^k for primes p not dividing kQ(1) + Q'(1), a binomial expansion shows the exact power p^k (Taylor expansion P(n + k) − P(k) ≡ nP'(k) mod n² is the same idea).

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Substitute a = 1/x etc. (so xyz = 1); the sum becomes Σ x³/(2y + z)², and Hölder with the weights (2y + z) gives Σ x³/(2y + z)² · (Σ(2y + z))² ≥ (x + y + z)³, i.e. the sum is at least (x + y + z)/9 ≥ 1/3 by AM-GM. Equivalent standard routes: Cauchy–Schwarz applied twice, or termwise AM-GM against (ab + 2ac)/27. A convexity route applies weighted Jensen to t ↦ 1/t² with weights x. A third family homogenises with the tailored substitution a = x⁶ (or a = vw/u²) and finishes with Titu plus Muirhead / weighted AM-GM on the resulting bunched sums.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Geometric inequality via the Erdős–Mordell lemma. With D, E, F the feet from P and S the area, 2S = a·PD + b·PE + c·PF ≤ a(PA + PD) because the altitude from A is at most AP + PD; this gives a·PA ≥ b·PE + c·PF. Reflecting P in the bisector of angle A swaps the roles of PE and PF, giving a·PA ≥ c·PE + b·PF. Adding, PA ≥ (b + c)(PE + PF)/(2a); since h_b + h_c = 2S(1/b + 1/c), the left side is at least Σ bc(PE + PF)/(4aS), and regrouping by PD, PE, PF and AM-GM (b/c + c/b ≥ 2) compares it with 2S = Σ a·PD. The lemma can also be proved by Pappus's area theorem on parallelograms built by translating P.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: First show that the circle tangent to AB, AC at F, E is the incircle of ARS, with RS parallel to BC. With X, Y the touch points of the incircle of ABC on CA, AB, the homotheties CMN → CAB and BPQ → BCA give NE ∥ BX and QF ∥ CY; together with AE = AF and AX = AY, the figure (A, E, F, lines NE, QF) is the image of (A, X, Y, lines BX, CY) under a homothety at A, so ARS is homothetic to ABC and E, F are its touch points. Equivalent routes use homotheties centred at E and F (mapping the small incircles to the circle through E, F, with the tangent line through the arc midpoint parallel to BC), or Menelaus twice plus the tangent lengths s − b, s − c to prove RS ∥ BC. Finish by angle chasing: the incentre J of AEF has ∠EJF = 90° + A/2, while the touch point on RS sees EF under 90° − A/2, so J lies on the incircle.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Let b_n = a_n − a_{n−1}. Because ⌊n/k⌋ − ⌊(n − 1)/k⌋ is 1 when k | n and 0 otherwise, the recurrence collapses to b_n = Σ_{d | n, d < n} b_d, i.e. Σ_{d|n} b_d = 2b_n for n > 1; Möbius inversion (or a Dirichlet-convolution identity) then shows by induction that p^{k+1} | n forces 2^k | b_n for any prime p (the same 2-adic bound also follows by a direct induction on the divisor sum, without Möbius). By the Chinese remainder theorem there are infinitely many runs of 2^2010 consecutive integers, each divisible by a high power of a different prime; along such a run b_n ≡ 0, so a_n is constant mod 2^2010 while n runs through every residue, giving a_n ≡ n.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Reformulate on the graph with vertex set T and edges between non-coprime numbers: good subsets are the dominating sets, and the claim holds for every finite graph. Double count ordered pairs (A, B) of subsets with every cross pair coprime (no edges between A and B): the swap (A, B) ↦ (B, A) is an involution whose only fixed point is (∅, ∅), so the number of such pairs is odd. For fixed A the admissible B are exactly the subsets of the set of vertices not dominated by A, so A contributes 2^{#undominated}, which is odd exactly when A is good. Hence the number of good subsets is odd. Alternatives: sum the 0/1 indicator polynomial of domination over {0,1}^n and reduce mod 2, where only symmetric full-support terms survive; or inclusion–exclusion over the neighbourhood families of non-good subsets.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The angle conditions say P and Q are isogonal conjugates in ABC. Key observation: the isogonal conjugate of A with respect to triangle BPC is the reflection Q' of Q in BC, so ∠APB + ∠DPC = 180° holds exactly when P, D, Q' are collinear, and symmetrically the second condition says Q, D, P' are collinear (P' the reflection of P). The quadrilaterals BPCQ' and BP'CQ are mirror images in BC, so PQ' and P'Q cross BC at the same point; the two conditions define the same D. Other routes: the inellipse with foci P and Q touches BC at the required D (each focal segment bisects the angle between tangent points, then an angle sum); or Steiner's isogonal ratio theorem on BC with trig Ceva reduces both conditions to the same ratio BD/DC. Trigonometric route: the law of sines in DPB, DPC and in AQB, AQC (using the isogonal angle equalities) gives BD·sin APB/(CD·sin APC) = AB·sin AQC/(AC·sin AQB); the same in DQB, DQC and PCA, PBA, multiplied together, yields sin DQC·sin AQC = sin DQB·sin AQB. Product-to-sum turns this into cos(DQC − AQC) = cos(DQB − AQB), and since all angles lie in (0°, 180°) and Q is interior, DQB + AQC = 180°.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Both sides count surjections from an m-set onto n colours (n!·S(m, n)). The right side is inclusion–exclusion over the colours left out. For the left side, record the positions where a new colour first appears; the gaps between consecutive first appearances form a composition (a_1, …, a_n) of m, and after the i-th new colour each later object in that gap may take any of the i colours already used, and the first appearances themselves contribute n·(n − 1)⋯1 = 1·2⋯n choices, so the composition carries weight exactly 1^{a_1}·2^{a_2}⋯n^{a_n}. Alternatives: the left side is the coefficient of x^m in n!·x^n/((1 − x)(1 − 2x)⋯(1 − nx)), and the partial-fraction (Lagrange interpolation) identity checked at x = 1/k matches the right side; or prove the recurrence f(n, m) = n[f(n, m − 1) + f(n − 1, m − 1)] and induct with Pascal's rule.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Answer: no. Suppose C(3k, k) ≡ 1 mod p = 6k + 1; then C(3k, j) ≡ 1 for j = 0, k, 2k, 3k. Take ζ of order k mod p (a power of a primitive root). The roots-of-unity filter gives (1/k)·Σ_i (1 + ζ^i)^{3k} ≡ C(3k, 0) + C(3k, k) + C(3k, 2k) + C(3k, 3k) ≡ 4. But 3k = (p − 1)/2, so by Euler's criterion each term (1 + ζ^i)^{3k} is 0 or ±1 mod p, and a sum of k such terms cannot be ≡ 4k mod p since |4k|, |2k + 1| exceed k. Alternatives evaluate a Legendre-symbol sum such as Σ((n^4 + n)/p) or Σ((1 + x^3)/p) via power sums Σ n^ℓ ≡ −[p − 1 | ℓ], getting −1 − C(3k, k), and reach a contradiction by parity and the three roots of x^3 = −1 (quadratic reciprocity gives (−3/p) = 1), or by counting points on x^2 + y^3 = 1 (Hasse–Weil bound).

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Put the missing cell in a corner. The two board edges next to it have lengths 2^m − 1 and 2^n − 1, and writing 2^k − 1 as a sum of distinct powers of 2 needs at least k terms (minimal binary representation), so the m + n tiles must each touch one of these two edges, one tile per binary digit. Counting then works by an injection into orderings: take the tile covering the far corner (at most m + n candidates), remove it, and repeat, or (official route) walk along the two edges and record the order in which the tiles are met; the order determines the tiling, giving at most (m + n)!. Inductive alternatives: the largest tile must span the board between two opposite sides (extremal casework on its dimensions), so removing it and sliding the pieces together halves the board; or insert a full-size tile into a smaller tiling along an unblocked grid line, where counting the blocked lines leaves at most m + 1 or n + 1 positions.
