problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The triangles A O_B B and A O_C C are isosceles with equal apex angles (both twice angle ADB), so A is the centre of the spiral similarity taking O_B B to O_C C, hence also O_B O_C to BC: A is the Miquel point of the cyclic quadrilateral B O_B O_C C, and triangle A O_B O_C is similar to ABC. Standard Miquel facts then give the cyclic quadrilaterals A O_C X B and A O_B X C (equivalently, AX is perpendicular to the line from A to the intersection of BC and O_B O_C), and an angle chase finishes; the cyclic hypothesis forces angle BAD = 90° − (2B + C)/3, so angle DAH = (B − C)/3 (D cannot in general be constructed with ruler and compass). Other routes: radical axes of (ABC), (A O_B O_C) and the given circle concur at a point R, and a cyclic quadrilateral through the foot of the altitude gives the angle; or inversion, either in the given circle (A is the inverse of B O_C ∩ C O_B) or the √(bc) inversion, which turns it into a reflection statement. Trigonometric route: from the isosceles triangles, the cyclic condition becomes an equation in θ = angle BAD whose solution is θ = 90° − (2B + C)/3. The law of sines in the triangles at B and C and trigonometric Ceva for the cevians AX, BX, CX then compute angle XAB = 90° − (B + 2C)/3, so angle XAD = (B − C)/3 = angle DAH. A variant expresses the radius of (A O_B O_C) as R/(2cos((B − C)/3)) and checks that AX bisects angle DAO through a trigonometric identity.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Answer: c(n) = 1/lcm(1, 2, …, n). Shift so that b = 0 and f(0) = 0, and write f in the binomial basis, f(x) = Σ c_k·C(x, k) with integers c_k (Newton interpolation for integer-valued polynomials). Since C(m, k)/m = C(m − 1, k − 1)/k, the quotient f(m)/m is a sum of fractions with denominators dividing k ≤ n, so L·f(m)/m is an integer and the bound 1/L holds whenever f(m) ≠ 0. For equality take m = L: the gcd of C(L, 1), …, C(L, n) is 1, because for each prime p with p^e ≤ n < p^{e+1} the binomial C(L, p^e) is prime to p (Lucas, or a direct valuation count), so Bézout gives integers c_k with Σ c_k·C(L, k) = 1. Swapping the two minima, c(n) is exactly min over x of gcd(C(x, 1), …, C(x, n))/|x|.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Answer: 2/3. The triangles ABP and QBC are similar (angles 45°, 75°, 60°), so the spiral similarity at B gives ABQ similar to PBC with ratio BA/BP = sin 60°/sin 45° = √(3/2), hence AQ = √(3/2)·CP. Reflect C in M to get D, so ADPC is a parallelogram and AD = CP. An angle chase gives angle QAD = 105° = angle RAC, so angle RAQ = angle CAD; with AQ/AD = √(3/2) = QR/DC (as QR² = 6CM² = (3/2)·CD²), the obtuse-angle side-side-angle criterion gives triangle AQR similar to ADC, and AR/AC = √(3/2). Equivalent: the quadrilateral similarity C P B C' ~ Q B A R, or define R through that similarity and check that it meets both conditions (phantom point).

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Answer: (2, 2) and the pairs (t² + 1, (t + 1)² + 1), ((t + 1)² + 1, t² + 1) for t ≥ 0. Modulo mn − 1, n is invertible with inverse m, and (n² − n + 1)² ≡ n²(m + n − 1)², so the condition is equivalent to mn − 1 | (m + n − 1)², which is symmetric. Vieta jumping on k = (m + n − 1)²/(mn − 1): the quadratic in m has a second root m' = ((n − 1)² + k)/m, and at a minimal pair the size inequality n(m − n + 1) ≤ 2 leaves only (2, 1) and (2, 2), so k ∈ {3, 4}; k = 3 gives only (2, 2), and k = 4 is the conic (m − n)² − 2(m + n) + 5 = 0, whose solutions are consecutive squares plus one. Equivalent descent: the complementary divisor (n² − n + 1)² = (mn − 1)(m'n − 1) gives a ladder of solutions, with inequalities pushing down to n ≤ 2.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: As a tournament, the hypothesis says there is no directed cycle of length M + 1. Key lemma: then there is no cycle of length M + 1 or more at all (a longer cycle can be shortened by one vertex using the tournament edges, by casework or by removing a vertex and splitting the rest). Structure: take a maximal cycle; every outside vertex beats all of it or loses to all of it, and every "strong" vertex beats every "weak" one, so the tournament splits into a chain of strongly connected blocks A_1 → A_2 → …, each with a Hamiltonian cycle of length at most M. Number the blocks in order and each block along its cycle in reverse; then any two players at least M − 1 apart are in different blocks or ordered correctly. Inductive alternative: an M-cycle C splits the others into those beating all of C and those beaten by all of C, the former beat the latter through C, and induction on N (base case M = 2 is a transitive tournament) labels the parts.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Answer: (2, 4, 6) only. Shift by the solution: x³ − 3x − 2 = (x − 2)(x + 1)², y³ − 12y − 16 = (y − 4)(y + 2)², z³ − 27z − 54 = (z − 6)(z + 3)², so the system reads −12(y − 4) = (x − 2)(x + 1)², 3(z − 6) = (y − 4)(y + 2)², 27(x − 2) = (z − 6)(z + 3)². Comparing signs: x > 2 forces y < 4 from the first equation and z > 6 from the third, but then the second forces y > 4; x < 2 is symmetric; so x = 2, and then y = 4, z = 6. Equivalently multiply the three equations and cancel the nonzero product to get a negative product of squares, or scale x = 2a, y = 4b, z = 6c to the Chebyshev form 4t³ − 3t and chase the same inequalities. Eliminating x and y via z = 3u gives a polynomial with the factor (u − 2) times a square.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Work in F_p. Exponents matter only modulo p − 1 on the nonzero residues (Fermat), so take 0 ≤ i, j, k ≤ p − 2; then i + j + k is 0, p − 1 or 2(p − 1), and the last case reduces to the middle one by replacing each exponent e with p − 1 − e (the product is inverted). Suppose i + j + k = p − 1. Then (x − a)^i(x − b)^j(x − c)^k − 1 is a monic polynomial of degree p − 1 vanishing at every residue except a, b, c, where it equals −1. Contradictions: its values sum to −3, while a monic polynomial of degree p − 1 sums to −1 over F_p (power sums Σ x^ℓ ≡ 0 for p − 1 ∤ ℓ); or it agrees everywhere with (x − a)^{p−1} + (x − b)^{p−1} + (x − c)^{p−1} − 2, whose leading coefficient differs, so their difference is a nonzero polynomial of degree p − 1 with p roots (Lagrange). A third route cancels a factor to get a polynomial of small degree with p − 3 roots and finishes by cases.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Sum of squares. With x = 1/a, y = 1/b, z = 1/c the inequality becomes Σ a(b² + c²)² ≥ Σ a³(b + c)², i.e. Σ a²(b + c)(a − b)(a − c) ≥ 0, a Schur-type sum (Vornicu–Schur), and in fact LHS − RHS = Σ a(b − c)²(b + c − a)² identically. Directly in x, y, z the difference is Σ x³(y − z)²(xy + xz − yz); after yz = a, zx = b, xy = c the coefficients are nonnegative when a, b, c form a triangle, and otherwise a direct bound handles a = b + c + t; or apply the S_a, S_b, S_c criterion (S_b ≥ 0, S_a + S_b ≥ 0, S_c + S_b ≥ 0 for a ≥ b ≥ c). The proposer's intended route multiplies by x + y + z and expands.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: every odd n ≥ 7. Removing any coin leaves an even total, so all weights have the same parity as the total; take a set with minimal total (or divide by the gcd) so the weights are not all even, hence all odd, the total is odd and n is odd. n = 3 is impossible at once, and n = 5 falls to casework on which of the few possible splits occur when each coin is removed. For odd n ≥ 7 the weights 1, 3, …, 2n − 1 work: one needs signs ± on these numbers whose signed sum equals each removed weight (equivalently, splittings with difference 0 and with difference 2). An explicit table handles n = 7, and induction passes from n to n + 2 by appending 2n + 1 and 2n + 3 with opposite signs, flipping a pair of consecutive odd numbers when the two new weights themselves are removed.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: As the inscribed equilateral triangle PQR varies, its Miquel point M with respect to ABC stays fixed: an angle chase gives angle BMC = A + 60° and its cyclic versions, so M is the first isodynamic point. In the circle AQRM the chord QR equals 2R_A·sin A, which is smallest when AM is a diameter, i.e. when MQ ⊥ CA and MR ⊥ AB; so the minimal triangle is the pedal triangle of M (equivalently, comparing PQR with that pedal triangle by the spiral similarity at M, or by congruent right triangles MPP', MQQ', MRR', shows the pedal triangle is smaller). The perpendiculars from A, B, C to the sides of a pedal triangle of M concur at the isogonal conjugate of M (here the first Fermat point), which proves the orthology; the argument works for any fixed shape. An alternative via circumscribed equilateral triangles and [ABC]² = [DEF]·[D'E'F'] reaches the same point. Complex numbers on the unit circle: with ω a primitive cube root of unity, p + qω + rω² = 0 encodes the equilateral triangle; conjugating the conditions P ∈ BC, Q ∈ CA, R ∈ AB expresses q − r through r = ta + (1 − t)b, and minimising |q − r| over real t fixes r. The conditions AX ⊥ QR and BX ⊥ RP then give an equation for x that is invariant under the cyclic shift a → b → c, so CX ⊥ PQ as well.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: 3750. Join two points when they are harmonic; the graph has no K5, so Turán's theorem bounds the number of edges by the complete 4-partite count 3750, attained by 25 points near each of (±3/4, 0) and (0, ±3/4). No K5: among five points sorted by x, Erdős–Szekeres gives three with monotone y, and taxicab distance is additive along such a triple, so the outer pair has distance > 2. Alternatives rotate by 45° to the maximum metric: then five pairwise harmonic points lie in a 2 × 2 square, and pigeonhole on four unit squares gives two at distance ≤ 1; or colour each clique edge by the coordinate that attains the maximum, so that a two-colouring of K5 without a monochromatic triangle must contain a monochromatic 5-cycle, which is impossible on a line.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Suppose n⁷ + 7 = k². Modulo 4 forces n ≡ 1 (mod 4) (n ≤ −2 gives a negative number, n = 0, −1 fail). Add 121: k² + 11² = n⁷ + 2⁷ = (n + 2)·M with M = n⁶ − 2n⁵ + … + 64. Since n + 2 ≡ 3 (mod 4) it has a prime factor p ≡ 3 (mod 4), and such a prime dividing a sum of two squares divides both (−1 is a non-residue mod p), so p = 11 and 11 | k; as −1 is a non-residue mod 11, v_11(k² + 121) = 2 exactly. Finish either by lifting the exponent, v_11(n⁷ + 2⁷) = v_11(n + 2) + v_11(7) = v_11(n + 2), which must be odd (n + 2 ≡ 3 mod 4 with 11 its only 3-mod-4 prime), giving a contradiction with 2; or by coprimality of n + 2 and M (their gcd divides 448, and 7 is excluded since 5 is a non-residue mod 7), so, both factors being ≡ 3 (mod 4), the one not divisible by 11 has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) other than 11, a contradiction.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: View P_n = (a_n, b_n) as lattice points: the condition says the angle at P_n in triangle P_{n−2}P_{n−1}P_n is right, i.e. P_n lies on the circle with diameter P_{n−2}P_{n−1}. Hence the squared step length d_n = |P_nP_{n+1}|² is a non-increasing non-negative integer (Pythagoras; equivalently, for the difference vectors, Cauchy–Schwarz on the condition), and it drops by at least 1 unless the right triangle is degenerate. So d_n is eventually constant; if the constant is positive, the equality case forces each step to reverse the previous one (P_{n+2} = P_n, period 2), and if it is 0 the sequence is eventually constant. Either way a_k = a_{k+2008} for large k.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Answer: k = 1, approached by a degenerate configuration in which A lies on BD, A_1 = D_1 = A and B_1, C_1 are midpoints, so A_1B_1C_1D_1 is a medial triangle and the two smallest corner areas are 0 and a quarter. Key lemma: a triangle inscribed in another has area at least the smallest of the three corner triangles (affine map making it equilateral; if every corner were larger, every vertex angle would be below 60°). For the bound, either some corner area is at most an adjacent piece of A_1B_1C_1D_1, and the lemma applied to a suitable triangle finishes, or all corners are large, and after an affine normalisation of the diagonals of A_1B_1C_1D_1 a ratio comparison around the four vertices gives a cyclic contradiction. Several short write-ups apply the lemma to a triangle that is not actually inscribed, a gap pointed out in the thread. Barycentric route: for points on the sides with parameters d, e, f, the inscribed triangle has area [ABC]·(def + (1 − d)(1 − e)(1 − f)), which proves the corner lemma and two variants for points on extended sides; a case split on whether AB ∥ CD or where AB and CD meet assembles them into S ≤ S_1. The second case of the synthetic route is itself a coordinate computation.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The fixed point is the A-Dumpty point X (midpoint of the A-symmedian chord), the centre of the spiral similarity taking B to A and A to C; it lies on the symmedian, which gives the angle condition. The parallels give BR/RA = BP/PC = AQ/QC, so that spiral similarity also sends R to Q, and the centre of a spiral similarity taking R to Q while sending line AB to line AC lies on the circle through A, R, Q. Other complete routes: the power-of-a-point difference between (AQR) and (ABC) is linear along BC and constant at the symmedian foot; an angle chase with Miquel's and Reim's theorems; or the √(bc) inversion with reflection, which turns the claim into a collinearity proved by a spiral similarity. Barycentric coordinates: with P = (0 : m : n), the points are Q = (m : 0 : n) and R = (n : m : 0), the circle (AQR) has a short explicit equation, and substituting the symmedian (t : b² : c²) gives t = b² + c² − a², independent of m. Complex numbers with A = 0: the parallels give bq + cr = bc, the fixed point is x = bc/(b + c), and both the angle condition and the concyclicity reduce to checking that explicit ratios are real.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: one submission suffices. Start with red > blue > 0 (for instance 2 and 1); by induction the red number stays larger than the blue one, and at each step the new blue number is the old red one. From the final pair, the division algorithm undoes the last step: the old blue number is smaller than the old red number (= the current blue one), so the quotient of red by blue is exactly the last k and the remainder is the previous blue number. Backward induction recovers every k_i — this is the Euclidean algorithm, i.e. the continued fraction of the final ratio.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Answers: for squarefree n = ∏ p the count is ∏ p^p, and for cube-free n = ∏ p·∏ q² it is ∏ p^p·∏ q^{3q}. The count is multiplicative by the Chinese remainder theorem (signatures mod mn correspond to pairs of signatures mod m and mod n, since f(x) mod m depends only on x mod m). Mod p every sequence occurs (Lagrange interpolation). Mod p²: f(x + p) ≡ f(x) + p·f′(x), so the values on 0, …, 2p − 1 determine the rest and the values on p, …, 2p − 1 are fixed mod p, giving at most p^{2p}·p^p, and corrections of the form p·h(x) and x(x − 1)…(x − p + 1)·g(x) show that all are attained. Alternatively, write f in the binomial basis Σ a_k·C(x, k); f has integer coefficients exactly when k! | a_k, and counting the residues of a_k mod p² allowed by v_p(k!) gives the same p^{3p} (and the general prime-power count).

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Q is the Miquel point of the complete quadrilateral formed by lines AB, CD, AC, BD: it is the centre of the spiral similarity taking C to A and D to B (because P = AB ∩ CD lies on both circles), hence also the one taking C to D and A to B, so the circles QXDC and QXAB pass through Q. With these extra cyclic quadrilaterals, Reim's theorem on ω1 and circle CXDQ (parallels PY ∥ DX) shows Y lies on line QX, and the same argument on ω2 with PZ ∥ CX puts Z on QX. Equivalently, define Z' as the second intersection of line XQ with ω2 and angle-chase that PZ' ∥ AC. An inversion centred at P turns the claim into the concyclicity of two quadrilaterals, again settled by angles.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Since the multisets of differences agree, so does the sum of all nonnegative differences; for a sorted sequence that sum is Σ (2i − n − 1)·a_i, and with equal totals this gives Σ i·a_i = Σ i·b_i. Abel summation rewrites Σ i·a_i as n times the total minus the sum of the first n − 1 partial sums, so the partial sums of a and of b have the same total. Each partial sum of a is at most the corresponding one of b, so adding the n − 1 inequalities forces equality in every one, and then a_i = b_i term by term. A second route: the sum of squared differences is also determined, and n·Σa_i² = (Σa_i)² + Σ_{i<j}(a_i − a_j)², so Σa_i² = Σb_i²; the partial-sum condition says a majorizes b, and strict convexity of x² (Karamata) gives Σa_i² > Σb_i² unless the sequences coincide.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Write z = cos θ + i sin θ. Since cos kθ is rational, z is a root of x^{2k} − 2cos(kθ)x^k + 1, and likewise of the analogous polynomial for k + 1; both lie in Q[x]. If θ were not a rational multiple of π, the roots of the first are cis(±θ + 2πj/k) and of the second cis(±θ + 2πj/(k + 1)), and since k and k + 1 are coprime the only common roots are z and its conjugate, so their gcd is x² − 2cos θ·x + 1, which would lie in Q[x] — contradicting the irrationality of cos θ. Hence θ = (p/q)π, and then 2cos(kθ) is a sum of a root of unity and its conjugate, an algebraic integer; being rational, it is an integer (Niven), so cos kθ and cos (k + 1)θ lie in {0, ±1/2, ±1}. Thus kθ and (k + 1)θ are multiples of π/6 (more precisely of π/3 or π/2), and their difference θ, lying in (0, π/2) with irrational cosine, must be π/6. Variants: Chebyshev polynomials T_n(2cos x) = 2cos nx with a second common root, or Bezout for coprime exponents.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Answer: no — for all a, b some n has a | b^n − n. Take a minimal counterexample a. The powers b^i mod a are eventually periodic with period d < a (d divides the order of b modulo the part of a coprime to b, at most φ(a) < a). Proving the stronger claim that infinitely many n work, minimality applied to d (with the same b) gives arbitrarily large k with d | b^k − k, so k can be taken beyond the preperiod, and n = b^k satisfies b^n ≡ b^k ≡ n (mod a). Alternatively, the power tower b, b^b, b^{b^b}, … is eventually constant modulo every a (strong induction on a via Euler's theorem and φ(a) < a), so a tall enough tower n works, since b^n is the next tower term. A third route iterates φ down to 1, and a fourth inducts on the prime factorisation, lifting a solution modulo m to one modulo mp with the Chinese remainder theorem.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Intended solution: AT is the A-symmedian, so the law of sines in the two halves gives BT/AT = MC/AM with M the midpoint of BC, hence TC1/TA = MC/MA. The right angles at M and A make T, M, A, S concyclic, so angle AMC = angle ATC1, and SAS similarity gives AMC ~ ATC1; the spiral similarity at A sending M to T and C to C1 then sends B to B1, so ABC ~ AB1C1. Other complete routes: with K = BB1 ∩ CC1 and R = B1C ∩ C1B, R is the orthocentre of KB1C1, the tangents TB, TC touch the circle through K, B, C, R, and A is the Miquel point of B1BCC1, whose spiral similarity gives the claim; inversion centred at T with radius TB fixes ω and the circle through B, C, B1, C1 and swaps the relevant points; poles and polars with respect to the circle (T, TB) identify the second intersection of AT with ω as that orthocentre.

synthetic.explanation: Intended solution: AT is the A-symmedian, so the law of sines in the two halves gives BT/AT = MC/AM with M the midpoint of BC, hence TC1/TA = MC/MA. The right angles at M and A make T, M, A, S concyclic, so angle AMC = angle ATC1, and SAS similarity gives AMC ~ ATC1; the spiral similarity at A sending M to T and C to C1 then sends B to B1, so ABC ~ AB1C1. Other complete routes: with K = BB1 ∩ CC1 and R = B1C ∩ C1B, R is the orthocentre of KB1C1, the tangents TB, TC touch the circle through K, B, C, R, and A is the Miquel point of B1BCC1, whose spiral similarity gives the claim; inversion centred at T with radius TB fixes ω and the circle through B, C, B1, C1 and swaps the relevant points; poles and polars with respect to the circle (T, TB) identify the second intersection of AT with ω as that orthocentre.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Write P in the Newton basis at the odd points 1, 3, 5, …: P(x) = b1 + (x − 1)(b3 + (x − 3)(b5 + …)). At odd x, the product (x − 1)(x − 3)…(x − 2k + 1) is divisible by 2^k·k!, so modulo 1024 only b1, …, b11 matter and each b_{2k+1} matters only modulo 2^{10 − v2(2^k k!)}; the possible remainder sequences number at most 2^{10+9+7+6+3+2} = 2^37. A complete sequence hits every odd residue, which forces b1 odd and b3 odd (if b3 were even, every value would be congruent to b1 modulo 4), removing two factors of 2 and leaving at most 2^35. An equivalent version reduces P modulo the polynomials 2^j·(x − 1)(x − 3)… that vanish mod 1024 on odd x, leaving a degree-5 polynomial with bounded coefficients and two parity conditions; another expands P(x + 32k) by Taylor's formula and counts with v2(k!) in the binomial basis.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: f(1) = 6 and f(n) = 4n + 1 for n ≥ 2. In graph language a 3-connector has no independent set of size 3 and a windmill is a vertex whose neighbourhood contains a matching of n edges. Lower bounds: the 5-cycle has no triangle, and two disjoint cliques on 2n vertices are a 3-connector in which every connected piece is too small. For the upper bound fix a vertex A: its non-neighbours are pairwise adjacent, so if there are at least 2n + 1 of them they already contain a windmill. Otherwise A has at least 2n neighbours, and since any three of them contain an edge, edges can be peeled off greedily to build n − 1 disjoint blades, and a last blade unless exactly two non-adjacent neighbours V1, V2 remain. In that case each of the 2n non-neighbours (a clique) is joined to V1 or V2, so by pigeonhole V1 (say) has two neighbours in the clique, and a windmill centred at one of them uses V1 and pairs of clique vertices. For n = 1 the same vertex split is the R(3, 3) = 6 argument.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let the circle through B, Q, H meet BC again at R. By Miquel's pivot theorem in triangle ABC with A, Q, H, P concyclic, the circle through C, P, H also passes through R. Angle chasing gives angle PRQ = 180° − 2A, which is supplementary to the central angle QOP, so O, P, R, Q are concyclic for every choice of ω; RH bisects angle PRQ (OP = OQ), so R lies on line OH, and H is the incentre of triangle PRQ, just as H is the incentre of the orthic triangle DEF. More angle chasing gives triangle RPQ similar to DEF and isosceles triangles RBQ, RCP, so CR/BR = RP/RQ = ED/FD; with the tangency, this R is the tangency point. Other complete routes: a spiral similarity at H taking the orthic configuration (AFHE, nine-point circle) to (ω, circle OPQ); a lemma that the perpendicular bisectors of BQ and CP meet on BC, proved with trigonometric lengths, followed by the same angle chase; and Pascal's theorem on a hexagon inscribed in ω (with B1, C1 the second intersections of BH, CH) which puts the tangency point on QC1 and PB1, then the sine rule and similar triangles finish. Complex numbers with ω as the unit circle (A, H, P, Q on it): the feet of the perpendiculars from H give B and C as line intersections, the condition that R on BC lies on circle OPQ is a quadratic in the conjugate of R, and tangency (a double root) becomes the relation x³ + wyz = 0 between the four unit-circle points; R is then explicit and CR/BR simplifies to the same expression as ED/FD = (sin C cos C)/(sin B cos B). A trigonometric length computation (BQ and CP in terms of the angle at H) proves the key lemma that the perpendicular bisectors of BQ and CP meet on BC.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Answer: k = 16/9. Write f(t) = t² − t + 1 = (t − 1/2)² + 3/4, so x = 0, y = z = 1/2 forces k ≥ 16/9. For the bound, assume x ≤ 0 and read 16/9·f(x)f(y)f(z) − f(xyz) as a quadratic in x: its leading, linear and constant coefficients are kf(y)f(z) − y²z², −(kf(y)f(z) − yz) and kf(y)f(z) − 1, and for k = 16/9 they have the right signs because f(y)f(z) ≥ 9/16 and, using f(1/t) = f(t)/t², f(y)f(z) ≥ 9y²z²/16 (then AM-GM handles the middle one). Equivalently prove the two-variable lemma 4f(x)f(y) ≥ 3f(xy) when x, y are not both positive (a quadratic in x with nonpositive discriminant) and apply it twice. Other complete routes: an explicit sum-of-squares decomposition in x, and a sign-case analysis that fixes the product xy, applies Cauchy–Schwarz to f(x)f(y), and splits on z ≥ 1 or z ≤ 1 with the bounds f(z) ≥ 3z²/4 and f(z) ≥ 3/4.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Answer: d_n = 2(4^n − 1)/3 + 1 = (2^{2n+1} + 1)/3. Call a number n-good if it is a sum of n signed powers of two. If x is n-good then so is 2x, and x − 1, x + 1, x + 2 are (n + 1)-good, so 4x − 1, …, 4x + 2 are (n + 1)-good; by induction every positive integer up to 2(4^n − 1)/3 is n-good. For the other direction take a shortest representation: two equal terms ±2^i can be merged, so it is a signed binary expansion with digits in {−1, 0, 1}, and padding (2^l = 2^{l+1} − 2^l) shows n-good implies m-good for m ≥ n. The target is 3 mod 4, so its last two digits are (0, −1) or (1, 1) (the third option is never shortest); each case reduces to a smaller number of the same shape with one or two fewer terms, which is not good by induction.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: n·C(n − 4, 4)·2^{n−9}. The two interior triangles are joined by a strip of triangles, and each of the other four sides of the two interior triangles carries a fan-like tower of at least one triangle cut off by that diagonal. Built up from its base, every triangle of a tower or of the strip has exactly two choices for which of its free sides is a polygon side (the top of a tower is forced), giving 2^{n−8} triangulations once the five sizes are fixed. The sizes are nonnegative integers with a fixed sum n − 8, so stars and bars gives C(n − 4, 4) choices; the apex of one interior triangle can be any of the n vertices, and each triangulation is counted twice (the two interior triangles swap roles). The alternative proof counts triangulations of a polygon whose triangles all touch a red side: 2^{m−3} with one blue side and C(k + l, k) with two blue sides (by recursion or a word of k pluses and l minuses read off while walking through the triangles), then sums over the regions cut off by the interior triangles.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The rotation about A through the common angle θ takes triangle APC to triangle ABQ, so PC = BQ, the lines BQ and CP meet at angle θ, and A, P, B, R and A, Q, C, R are concyclic; hence angle BOC = 2θ. Composing the rotation about A by −θ, the rotation about O by 2θ (which takes B to C) and the rotation about A by −θ again gives a map with total angle zero that sends P to Q, so it is the translation by PQ; following A through the three rotations shows that A moves perpendicular to OA, so AO ⊥ PQ. Other complete routes: reflect C in AQ to C' and use the spiral similarities ABC' ~ APQ and CAO ~ CC'B to compare directions; take the circle through A and the second intersections of the two circles with AQ and AP, whose centre I satisfies IA ⊥ PQ, while PQ is the radical axis of that circle and circle BCR (equal powers), so IO ⊥ PQ as well; or use the criterion AO ⊥ PQ ⇔ AP² − AQ² = OP² − OQ², with OP² − OQ² read off from powers with respect to circle BCR and Stewart's theorem in triangles ACP and ABQ. Complex numbers with A = 0 and z = e^{iθ}: P = b/z and Q = cz, and since angle BOC = 2θ with OB = OC, (b − o)/(c − o) = z², so o = (q − p)/(z − 1/z); then o/ō = −(q − p)/(q̄ − p̄), which is exactly AO ⊥ PQ. Barycentric coordinates on triangle BRC (A on the bisector of angle BRC) also work: P and Q come from the circles through A, R, B and A, R, C, and the perpendicularity criterion for displacement vectors expands to zero. A third computation evaluates OP² − OQ² by the law of cosines in triangles POB and QOC and trigonometric identities, getting AB² − AC² = AP² − AQ².

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: m = 2n − 1. Each element lies in exactly two of the 2n sets, and two sets share at most one element, so every element is the unique common element of one pair of sets; double counting (element, pair of sets containing it) gives mn ≤ C(2n, 2), that is m ≤ 2n − 1. Equivalently, treat the 2n sets as vertices of a graph and each element as the edge joining the two sets that contain it: condition (b) says the graph is simple, so it has at most C(2n, 2) edges and each vertex has degree m. Equality is reached by the complete graph on 2n vertices (each set is the set of edges at one vertex), which can also be written out greedily: each new set takes one fresh-ordered element from every earlier set and fills up with unused elements. A third view is the 2n × mn incidence table with m marks per row and two per column, where (b) forbids rectangles.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The point reflection in the nine-point centre N (the midpoint of OH) swaps O and H and takes triangle ABC to a congruent triangle A'B'C' with circumcentre H and orthocentre O. Since AH = 2·OM (M the midpoint of BC), the midpoint X of AH is the image of M, so it lies on B'C', and B'C' is the perpendicular bisector of AH; the parallelogram condition puts P1 on B'C', so OQ1/OP1 = HP1/OP1 = AP1/OP1. Similar triangles turn this ratio into A'O/(2·OJ) with J the foot of the altitude from A', and the three ratios OJ/A'J are area ratios [B'OC']/[A'B'C'] summing to 1, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives the bound. A second synthetic step used by the trigonometric solutions: the reflection H1 of H in BC lies on the circumcircle, and an angle chase with similar triangles H1HQ1 ~ H1AO shows that O, Q1, H1 are collinear and HQ1 + OQ1 = R. Trigonometry: HQ1 = 2R cos B cos C / cos(B − C) from the sine rule in triangle HBQ1 and OQ1 = R cos A / cos(B − C) from the cosine rule in triangle OBQ1, so OQ1/OP1 = OQ1/HQ1 = cos A/(2 cos B cos C); AM-GM reduces the sum to cos A cos B cos C ≤ 1/8, which is Jensen for the concave function log cos (or a product estimate with sin 2B + sin 2C ≥ 2√(sin 2B sin 2C)). Complex numbers with the circumcircle as the unit circle give p1 and q1 explicitly and the same ratio as a modulus.

A second synthetic step used by the trigonometric solutions: the reflection H1 of H in BC lies on the circumcircle, and an angle chase with similar triangles H1HQ1 ~ H1AO shows that O, Q1, H1 are collinear and HQ1 + OQ1 = R.

For 3000 random acute triangles OQ1/OP1 = cos A/(2 cos B cos C) (max deviation 1.8e-8) and the sum is at least 3 (minimum 3.0009; check_2005.py).

analytic.explanation: Trigonometry: HQ1 = 2R cos B cos C / cos(B − C) from the sine rule in triangle HBQ1 and OQ1 = R cos A / cos(B − C) from the cosine rule in triangle OBQ1, so OQ1/OP1 = OQ1/HQ1 = cos A/(2 cos B cos C); AM-GM reduces the sum to cos A cos B cos C ≤ 1/8, which is Jensen for the concave function log cos (or a product estimate with sin 2B + sin 2C ≥ 2√(sin 2B sin 2C)). Complex numbers with the circumcircle as the unit circle give p1 and q1 explicitly and the same ratio as a modulus.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The statement needs n ≥ 2. The probability is exactly the product of 1 − p^(−p) over primes p ≤ n. A polynomial is special exactly when, for every prime p, it is not identically zero modulo p (if some prime divides every value, k = p fails; otherwise the Chinese remainder theorem combines non-zero residues for the primes of k and periodicity gives infinitely many values coprime to k). A monic polynomial of degree n cannot vanish on all of F_p when p > n (too many roots). For p ≤ n, reduce modulo p and modulo x^p − x: since n! is divisible by p, the reduced coefficients are uniform, and exactly one of the p^p residues of degree below p is the zero function (Lagrange interpolation), so the chance of vanishing is p^(−p); the Chinese remainder theorem makes different primes independent. The p = 2 factor gives the upper bound 3/4, and the lower bound follows from the union bound with the sum of p^(−p) below 0.29, or from an Euler-product comparison with 1/ζ(8).

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: The coefficients are chosen so that f(x) = g(2x) − g(x). Adding this at x = 1, 2, 4, …, 2^n telescopes to f(1) + f(2) + … + f(2^n) = g(2^(n+1)) − g(1) = 0 (equivalently, expand each coefficient with the geometric series 1 + 2^k + … + 2^(nk)). Either all these values are zero, and x = 1 is a positive zero below 2^n, or two of them have opposite signs, and the intermediate value theorem gives a zero strictly between two of the points 1, 2, …, 2^n.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: the sets with at most two points and the four vertices of a (non-degenerate) parallelogram. Three collinear points admit no parallelogram, and three points alone have no fourth point. For larger sets take a triangle ABC of maximal area: one of the three possible fourth points D is in S, and every point of S lies in the parallelogram ABCD, since a point outside it would form a larger triangle with two of its vertices. A fifth point E inside ABCD then fails with a side AB: the three candidates for the fourth point are the reflection of E through the midpoint of AB and the translates of E by ±AB, all outside ABCD. A second complete route projects S onto a generic line; looking at the largest projections forces x_i + x_(n−i) = x_n and x_i + x_(n−1−i) = x_(n−1), so the projections form an arithmetic progression, and the middle term then has no partner once there are five or more points.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The angle conditions make the circles ABP and ACP tangent to BC, so line AP, their radical axis, bisects BC at its midpoint M (equivalently MB² = MP·MA = MC² from similar triangles MAB ~ MBP and MAC ~ MCP); P is the A-humpty point. The key claim is that Q is where the tangent to the circumcircle at A meets BC: that point Q0 satisfies Q0A² = Q0B·Q0C and Q0B/Q0C = AB²/AC², and the same ratio holds for the point of BC on the perpendicular bisector of AP. Then the angles at A and M are right, so Q, A, O, M are concyclic and an angle chase gives angle AQP = 2·angle OQB. Other complete routes: the reflection P' of P in BC lies on the circumcircle and ABP'C is a harmonic quadrilateral, so the tangents at A and P' meet on BC (directly, or via poles and polars); a circle centred at Q through A, P and P' with OQ ⊥ AP'; inversion at A with radius AP, or the √(bc) inversion that sends P to the pole of BC; and a linear-function argument for PX² minus the power of X along BC.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: This is the contrapositive of Aczél's inequality with both constants equal to 1. Write A and B for the two sums of squares and C for the inner product. The hypothesis makes (A − 1)(B − 1) positive, so A and B lie on the same side of 1, and it remains to rule out A, B < 1. Quadratic route: (x − 1)² − Σ(a_i x − b_i)² is a quadratic with positive leading coefficient whose discriminant is negative by hypothesis, yet its value at x = 1 is −Σ(a_i − b_i)² ≤ 0. Manipulation route: rearrange the hypothesis to AB − C² > A + B − 2C ≥ 2(√(AB) − C) by AM-GM, factor as (√(AB) − C)(√(AB) + C − 2) > 0, and Cauchy–Schwarz (C ≤ √(AB)) forces √(AB) > 1. Optimization route: with C = |a||b| cos θ, the right side is smallest at cos θ = 1 when |a||b| ≤ 1, which leaves (|a| − |b|)² < 0.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answers: (a) (n − 1)^n − (n − 1); (b) (n − 1)((n − 2)^(n − 1) − 1). Only the cyclic differences matter: each sequence is a choice of a_0 together with n differences summing to 0 mod n. Inclusion–exclusion over the violated conditions: k forced differences glue neighbours together and leave n^(n − k) sequences, except when all n are forced, where the forced values must themselves sum to 0 mod n (true for odd n in part (a)); the binomial theorem then collapses the sum. In part (b) each violated condition has two forced values, and the all-forced term asks for subsets of {1, …, p} with sum divisible by p; these are counted by orbits under the cyclic shift, which have size p because p is prime. Recursive route: count tuples of nonzero shifted differences by their running sum, c(k, l) = (n − 1)^(k − 1) − c(k − 1, l), solved by induction; for part (b) the unrolled recurrence again needs the subsets with sum divisible by p, which the p-th roots of unity count as C(p, k)/p for each size k.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answer: n = 561. Walk around the polygon and record the side vectors: they point in pairwise different directions, the rightward and leftward moves each total at most 2003, and likewise vertically, so the sum of |x| + |y| over all sides is at most 8012. Replacing each side by its primitive direction can only shorten it, and there are exactly 4φ(m) primitive vectors with |x| + |y| = m (4 for m = 1). The 560 primitive vectors with |x| + |y| ≤ 21 have total length 7988, and any further side costs at least 22, so a 562-gon would need at least 7988 + 44 > 8012. Sorting those 560 vectors by angle gives a convex polygon of width and height 1997; for 561, trade two length-21 vectors for three of length 22 with the same sum, so that width and height grow to exactly 2003.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: A lies on AD, the radical axis of the two circles, so if they meet AB and AC again at X' and Y', then AX'·AB = AY'·AC and BCY'X' is cyclic. Angle chasing then puts X, X', D, Y', Y on one circle, so XY is antiparallel to X'Y' with respect to angle A and hence parallel to BC. Other complete routes: Menelaus in the triangles cut off by S = AD ∩ BC reduces the claim to SF/BF = SE/CE, which is the equal power of S; Desargues for triangles DXY and D'BC (in perspective from A), with an auxiliary line RS shown parallel to BC by a cyclic-quadrilateral chase; a composition of homotheties centred at S and D; and the dual Desargues involution on BC, which the equal powers from S force to be an inversion fixing the point at infinity. Barycentric coordinates. On the reference triangle DEF the circle through D, E and the second common point has a simple equation, B and A come out explicitly, and X and Y share the same coordinate pattern, so XY ∥ EF. On ABC with E = (0, e, 1 − e), F = (0, 1 − f, f) and D = (p, q, r), the lines DE and DF give AY/YC and AX/XB directly, parallelism reduces to fq = er, and that is exactly the equal power of S = (0 : q : r) on BC.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: It is enough to give an infinite family of pairs of orthogonal integer vectors B, D of equal integer length, with primitive coordinates, unequal weights and pairwise different planes. A clean family is B = (1, 2n, 2n²), D = (2n, 2n² − 1, −2n): both have length 2n² + 1, their dot product vanishes, B is primitive because of the coordinate 1 and D because gcd(2n, 2n² − 1) = 1, the weights 2n² + 2n + 1 and 2n² + 4n − 1 differ for n ≥ 2, and the normals differ. It comes from parametrising the plane orthogonal to B rationally and solving the resulting Diophantine conditions (x² = 2yz). A second family comes from setting the first coordinates equal and splitting the equal-length and orthogonality conditions into products of factors, each solved by a two-parameter factorisation.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Unwinding the recursion, f(n) is the base-3 digit string of n read in base −3/2. The range is exactly the dyadic rationals k/2^l. Every value has a power of 2 as denominator. Injectivity: if two digit strings give the same value, clear denominators to get Σ d_i (−3)^i 2^(m − i) = 0, and reducing mod 3 kills the last digit difference, then peel off one digit at a time; equivalently, a minimal counterexample with different last digits would need f(s) − f(u) = −2(v − t)/3, whose denominator contains 3. Surjectivity: all integers are reached, by carrying in base −3/2 or by descent (n is reached once the smaller number −2(n − r)/3 is, where r is the residue of n mod 3, with small cases by hand), and then induction on the power of 2 in the denominator, choosing the last digit to make the numerator divisible by 3.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answers: the minimum of f is 668 and the maximum is 1334. Minimum: for (1, 2) the chosen numbers must be at least 3 apart, so f(1, 2) = 668. For every other pair a periodic construction with period 3b gives at least a third of the numbers: in the first b positions take alternate blocks of length a (starting with a chosen block), in the next b positions take exactly the complementary positions, and leave the third b positions empty. Differences of a stay inside alternating blocks or cross into a complementary or empty block, and differences of b always land in a complementary or empty block; a truncated last period still keeps at least a third, which gives 668. Maximum: split 1, …, 2003 into the residue classes mod b; each class is a chain with step b in which no two neighbours can both be chosen, so a chain of length L contributes at most ⌈L/2⌉. Summing over the chains gives at most 1334 for every b except b = 668, where the bound 1335 forces a specific set that the difference a then breaks. The set {1, …, 667} ∪ {1336, …, 2002} shows f(667, 668) = 1334.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Write the six small triangles around P in terms of the areas x, y, z of PBC, PCA and PAB: each cevian splits a triangle such as PAB in the ratio y : x, so [PAF] = yz/(x + y) and similarly for the others. The condition becomes a rational identity in x, y, z that clears to (x + y + z)(x − y)(y − z)(z − x) = 0, and two equal areas among PAB, PBC and PCA mean exactly that P is on a median. A Ceva version uses the side ratios a, b, c with abc = 1: expressing 1/(1 + a) and its cyclic versions as sums of small areas and using that alternate small triangles total half of [ABC] gives (a − 1)(b − 1)(c − 1) = 0. A variant writes Ceva with differences of opposite small areas and gets xyz = 0, that is, one of EF, FD, DE parallel to a side. Barycentric coordinates with P = (r : s : t): D, E, F are (0 : s : t), (r : 0 : t), (r : s : 0), each small area is a 3 × 3 determinant such as st/((r + s)(r + s + t)) times [ABC], and the difference from one half factors as (r − s)(s − t)(t − r)(r + s + t) over a positive denominator, so the identity holds exactly when two coordinates of P agree.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Answer: the cyclic shifts of (2, 5, 3). The primes are distinct. From p | q^r + 1 the order of q mod p divides 2r but not r, so it is 2 or 2r, and similarly for the other two pairs. If an order is 2r, then 2r | p − 1, so p ≡ 1 mod r, which clashes with r | p^q + 1 unless r = 2; if all three orders are of the form 2·prime the inequalities 2r ≤ p − 1, 2p ≤ q − 1, 2q ≤ r − 1 add to a contradiction. Order 2 with odd primes forces p | q + 1 (p | q − 1 would give p | 2), and the conditions then propagate to q | r + 1 and r | p + 1, impossible for three odd primes because it would need p < q < r < p. So one prime is 2, say p = 2; then r | 2^q + 1 forces the order of 2 mod r to divide gcd(2q, r − 1), which leaves r | 3, so r = 3 and q | 10 gives q = 5.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Answer: f ≡ 1. The same square m² can be written as (m − n)(m + n)-type pairs for several n, which gives relations such as f(m − 2)f(m + 2) = f(m − 1)f(m + 1), and so all values are determined by f(1), f(2), f(3). Computing f(4), …, f(9) in two ways forces f(2) = f(1)², f(3) = f(1)³ and finally f(1)³ = 1, after which strong induction gives f ≡ 1. Taking p-adic valuations turns the equation additive, g(m + n) + g(m − n) = g(m²), so g satisfies a linear recurrence with three free initial values, and two different representations of the same squares force all three to vanish. Alternatively the even values form a geometric progression A·B^n, and comparing exponents of B in f(4n)f(6) = f((2n + 3)²), which grow at different rates in n, forces A = B = 1. A fourth route shows f has periods 3 and 5, hence is constant.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Multiply by the positive product sin(A + B) sin(B + C) sin(C + A) and use sin(A − B) sin(A + B) = sin²A − sin²B: with a = sin A, b = sin B, c = sin C the claim becomes Σ a(a² − b²)(a² − c²) ≥ 0, which is Schur's inequality in a², b², c² with exponent 1/2 (or the generalised Vornicu–Schur form). The direct route is the usual Schur ordering argument on the trigonometric terms: with A ≤ B ≤ C the term for the smallest angle is non-negative, and the remaining two terms compare through sin C ≥ sin B and the same product identity.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The common point is the orthocentre H' of the contact triangle T1T2T3. The key claim is that the circle through T1, P1, T2 is the reflection of the incircle in T1T2; since the reflection of an orthocentre in a side lies on the circumcircle, H' is on all three reflected circles. One way to see the claim: the centre of (T1P1T2) lies on the bisectors of the angles at C and at H1 of triangle CH1H2, so it is the incentre of CH1H2, and the similarity CH1H2 ∼ CAB scales CI by cos C, which is exactly where the reflection of I in T1T2 sits. Another: the isosceles triangles H1P1T1 and AT3T2 are similar, which gives an angle equality making P1 the reflection of a point of the incircle in T1T2. A third uses the rhombus formed by I and the reflected centre to identify that centre with the orthocentre of CT1T2, then reflects T1 across a diameter. Trigonometry: the law of sines in triangle T1P1T2 gives the ratio of its two base angles' sines from T1T2 = 2r cos(C/2)-type lengths and T1H1, and their sum is known from the angles at H1, so ∠T1P1T2 = 90° + C/2 = 180° − ∠T1T3T2; hence the circle is the incircle reflected in T1T2.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Since A = π − B − C, product-to-sum turns each difference cos((B − C)/2) − sin(3A/2) into 2 sin((A − B)/2) sin((A − C)/2), so the claim is a Schur-type sum of products of half-angle differences; ordering the angles and using that sine is increasing on the relevant range makes the two possibly negative terms dominated by the third, as in the proof of Schur's inequality. Equivalently, the half-angle formulas in terms of the sides reduce it to Σ (c − a)(c − b) sin(C/2) ≥ 0, where the weights are ordered like the sides. A short route pairs each cos((B − C)/2) with sin(3A/2) via sum-to-product, giving a sum of terms 2 sin(C/2 + A) cos((C − A)/2), each at most 2 cos((C − A)/2). Another route rewrites cos((A − B)/2) through Σ sin A and sec(C/2), applies Chebyshev to the similarly ordered sequences, and then proves Σ (2 sin t − sin 3t) ≥ 0 over half-angles summing to π/2 by Jensen on the two smaller half-angles (the function is convex below arcsin(5/6)) and a one-variable factorisation. Equality holds for the equilateral triangle.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Show that f_p(x) modulo p³ (as a p-integral rational) does not depend on x. Expanding (px + k)^(−2) as k^(−2) − 2pxk^(−3) + 3p²x²k^(−4) modulo p³ reduces the claim to Σ 1/k³ ≡ 0 mod p² and Σ 1/k⁴ ≡ 0 mod p. The second is a power sum of residues: Σ k^(p−5) ≡ 0 mod p because p − 1 does not divide p − 5 when p > 5 (or by the closed formula for fourth powers). The first is a Wolstenholme-type congruence, proved by pairing k with p − k (which pulls out a factor p and leaves a fourth-power sum) or by reading it off the coefficients of ∏(x − k), whose low coefficients are divisible by p. Alternatively pair the terms for k and p − k in f_p itself, cross-multiply, and kill the x-dependence with the same fourth-power sum.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Answers: (1) not always, (2) always; more generally the property holds for every broken line exactly when k is a positive integer. For a non-integer k with m = ⌈k⌉, a broken line made of m − 1 open "squares" above P1Pn of decreasing heights, followed by their point reflections below, is symmetric about the midpoint; a horizontal chord between two of the upper squares has length at most m − 1 or at least m, so no chord has length P1Pn/k (for k = 2.5, P1Pn = 6 and the forbidden length is 2.4). For integer k, suppose S and its translate by P1Pn/k are disjoint. Take a highest and a lowest vertex with indices as close as possible; the sub-path between them cuts the horizontal strip into a left part, a right part and an enclosed part, the translate must lie entirely in the right part, and induction shows every further translate does too, while the reflected argument puts the backward translates on the left. Since P1 translated k − 1 times equals Pn translated back once, a point lies on both sides, a contradiction.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Induct on n. Colour an edge by the parity of its value. In every triangle the values satisfy x + y = z, so an even number of edges are odd; hence the odd edges form a complete bipartite graph, and one of its two sides has at least 2^(n−1) + 1 vertices, all of whose edges are even. Halving those values gives a function on 2^(n−1) + 1 points with values below 2^(n−2) that still satisfies the condition, so the induction hypothesis applies (for n = 1 all values are 0). A direct extremal proof even gives the stronger bound with 2n + 1 points and values below n: two zero edges at a vertex already force a zero triangle; otherwise deleting one endpoint of each zero edge leaves n + 1 points with no zero edge, and the edge AB with the largest label k leads, by pigeonhole on the labels CA with CA + CB = k, to two points X, Y at labels k/2, after which a fifth point produces a zero label. Another extremal argument counts how often each value can appear on edges from the endpoints of a maximal edge.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: EM/MC = 1/3 is the constant ratio. Since D is the incentre of CEM, CE is the reflection of CM in the bisector CD, so E lies on the C-symmedian; ME is the reflection of MC in AB. Let E' be the second intersection of the C-symmedian with the circumcircle: ACBE' is harmonic, so E'A/E'B = CA/CB = DA/DB, hence E'D bisects ∠AE'B and, with the two reflections, D is the incentre of CME', so E = E'. The median-length formula with AC² + BC² = 2AB² gives GA/GB = CA/CB for the centroid G, which identifies E with the reflection of G in AB, so EM = GM = MC/3; equivalently the ratio lemma together with Stewart's theorem (CM² = 3AM²) gives EM/MC = AM²/CM² = 1/3. If another ratio were constant, all triangles CEM would be similar, which fails because ∠CMA varies. An area version reflects C to C' and uses the pole P of AB: C'E/EM = CC'/MP = [CAC'B]/[ABP] = 2. Barycentric coordinates: D = (a : b : 0), CE passes through the symmedian point (a² : b² : c²), and EM is the reflection of CM in AB (through the foot (S_B : S_A : 0)), so E = (2a² : 2b² : −c²). The distance formula with a² + b² = 2c² gives CM² = 3c²/4 and EM² = c²/12, so EM/MC = 1/3, MC/CE = 3c²/(4ab) and CE/EM = 4ab/c², the last two non-constant. Trigonometrically, once E is on the circumcircle, the sine form of the ratio lemma and Stewart's theorem compute EM/MC = AM²/CM² = 1/3.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The quotient k = (m² + n²)/(mn − 1) is always 5, and the solutions are exactly the pairs of consecutive terms (in either order) of the two sequences 1, 2, 9, 43, … and 1, 3, 14, 67, …, both satisfying x_(j+1) = 5x_j − x_(j−1); explicitly they are combinations of ((5 ± √21)/2)^j. Viewing m² − knm + n² + k = 0 as a quadratic in m, the other root kn − m = (n² + k)/m is a positive integer, and for m > n > 1 it is smaller than m (because n(m − n)(m + n) ≤ 2m fails), so Vieta jumping descends to a pair with n = 1, that is (2, 1) or (3, 1), both with k = 5. Since k is preserved, it is 5 for every solution, and running the jumps backwards from the two base pairs (alternating a jump and a swap) generates all solutions.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Chain the recurrence over five consecutive steps and add the five inequalities. The four intermediate terms appear once on each side, as a_(n+i) on the left and a_(n+i)² on the right, and the five constants 1/5 add up to 1 = 4 · 1/4, so a_(n+5) − a_n² is at least a sum of four squares (a_(n+i) − 1/2)² and hence nonnegative. Applying the same bound five steps earlier gives a_n ≥ a_(n−5)² ≥ 0, and since squaring is increasing on nonnegative numbers, √a_(n+5) ≥ |a_n| ≥ a_(n−5)².

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: The sum equals (n!)²/2 + (−1)^n (2n + 1)!/(2n + 2). The shortest route splits each term: (2n + 2)(n − k)!(n + k)! = (n + k)!(n − k + 1)! + (n + k + 1)!(n − k)!, so the alternating sum telescopes to its two end terms. Alternatively, write k!(2n − k)!/(2n + 1)! as a Beta integral of x^k(1 − x)^(2n−k); summing the alternating terms under the integral is a geometric series and gives 1/(n + 1) for the full symmetric sum over k = 0, …, 2n, which folds at k = n onto the required half sum. A third write-up expands (1 − t)^(n−k) binomially and regroups by m = j + k with a Vandermonde-type count.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: This is Erdős's sum-free subset theorem. Choose a prime p = 3k − 1 larger than every element of A. For each a in A the multiples t·a (t = 1, …, p − 1) run over all nonzero residues, so a lands in the middle third {k, …, 2k − 1} for exactly k values of t. Averaging over t, some multiplier t puts more than |A|/3 elements of A into the middle third, i.e. at least 668 of the 2001. The middle third is sum-free modulo p (two of its residues add up to something in the outer thirds), so the elements of A that t sends there form a sum-free set B. A real-variable version replaces t mod p by a real multiplier r and the residues by fractional parts in (1/3, 2/3), integrating over r.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The answer is 7. Committees are proper colourings of the "hate" graph. Lower bound: seven senators where senator i hates i + 1, i + 2 and i + 3 modulo 7 (the rest arranged arbitrarily) have a hate relation between every pair, so they need seven committees. Upper bound by induction on the number of senators, with each hating at most three: there are at most 3m hate arrows among m senators, so some senator is hated by at most three others; remove that senator, split the rest into seven committees, and put the senator back into a committee that contains none of the at most six senators they hate or are hated by.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let D be where the perpendicular bisector of BC meets AC and E the foot from A to that bisector. Since DB = DC and ∠DBC = ∠C, BD bisects ∠B, so AD/DC = AB/BC; and AE ∥ BC gives AE/(BC/2) = AD/DC, hence AB = 2AE. An angle chase with ∠B = 2∠C shows that the trisector at angle A/3 from AB meets the bisector at a point P with ∠APE = 30°, so AP = 2AE = AB. The other trisector AQ then bisects ∠BAP in the isosceles triangle ABP, so it is the perpendicular bisector of BP: P is the reflection of B in AQ and QP = QB = QC. In triangle ABQ, PQ = QB < AB exactly when ∠QAB < ∠AQB; these two angles add up to 30° in this configuration, so the condition is ∠A/3 < 15°, i.e. ∠A < 45°, i.e. ∠B = 2∠C > 90°.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Substitute x = 1/a, y = 1/b, z = 1/c, so the hypothesis becomes xy + yz + zx ≥ 1 and the three claims become linear: 2x + 3y + 6z ≥ 6 and its two cyclic shifts. If two of them failed, adding those two linear forms would give 8x + 5y + 9z < 12 (up to the cyclic relabelling), but (8x + 5y + 9z)² is 144(xy + yz + zx) plus a sum of two squares, which is at least 144. Equivalently, the sum of the squares of two of the forms is at least 72(xy + yz + zx) by three AM-GM pairs. Other complete routes: scale the point so that one form equals 6 and maximise xy + yz + zx as a quadratic in one variable and then in the value t of the second form; AM-GM on the first form together with a case split on bc and a quadratic in b with negative discriminant for the sum of the other two; or a vector argument in which the cyclic shift acts as a 120° rotation in the plane orthogonal to (1, 1, 1), finished by Cauchy-Schwarz.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Compare areas. With the 135° angles, [ABC] and [ADC] are AB·BC and CD·DA times √2/4, so the right-hand side 2·AB·BC·CD·DA equals 16[ABC][ADC]. On the other hand [ABCD] = (1/2)AC·BD·sin θ, where θ is the angle between the diagonals, so (AC·BD)² ≥ 4[ABCD]² = 4([ABC] + [ADC])² ≥ 16[ABC][ADC] by AM-GM. Equality in the hypothesis forces sin θ = 1. Equivalently, drop perpendiculars BK and DL to AC: the hypothesis says BD² = 4·BK·DL, while BD ≥ BK + DL ≥ 2√(BK·DL), so equality forces BD ⊥ AC (with D the reflection of B in AC).

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The solutions are the pairs of consecutive terms (in either order) of the squares of the Lucas numbers 1, 4, 11, 29, … together with (1, 1), and of five times the squares of the Fibonacci numbers 0, 1, 3, 8, 21, …: (1, 1), (1, 16), (16, 121), …, (0, 5), (5, 45), (45, 320), …. Descent: g = gcd(m, n) divides 5. If g = 1, mn is a square, so m = a², n = b² with a² − 3ab + b² = 5; Vieta jumping a → (b² − 5)/a reduces every solution to (4, 1), so all of them lie on one recurrent sequence. If g = 5, m = 5a², n = 5b² with a² + b² − 1 = 3ab, handled the same way. Alternatively, completing the square gives (2m − 7n − 10)² − 45(n + 2)² + 180 = 0, so 15 divides 2m − 7n − 10 and (n + 2)² − 5u² = 4, a Pell-type equation whose solutions parametrise all pairs.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Build B by adding elements to A. First add some large distinct numbers so that the product exceeds the sum of squares. Then repeatedly add x = (current product) − 1: the new product is x times the old one and the sum of squares grows by x², and with this choice the surplus (product minus sum of squares) drops by exactly 1. The new elements are larger than everything before, so they are distinct, and after finitely many steps the surplus reaches 0. The choice of x is forced: asking the surplus to drop by one gives a quadratic with roots 1 and P − 1. Another route makes the surplus n = p − q and finds n new distinct numbers with x1² + … + xn² + q = p·x1⋯xn by Vieta jumping upward from (1, …, 1).

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Bound the maximum below by the average of the three squares; the claim then reduces to a + b + c + 3∛(abc) ≥ 2(√(ab) + √(bc) + √(ca)). With a = x⁶, b = y⁶, c = z⁶ this is Schur's inequality of degree three in x², y², z², followed by AM-GM (or Muirhead) to pass from the symmetric sum of x⁴y² to twice the sum of x³y³. Other complete routes keep the largest square: order a ≤ b ≤ c and note that, with a and c fixed, the left side is convex in b (or b only enters through a unimodal function), so it suffices to check b = a and b = c, where the inequality becomes a one-variable polynomial with a double root at 1; or substitute y = z + m, x = z + m + n and expand into a polynomial with only nonnegative coefficients; or factor the AM-GM gap of x², y², z² and compare with the extreme pair.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let M, N be the midpoints of AD and BC and P the intersection of the diagonals. It suffices to show ME = MF and NE = NF, since then MENF is a kite with axis MN. With R, S the midpoints of PD and PA, the midlines of triangle APD and the medians to the hypotenuses of the right triangles PFD and PEA give FR = MS and ES = MR, and an angle chase using ∠PAB = ∠PDC shows ∠MRF = ∠MSE, so triangles MRF and MSE are congruent. Equivalently, reflect A and D in F and E (or P in E and F): the inscribed-angle equality makes two triangles congruent (or two kites similar), and midlines give ME = MF. Other complete routes: F is the centre of a spiral similarity taking FRPS to FMEN; the Newton–Gauss line together with the Miquel point and the gliding principle; or, with X = AB ∩ CD, the reflection of P in N gives a line through X isogonal to XP in angle BXC, which is perpendicular to EF, and a homothety of ratio 1/2 at P carries it to the Newton–Gauss line. Complex numbers. With the diagonal intersection P at the origin, the right triangles PEA and PFD are similar, so A = e(1 + ik) and D = f(1 − ik) for a real k; then 2(M − E) = (f − e)(1 − ik) and 2(M − F) = (e − f)(1 + ik) up to the sign convention, and these have equal modulus, so M lies on the perpendicular bisector of EF (the same for N). On the unit circle instead, the foot formula gives 2e = a + b + p − ab·p̄ and 2f = c + d + p − cd·p̄, the chord-intersection formula gives p̄, and (e − f)/(m − n) simplifies to (ab + cd − ac − bd)/(bd − ac), which is purely imaginary.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Replacing (r, s) by (br, bs) permutes n modulo p, so one may take r = 1; since f(r, s) + f(r, −s) = p − 1, the lower bound for all s implies the upper bound, and one may take 1 < s < p/2. Pairing n with p − n halves the count to n ≤ (p − 1)/2. Now count how the multiples s, 2s, … fall into the half-intervals [jp/2, (j + 1)p/2]: consecutive half-intervals receive almost equal numbers of multiples, so for moderate s the discrepancy is at most about s/2 + p/(2s), which is below (p − 1)/6 once p is large; for s near p/2 each half-interval receives one or two multiples, so no three consecutive n can land in the same half, and grouping n in triples gives the bounds (the residue class p ≡ 5 mod 6 needs a short extra parity argument). An exact version computes the block endpoints with floor functions (p = 2st + r) and shows that each block has at least a t/(2t + 1) ≥ 1/3 share in the required half, which proves the bounds for every prime p ≥ 7.

problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: Show that both sides satisfy the same first-order recurrence 2(n + 1)x_(n+1) = (n + 2)x_n + 2(n + 1) with x_0 = 1. For the right side this is immediate from its form; for the left side, write 1/C(n, k) = k!(n − k)!/n! and split the factor n + 2 as (k + 1) + (n + 1 − k), which turns the two shifted sums into the next sum. Alternatively, write k!(n − k)!/(n + 1)! as the Beta integral of x^k(1 − x)^(n−k), sum the geometric series under the integral, and compare with the integral of the geometric series for Σ 2^k/k; the difference has an integrand that is odd about x = 1/2. A probabilistic proof counts the expected number of common vertices of two random monotone paths across the n-cube: by linearity it is the left side, and conditioning on the second step gives the same recurrence. A generating-function proof verifies the recurrence through F(x) = Σ n! x^n.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Suppose an infinite family of corners has no two nested. Build points T_1, T_2, … inductively: take any corner C of the current family; every other corner of the family misses some point of C, and C is finite, so by pigeonhole one point T of C is missed by infinitely many of them; keep only those corners. Then no point of any later corner dominates an earlier T, so T_i dominates T_j coordinatewise only if i ≤ j, and since a finite set of points dominates only finitely many lattice points, a subsequence has no two comparable points. That contradicts Dickson's lemma: there is no infinite antichain of lattice points under coordinatewise order, proved by induction on n with the infinite pigeonhole principle applied to a coordinate bounded by a fixed point's coordinate.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Let X, Y, Z be the feet of the perpendiculars from P to BC, CA, AB. The key step is the Erdős–Mordell lemma a·PA ≥ c·PY + b·PZ: Y and Z lie on the circle with diameter PA, so YZ = PA·sin A, while the projection of YZ onto BC equals PY·sin C + PZ·sin B (each piece is a leg of a right triangle with a known angle), and a segment is at least its projection. Dividing the three lemmas by a³, b³, c³ and adding, each foot distance PX gets the coefficient b/c³ + c/b³ ≥ 2/(bc) by AM-GM, and a·PX + b·PY + c·PZ = 2[ABC] together with 4[ABC] = abc/R finishes. Another proof of the lemma uses areas: the altitude from A is at most AP + PX, which gives a·PA ≥ c·PZ + b·PY with the wrong pairing, and reflecting P in the bisector of angle A (its isogonal image) swaps the two feet distances.

problems.explanation: Alice wins by playing a_j = 2024j. problems.explanation: Treat (a_i, b_i) as points and (x, y) as a direction: the permutation is the order of the projections. Main 2010 P5 still needs supplied-source support. The 2024 shortlist is 9/12 classified; SL C2, G1 and G2 remain pending. Other rows retain individual official-source or analytic-route limitations. All 81 published shortlist labels and the separately keyed withdrawn 2019 papers have statements; 72 shortlist labels still await classification. The 2025 shortlist branch is unpopulated. Missing year branches are publication limits, not completed empty inventories.

coverage.title: USA TST · 2000–2026
coverage.text: 172 reviewed entries from the USA Team Selection Test for the IMO (TSTST and the TST for EGMO are not in scope), added from 2026 backwards. Official solutions are the USA TST archive (2025 onward) and Evan Chen's solution files; AoPS threads supply tags and alternative methods.

caveats: A forum check can find an incomplete proof; it does not certify every reply. Expand research notes for the exact outcome.
Official booklets, attributed reproductions and Compendium fallbacks are distinguished in each entry. Some original older booklets remain unavailable.
2016 N8 has a literal-versus-intended-statement caveat, retained in its research notes.
Main RMM problem numbers are preserved; A/C/N/G subjects are descriptive mappings. RMM main and SL IDs remain distinct; shortlist coverage and source gaps are explicit.
USA TST years are IMO years (TST 2026 was held in December 2025 and January 2026); problem numbers are the paper numbers, and subjects are descriptive mappings.
